award.projectOutComesReport:
Traditional imaging systems based on the human-eye architecture rely on a lens to project an image of the object of interest onto an array of photodetectors that can accurately map the intensity distribution of the incident light. At the same time, all information related to the local direction of light propagation and the phase profile of the incident field is lost in the image acquisition process. While this approach is clearly adequate for basic imaging tasks, capturing the additional information associated with angles and wavefronts would allow (in conjunction with specialized computational reconstruction algorithms) for more advanced capabilities. Examples include the ability to visualize transparent phase objects such as typical biological cells, to perform edge detection for automated image recognition, to produce focused images on all planes across a three-dimensional space in one shot, and to develop highly miniaturized lensless imaging systems based on the compound-eye architecture.

Motivated by these considerations, the main outcome of this research project has been the development of a new type of infrared image sensors that are uniquely sensitive to the direction of propagation of the incident light (Fig. 1). These devices consist of standard planar photodetectors coated with a plasmonic metasurface (i.e., rationally designed array of metallic nanoparticles of different shapes, sizes, and/or orientations) that only transmits light incident along a small geometrically tunable set of directions. Different metasurface architectures have been demonstrated, including structures optimized for wavelength-insensitive operation across a technologically relevant bandwidth, and directional photodetectors that can selectively sense a single predetermined state of polarization (either linear or circular). The latter devices may open up further application opportunities in the area of polarization vision, which is a promising avenue to increase visibility under conditions of low intensity contrast.

Additionally, this project has investigated the use of the proposed devices for the direct visualization of transparent phase objects by wavefront sensing (Fig. 2). Phase-contrast imaging in general is a promising technique for obtaining high-resolution images of biological tissue but typically requires bulky and complicated optical setups that can limit its widespread applicability. Computational studies carried out within this project have shown that suitably designed metasurface photodetector arrays can perform quantitative phase imaging of complex objects of practical significance (cancer cells), with enhanced system miniaturization, speed, and measurement simplicity compared to existing techniques. Furthermore, the edge-enhanced nature of the images recorded by these sensors can be exploited in a convolutional neural network to enable accurate classification of transparent biological cells with significant reduction in computational resources. More broadly, these results also highlight the great potential of combining the extreme design flexibility and size miniaturization of metasurface flat optics with the enhanced information processing capabilities of computational imaging. 

These activities have been carried out by six Ph.D. students at Boston University and thus have contributed to their professional development and training in multidisciplinary research at the intersection of optical physics, semiconductor device engineering, and data science. An undergraduate and a Master's student have also participated in related research endeavors for their thesis work. Finally, the device technology developed in these activities is promising for a long-lasting impact in multiple areas of machine vision, particularly through the development of novel instrumentation that could significantly expand the reach and functionality of quantitative phase imaging for biomedical microscopy.

award.abstractText:
Many crucial artificial intelligence applications in health sciences do not have sufficient practical data. Even when one collects incredible amounts of data, the data has significant gaps because of the unique circumstances (health conditions) of each patient. Training sizeable artificial intelligence systems on such data often results in an output that is either unacceptable for making decisive medical pronouncements or the systems do not perform any better than conventional methodologies. As such, the project's goal is to develop artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning algorithms that train rapidly, minimize errors, and do not require significant human expertise. The project's novelty is utilizing emerging quantum computing (QC) algorithms that offer the potential for rapid training of models and the ability to find better solutions quickly. In this project, QC will be applied to machine learning to demonstrate the efficacy of QC-based methods in two challenging applications: (a) seizure detection on encephalography signals and (b) automatic interpretation of digital pathology images. Positively impacting the two high-level applications will allow automated systems to approach domain expert (human) performance and increase the impact of this technology in the medical field, which will impact countless humans worldwide. Access to the highest levels of QC research will create career development opportunities, encouraging high schoolers to pursue computer and information science and engineering careers.  

In this project, adiabatic quantum annealing (QA) will be used to solve two significant computational challenges: (a) finding a global minimum and (b) sampling from complex probability distributions.  It will be demonstrated that training that utilizes QA-supported sampling can find better parameters than conventional parameter optimization approaches, and it also overcomes the deficiencies of current machine learning algorithms in challenging applications, such as seizure detection on encephalography signals and automatic interpretation of digital pathology images. Through these developments, it is also expected of this project to demonstrate that a wide range of configuration spaces (undirected probabilistic graphical models trained with a variety of application-relevant data) that have the property of "difficult to find local valleys in the probability distribution" to be easily sampled with QA. These findings will be applied to deep generative models for superior classification and pattern reconstruction accuracy. The ability of QA to reach difficult to sample regions of the configuration space will benefit many machine learning applications.

This project is jointly funded by Foundations of Emerging Technologies (FET) and the Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR).

award.abstractText:
Everything in the world deforms, so modeling high-quality deformations becomes a core algorithmic ingredient for serious and realism-driven visual applications such as high-fidelity animation, virtual reality, medical data analysis, surgical simulation, and digital fabrication/prototyping, to name just a few. While deformation has been studied for decades, deformable simulation is notorious for its costly computation. With the rapid development of sophisticated sensing devices and acquisition techniques, the complexities, scales and dimensionalities of the data have grown exponentially, and large-scale geometries are becoming ubiquitous in modern 3D data processing. Even with state-of-the-art hardware, a massive deformable simulation can still take hours, days, or even weeks. In this era of data explosion, increasing demands on both computing efficiency and simulation realism impose unprecedented challenges on this classic computing problem, so game-changing algorithmic techniques for large-scale, complex, and nonlinear deformable models are needed to empower future graphics applications.  If successful, this project will not only expand the frontier of physics-based simulation technologies, but also profoundly inspire broader computing communities beyond graphics and enable a variety of applications. 


During a deformable simulation, a nonlinear system needs to be repetitively solved in order to track the continuous shape evolution of the deforming body. A deformable object with complex geometry could house a large number of unknown degrees of freedom, and the resulting high-dimensional integration becomes prohibitive. To overcome this problem, this project will develop a re-branded deformable model which systematically integrates advanced simulation techniques and deep learning (DL) tools, specifically deep neural networks (DNNs). The hypothesis is that digital simulation provides us nearly unlimited noise-free training data, which should be fully exploited and leveraged to benefit unseen yet difficult simulation or computing challenges. Unlike existing data-driven methods that interpret the data with a closed-form formulation (e.g., using a convex interpolation), DNNs provide a universal mechanism to extract intrinsic features hidden behind the raw data in an end-to-end manner, and have already demonstrated significant outcomes in many long-standing computer vision problems like object detection, classification, and annotation. However, harnessing DL in physics-based simulation is not easy. While in theory one may still encode all of these parameters using a very high-dimensional input vector, the corresponding network would be extremely large and complex. Even if we manage to collect sufficient training data to optimize this net, a single forward pass of it may be slower than a conventional simulator, making DL completely unprofitable. In this project, we will thoroughly investigate those grand technical challenges, forge a collection of data structures and algorithmic techniques for the data-driven deformable simulation, and thereby pave the way for DL-based physics simulation to next-generation computer graphics.

award.abstractText:
Large-scale graphs with billions of edges are ubiquitous in many industry, science, and engineering fields such as recommendation systems, social graph analysis, knowledge bases, materials science, and biology. In particular, Graph Neural Networks (GNN), an emerging class of machine learning (ML) models, are increasingly adopted due to their superior performance in many tasks. Unfortunately, the progress towards training GNNs on large-scale real-world graphs is undermined by the lack of adequate systems support for ML practitioners. This project will develop fundamental research on algorithms, systems, and infrastructures to meet the pressing and growing need for GNN training systems that can scale to both large graph datasets and large expressive GNN models transparently to users. First, this project will develop split parallelism, a novel parallel training paradigm designed to support arbitrarily large-scale graphs and GNN models by scaling out to distributed and multi-GPU (graphics processing unit) systems. Split parallelism is tailored to the specific bottlenecks of GNNs and introduces a set of techniques to transparently split the training computation across GPUs. Second, this project will develop systems for scalable graph sampling, which can be a major performance bottleneck in GNN training. It will develop a novel fragment-based in-GPU sampling approach that transparently splits samples into multiple fragments to maximize data access locality and scalability.

Supporting large-scale graphs and GNN models will unleash innovation in a wide range of domains by making it easier for ML practitioners to develop large and expressive models without having to work around the scalability limitations of current GNN training systems. The project will develop novel approaches for parallel training and sampling and will introduce innovations in algorithms, infrastructure, and system design for the areas of general machine learning and graph analytics. This project will stress technology transfer to integrate the findings into popular open-source GNN training tools such as the Deep Graph Library (DGL). The PIs will also support colleagues at their department working on question answering using knowledge graphs. The project will improve the training of both graduate and undergraduate students, emphasizing demographic diversity.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This project developed new methods and software to make training graph neural networks (GNNs) practical and efficient at a very large scale. GNNs are a type of machine learning model that works on graphs: data that captures relationships among entities, such as people in a social network, users and products in a recommendation system, accounts and transactions in fraud detection, or papers and citations in scientific search. Many applications generate graphs with hundreds of millions of nodes and billions of edges, which quickly exceed the capacity of a single computer or graphics card (GPU) and require multi-GPU training systems and specialized software.

The central contribution of the project is GSplit, a multi-GPU training system based on a novel paradigm called split parallelism. Instead of having each GPU redundantly process overlapping parts of the graph, as in standard data-parallel training, GSplit splits each training batch across GPUs so that each device works on a different portion of the graph and exchanges only the information that needs to be shared. This avoids redundant computation and data loading. GSplit includes several novel key components: a split-parallel training engine that coordinates multi-GPU sampling, processing and communication for each batch, and an integrated probabilistic scheduling algorithm that splits work across GPUs extremely quickly and is mathematically guaranteed to balance load and minimize communication on average. Experiments show that GSplit can train GNNs up to 4.4 times faster than widely used systems such as the Deep Graph Library (DGL) and other research systems such as Quiver and P3, while achieving the same accuracy. The GSplit system and its supporting code have been released as open source, and techniques from this project can be applied to DGL itself, which recently added a conceptually similar feature called cooperative minibatching.

The project also delivered the first thorough comparison of two major parallelization approaches used in GNN training systems: mini-batch training, which samples part of the graph at each training iteration and is the focus of this project, and full-graph training, which processes the entire graph at each epoch. These approaches rely on different data management pipelines for partitioning data and parallelizing computation and communication at scale, leading to two distinct classes of GNN training systems. The study finds that mini-batch systems consistently converge faster than full-graph systems across multiple datasets, GNN models, and system configurations. It also shows that mini-batch training can typically reach similar or often higher accuracy, demonstrating that sampling is not inherently detrimental to accuracy. These results inform the design of future GNN training systems and help practitioners choose the right parallelization approach and training systems. All code and datasets from this study have been released for reproducibility.

The project produced additional contributions at the intersection of graphs and machine learning systems. GMorph is a software framework that accelerates AI applications that rely on inference over multiple deep neural networks. Rather than training a single multi-task model from scratch, GMorph performs model fusion by combining several independently trained models, potentially with different architectures, into a single, more efficient model using graph mutations. This eliminates redundant computation and reduces inference latency by 1.1 to 3 times while maintaining accuracy. The research team also designed an information-enhanced graph neural network (INGNN) to improve learning performance on graphs with varying degrees of homophily and heterophily, which describe whether linked nodes tend to share similar properties. INGNN integrates multiple graph features through an adaptive feature-fusion mechanism and outperforms 12 state-of-the-art message-passing GNNs, achieving an average rank of 1.78 across 9 real-world node-classification datasets. In addition, the project produced other contributions in related areas such as graph pattern mining systems, federated learning, and accuracy scaling for inference serving systems.

In terms of educational and outreach impact, multiple PhD, master, and undergraduate students received research training in deep learning systems, GPU programming, graph algorithms, and performance engineering. Students led or co-authored papers at top conferences in systems, machine learning, and data management, and moved into industry roles in machine learning and systems. The PIs integrated project ideas into new and existing graduate and undergraduate courses on databases and systems for machine learning, and developed an Early Research Scholars Program project to introduce undergraduates to GNNs and ML systems research. They also taught GNN and machine learning concepts in an outreach summer program for rising 10th graders from disadvantaged backgrounds, using hands-on notebooks to experiment with basic AI concepts.

award.abstractText:
This Mid-Career Advancement (MCA) project will study the evolution and taxonomy of the plant genus Hypoestes, a group of over 130 known species, most of which are native to the biodiversity hotspot of Madagascar. The diversity of this group in Madagascar is poorly known and evidence suggests that there are many undescribed species. To better understand the biodiversity and conservation status of the group in Madagascar, it is necessary to clearly identify species and understand their evolutionary relationships. This project will use DNA sequence and other data to identify species and reconstruct their evolutionary history, laying the groundwork for an improved taxonomy and understanding of biodiversity in the group. This MCA project will allow the principal investigator to work with an expert collaborator to develop new skills that  will enhance their research and training program, generate opportunities for undergraduate and graduate student research experience, and provide for public education and engagement through outreach programs at the Missouri Botanical Garden.

A phylogenetic study of Hypoestes will be conducted using the Angiosperms-353 probe set. This method consistently supplies over 100,000 base pairs of low-copy nuclear DNA sequences and can be used on degraded DNA. Most samples will be extracted from herbarium specimens using a modified CTAB method. Specimens will be tentatively identified using an unpublished resource prepared by the PI and comparison to online type specimen images. Some will be identified as possible new species, and  undergraduate research interns will aid in species descriptions. Five other genera of tribe Justicieae will be used as outgroups. Genomic libraries will be prepared using commercial kits, pooled, enriched using the Angiosperms-353 myBaits® Expert Panel target capture kit, multiplexed, and sent to a commercial laboratory for Illumina® sequencing. Four different analytical methods will be used to produce gene and species trees from cleaned and aligned sequence data. Two methods will be used to produce dated trees calibrated using Acanthaceae fossils, and ancestral geographic ranges will be predicted. An infrageneric classification of Hypoestes globally will be proposed, which will recognize subgroups supported by both molecular and morphological characters.

award.abstractText:
Rapid proliferation of mobile technologies, manifested by a boom in smart phones and mobile video, along with the emergence of new verticals such as industrial IoT and autonomous vehicles, placed high demand on the communications infrastructure and motivated the introduction of 5G cellular systems. Compared to its 4G/LTE predecessor, 5G systems promise to deliver orders of magnitude higher data rates, significantly lower end-to-end latency, much denser connectivity, seamless coverage, high reliability, and longer battery lifetime. Facilitating these performance gains are advances on multiple fronts, most notably access to new swaths of the radio frequency (RF) spectrum. In addition to opening new spectrum above 24 GHz for 5G systems, the FCC and other regulatory bodies also created new opportunities at mid-bands below 7 GHz (“beachfront spectrum”). These bands exhibit favorable propagation characteristics that enable wide-area coverage at high data rates.

This project focuses on addressing coexistence challenges over three recently available mid-bands: the C-band (3.7-3.98 GHz), the CBRS band (3.55-3.7 GHz), and the recently unlicensed 6 GHz bands (5.925-7.125 GHz).  These bands have been only recently allocated for commercial wireless systems, which will have to coexist on these bands with a wide variety of incumbents, including Navy radar in 3.55–3.7 GHz CBRS band, point-to-point microwave links and passive radioastronomy receivers (e.g., the Methanol line) in the 6 GHz bands, and adjacent radar altimeters in the 4.2–4.4 GHz band. The proposed research agenda includes three thrusts. In the first thrust, the PIs will focus on coexistence and interference mitigation in the C-band. Despite extensive media coverage of the potential of 5G interference onto radar altimeters, there is a lack of rigorous, unbiased analyses and measurement of such interference in realistic operational scenarios. The PIs will accurately characterize C-band interference and establish the conditions under which it may occur. Novel machine learning (ML) techniques will be developed for real-time detection of interference and mitigation of its impact by adapting the 5G transmission parameters. The second thrust focuses on coexistence and interference mitigation in the CBRS band, particularly secondary coexistence between Tier 3 (GAA) users, which is quickly emerging as a bottleneck to efficient use of the band. Protocol-based and ML-based solutions will be explored. The third thrust focuses on coexistence in the unlicensed 6 GHz bands, where ML-based protocol classification designs will be explored to allow a given device to detect the underlying protocols of other devices and adapt its parameters accordingly. The proposed solutions will be evaluated via simulations and field measurements. These solutions are expected to have broader applicability beyond the specific studied bands. Research outcomes from this project will be shared with industry and will be provided to the FCC as case studies to facilitate subsequent policy making in other bands. The proposed research will be fully integrated into the educational plan by incorporating its outcomes in newly designed and existing courses as well as training undergraduate and graduate students via mentoring, participation in test-bed development, and special projects. The project contains a detailed plan to broaden participation of underrepresented groups via various channels established in the past years.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.abstractText:
Graph neural networks (GNNs), which translate the success of deep learning to graph-structured data, have numerous applications spanning from recommendation systems and fraud detection to medicine to finance. In such applications, the extent to which similar entities connect with each other---known as homophily---is unknown and cannot be computed empirically due to limited labeled data. Though homophily is common, it is not universal; there are important real-world settings where "opposites attract", leading to heterophily (low homophily). By moving beyond a reliance on graph homophily and introducing new GNN models, this project will generalize GNNs to work effectively in a wider range of domains. It will also help rectify some negative consequences of GNNs that are tailored to homophilous graphs, including biased, unfair, or erroneous predictions when applied to heterophilous data. Focusing on robustness, fairness, and explainability will help support accountable algorithmic decision-making in the domains where GNN models are employed. In addition to research, this project will support the training of a diverse cohort of undergraduate and graduate students at the University of Michigan, the New Jersey Institute of Technology, and Michigan State University via integration of this research in advanced courses, capstone projects, and other opportunities to directly contribute to this research program.

The inability of GNNs to generalize their strong performance on homophilous or assortative graphs to many heterophilous graphs has attracted significant attention, and has led to empirical demonstration of the existence of "good heterophily", where GNNs can perform well. However, there is still limited understanding about the types of heterophily that are easy or difficult to handle with GNNs, especially beyond the limited, typically-studied settings (i.e., node classification on small homogeneous graphs). This project will advance the theoretical underpinnings of the interplay between different types of heterophily and GNNs, considering properties beyond just accuracy, which are necessary for deployment. Specifically, it will contribute: (a) New Theory: It will formally characterize the heterophily-related challenges of GNNs to provide a deeper understanding into "good" and "bad" heterophily, and enhance our understanding of "good" types of heterophily, which some architectures can model effectively, but have been vastly ignored until now. (b) New Models: Based on the new theory, it will introduce new GNN designs and architectures that not only have strong performance across different levels and types of heterophily, but are also robust, fair, and transparent, which are crucial for algorithmic decision-making. (c) New Applications: The project will also go beyond the traditional tasks and heterophilous network types investigated in the literature, and will include exploration of high-impact applications along with collaborators in academia and industry.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.abstractText:
Machine learning has become a highly successful and practical tool for understanding data, enabling new technologies, and aiding human decision-making.  However, its increased use in applications that impact people has also led to a number of concerns.  These include concerns about the fairness of decisions made, concerns about incentives generated and the effect of strategic behavior on accuracy of these systems, and concerns about the impact of classification decisions on societal welfare.  This project aims to develop theoretical frameworks that advance the foundations for machine learning systems that address these concerns. In particular, the high-level goal of this work is to be able to provide clean guarantees both to those using these systems and to those affected by the decisions they make.

Specifically, this project is centered around three main research directions.  The first is to advance the understanding of fairness in machine-learning and algorithmic contexts, with emphasis on the interaction between fairness conditions and biased training data, and on implementing fairness conditions in multi-stage decision systems.  The second direction involves strategic classification, which is the problem of making classification decisions on agents that have the ability to modify their observable features to a limited extent, and who may do so if it leads to a decision they prefer. This work will tackle a number of fundamental problems in the design of algorithms with provable accuracy guarantees in such settings, especially for the challenging case of online sequential decision-making.  The third direction involves impacts on societal welfare, and development of learning algorithms that combine classic accuracy goals with goals that involve incentivizing societally-beneficial behaviors.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
The goal of this project was to advance the mathematical foundations for machine learning systems that interact with people, in which the impact of classification decisions on behavior and society, as well as issues such as transparency and fairness, need to be considered in addition to just the accuracy of the system on data given.

One main direction concerns the mathematics of algorithmic classifiers for settings such as college admissions or loan approvals, where individuals may want to take actions in order to improve their classification.  Our work here helped to develop foundations for "incentive-aware" machine learning algorithms that operate well even when individuals have full knowledge of the classification system.  It is hoped that such algorithms can make firms and other decision-makers more willing to fully publicize their decision processes, and indeed even incentivize them to do so.

A second, closely-related direction concerns development of algorithms to help individuals respond to algorithmic classification schemes.  These algorithms interact with their user and produce personalized policies that the individual could use to determine how best to achieve the classification they are aiming for.

A third direction involved advancing the mathematical foundations of trustworthy AI systems.  We specifically investigated methods that provide justification for their outputs by connecting their predictions or decisions to specific subsets of their training data that led to that decision.

Finally, this work developed a mathematical model designed to explain, at least at a high level, the societal phenomenon of "pessimism traps" in which communities get locked into a self-reinforcing cycle of negative behavior, and what kinds of interventions might help to break them.  Our model suggests that temporary "information-revealing subsidies" can allow individuals to step out of these cycles and help lead their communities out of these traps.

award.abstractText:
Graph mining is an emerging field with a wide spectrum of applications across many disciplines, such as social media and healthcare. Examples of applications include finding groups of users in social networks (e.g., Facebook), which is useful for a personalized recommendation, and detecting drug-drug interactions, which may cause dangerous side effects on health. In graph mining, many useful methods can be applied to small graphs effectively. However, the ever-increasing size of real-world networks is a major challenge for these methods due to their high computational and space costs. This project aims at developing novel graph compression (summarization) methodologies that facilitate efficient analysis of large graphs and advancing a wide spectrum of graph-related applications. Graph compression aims to create a smaller graph from a massive graph. Compressing graphs achieves several benefits, including but not limited to 1) significant speed-up for current graph mining algorithms, 2) memory space and communication cost reduction, 3) improved data privacy, 4) more effective graph visualization. This project will provide research opportunities to graduate students, especially female and underrepresented students, in graph mining and its real-life applications. The PI will also incorporate the results of the research in undergraduate and graduate-level courses.

Graph compression algorithms reduce the complexity and size of large graphs while maintaining the crucial information of the original graph in the smaller graph. Such reductions are essential to scale up or scale out existing algorithms to better manage, query, store, and display them. The investigator will design graph compression methods that preserve the desired structural information of graphs, including similarity and cohesiveness, specific to the selected graph mining problems. This project will: 1) explore the spatial locality property of graphs by taking the structural information from different aspects, including similarity of nodes and cohesiveness of subgraphs; 2) develop the corresponding novel structure-aware compression methods to tackle the challenges brought by large real-world networks; and 3) build more tailored architectures with proposed compression methods for various problems, including network embedding and community search and evaluate them on real-world applications such as link prediction, node classification, anomaly detection, and community detection. Its outcomes will be disseminated through publications, tutorials, workshops, as well as open-source tools, code, and datasets.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This project advanced the theoretical foundations and practical applications of structure-aware graph compression. The goal was to develop novel algorithms that effectively reduce the size of large-scale graphs while preserving their essential structural properties, thereby enabling more efficient storage, computation, and analysis. 

Key Outcomes:

Algorithm Development and Analyze:
We designed and implemented new compression techniques that leverage similarities and structural patterns in graphs, such as motifs. and communities, preserving task-relevant graph properties. We analyzed trade-offs between compression ratio and task accuracy for various downstream tasks.

Applications in Graph Learning on  Biological and Social Networks:
We demonstrated that compressed graphs retain high performance in machine learning tasks including  network embedding and graph neural networks (GNNs) trained on compressed graphs for classification and utilized for many real world applications including drug drug interaction, sequence classification, event prediction, molecular property prediction.

Open-Source Tools and Datasets:

We released  publicly available Python libraries as the implementation of our graph compression methods and benchmarked them on real-world datasets. This contributes to reproducibility and facilitates adoption by other researchers and practitioners.

Student Involvement and Training

The project supported undergraduate and graduate students, providing hands-on research experience in graph algorithms, compression, and machine learning. Several students presented at workshops and conferences, contributing to workforce development in data science.

Dissemination of Results

Research findings were published in peer-reviewed venues in data mining and machine learning (e.g., KDD, ICDE, CIKM, PAKDD, ECMLPKDD), and results were shared through invited talks and departmental seminars.

 

By reducing computational and storage overhead, the project enables the use of large-scale graph data in resource-constrained environments, including mobile platforms and edge devices. The outcomes of this work have potential applications in public health, cybersecurity, and social network analysis, where understanding large-scale relationships is critical. The research results have also led to the development and update of multiple undergraduate and graduate courses at GSU.

award.abstractText:
Community paramedicine programs are designed to provide expedited and customized care to underserved and often vulnerable populations seeking repeat assistance through emergency 9-1-1 services. While evaluations show that these programs are effective at reducing use of emergency services and saving cities money, knowledge of how successful these programs are at improving the quality of life for the clients they serve and whether they serve the community equitably is limited. This participatory action research project explores the perspectives of San Francisco Fire Department Community Paramedicine Division’s vulnerable clients and the paramedicine staff. The goals in Stage 1 are to identify indicators of success as defined by clients and staff and develop a method to meaningfully measure progress toward successful outcomes. The project aims to consolidate data from several distinct community paramedicine programs to better understand the client population. Insights from this project will be used to develop, pilot, and evaluate interventions to improve effectiveness and equitable delivery of community paramedicine services in San Francisco and other communities across the United States. 

The vision for this project is to strengthen community paramedicine’s work to improve the quality of life and resilience of residents of San Francisco who rely heavily on emergency services. Existing metrics to evaluate community paramedicine programs focus only on cost-savings and efficiencies and not on the experiences of vulnerable clients and community paramedics. The research team will be measuring success at the individual- and community-level, tracking how equitably these programs are being delivered, and developing strategies to reduce burnout and moral injury among community paramedics. The Stage 1 activities are guided by three core questions: 1) how do community paramedicine staff, clients, and municipal stakeholders define success for community paramedicine programs?; 2) what are useful metrics to measure equitable delivery of community paramedicine programs and what data should be routinely collected to assess these metrics?; and 3) what interventions could improve the coordination, design, equitable delivery, and/or efficiency of community paramedicine services? The Stage 2 pilot will test best practices that could be scaled and adopted by other community paramedicine programs that share the goal of serving vulnerable populations.

This project is in response to the Civic Innovation Challenge program—Track B. Bridging the gap between essential resources and services & community needs—and is a collaboration between NSF, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Department of Energy.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Community Paramedicine (CP), also known as mobile integrated health, is an approach to providing customized care to community members and alleviating strain on emergency services. In San Francisco, community paramedics work on several street teams responding to residents experiencing homelessness, drug overdoses, and crises related to mental health or substance abuse.

 

This planning grant was a collaboration between San José State University researchers and the San Francisco Fire Department (SFFD) CP Division and focused on two major challenges facing community paramedicine, emergency medical services, and prehospital care. The first challenge is equity. Work to understand and mitigate disparities within EMS and CP practice is significantly behind other aspects of the healthcare system. As these programs develop and expand, it is critical to build equity into the design and implementation of these programs and share best practices through the field in order to improve outcomes for the vulnerable populations served. The second challenge is that community paramedics are exposed to an entirely different set of moral dilemmas and pressures due to expanding the scope of work for paramedics beyond emergency medical care and hospital transport to supporting clients experiencing homelessness, addiction, and serious mental illness in the community. This work puts community paramedics at risk of moral injury - a mental health injury stemming from perceived transgression of deeply held moral values. Moral injury can not only harm community paramedics, but impedes their ability to serve clients and can create structural challenges for municipalities, as moral injury is associated with burnout and attrition.

 

During the Stage 1 Planning Grant, researchers met with CP and SFFD leadership over 20 times. We conducted six two-hour focus groups with CP division members exploring how members view success of programs, points of frustration and satisfaction, understanding of equity, and experiences of moral distress and injury. We thematically analyzed the data and reported our findings back to members of the CP division. We also separately discussed findings with CP leadership to develop a shared understanding of the findings. From our analysis of focus group responses, we developed a working conceptual model for moral injury in CP practice to demonstrate how exposure to potentially morally injurious events (PMIEs) experienced during work can lead to moral distress, or more severe moral injury. The focus groups also yielded valuable insights into solutions to the problems experienced by clients and CP members. To harness the insights from these focus groups for the development of our Stage 2 pilot proposal, SJSU investigators developed a participatory brainstorming activity for CP members to generate new ideas, comment on previously suggested ideas, and vote up/down these proposed solutions to the challenges identified.

 

We also examined de-identified encounter log data from over 10,000 Street Response Team calls and analyzed these records for data quality and to identify a starting point for tracking equity in service delivery. We found extensive and systematic missingness in demographic data. In the focus groups, CP members expressed discomfort with collecting these data, noting that it felt transactional and often inappropriate, and that the narrow options for classification did not match client’s reality. We met with the SFFD Chief of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion to better understand the equity context in the organization and developed a multi-prong approach to strengthen data equity for our Stage 2 pilot proposal.

 

Investigators also held multiple conversations with RAMS peer-based services and conducted a focus group with RAMS peer supervisors who work with CP on the street response teams. RAMS has over a decade of experience in peer-based services, providing certification and training to individuals who have personal lived experience with mental health and/or substance use challenges to become peer counselors. Recognizing the value of the unique peer specialist perspective, we expanded the collaborative team for our Stage 2 proposal to include RAMS. We also brought on Co-PI Dr. Shira Maguen, who is an expert in moral injury. Dr. Maguen recently developed and validated a scale to assess moral distress and injury in civilian populations, including among first responders (the Moral Injury and Distress Scale, MIDS), which will be utilized in Stage 2 to provide the first quantitative assessment of moral injury and moral distress among community paramedics.

 

The intellectual merit of this planning grant includes the development of a conceptual model for moral injury in community paramedicine and emergency medical services and an initial equity analysis of community paramedicine data that can guide further efforts to understand, monitor, and improve equity. This work will be expanded during the Stage 2 award. Ultimately, the broader impacts of this project include improved quality of life for first responders and vulnerable residents, progress towards improving equity, and a model for successful transdisciplinary participatory action research to address critical problems.

award.abstractText:
Neurological/brain-related gait disorders affect many people and can be devastating to the mobility, independence, cognition, and self-esteem of an individual. Thus, early diagnosis and proper monitoring is key to giving an individual the proper care that can optimize their well-being. Yet, many individuals seek a medical opinion only after the disease has progressed for a while. Furthermore, once medical help is sought, many patients miss follow-up appointments to monitor the progress of their disease under therapy/medication. The situation can be much worse in impoverished/developing nations (or rural areas in US), due to the high cost of healthcare and/or lack of it for an average family.  Wireless signals, on the other hand, are ubiquitous these days, which open up the possibility of using them for sensing and learning about the environment. This is the main motivation for the proposed work, to introduce a new mathematical foundation and design methodology that enables everyday RF signals, such as WiFi, to detect, classify, and monitor gait disorders.  The proposed work can result in a considerable advancement towards developing an affordable home health system for gait disorder assessment.  Such a system can further work in partnership with medical professionals, for the diagnosis and monitoring of gait disorders. The project also has an educational component, targeting K-12 as well as under-represented groups.

This research proposes a new foundation for gait disorder assessment with ubiquitous RF signals. This is a considerably challenging problem, which is divided into four major tasks.  The first major goal proposes a new methodology that can translate the vast already-available online non-RF gait disorder datasets to RF data, enabling the creation of a large synthetic gait disorder RF datasets pertaining to different gait disorders. Such datasets are necessary for a methodical analysis/design, but currently lacking and prohibitively laborious to manually collect.  The second major task then proposes a new processing foundation that can mathematically characterize, for the first time, the general full frequency content of the received signal, and its high-energy epochs, enabling proper analysis of more complex movements.  The third objective then builds on the previous two to extract rich, efficient, and meaningful features from the received signal and design a robust machine leaning pipeline for the detection, classification, and monitoring of gait disorders, with an emphasis on understanding the feasibility and limitations. Finally, the last objective validates the proposed foundation with extensive experiments.

award.abstractText:
An abdominal aortic aneurysm is the most commonly diagnosed arterial aneurysm that is an abnormal bulge on the aorta associated with the gradual thinning of the vessel wall. With mortality as high as 80% in cases of ruptures, abdominal aortic aneurysm accounts for more than 10,000 deaths in the United States every year. One of the most common treatments is endovascular aneurysm repair, which redirects blood flow away from the aortic wall and bypasses the weak spots by implanting a covered stent graft in the aneurysm sac via a minimally invasive procedure. Among the stent recipients, 30% of them can experience persistent blood flow into the aneurysm sac, called ‘endoleak,’ leading to aneurysm expansion and rupture. Thus, blood pressure and flow near the stent should be periodically monitored. However, the commonly used imaging technique is highly dependent on patient compliance, and its repeatedly administrated iodinated contrast poses a risk of chronic kidney disease. As such, the overall objective of this research is to create a Smart Stent based on a flexible and battery-less membrane-based sensor and wireless bioelectronics with a deep-learning algorithm to realize automated diagnosis of endoleak. This collaborative research will integrate the scientific findings and discoveries with educational venues for students across disciplines (Electrical and Mechanical Engineering), generations (K-12 to lifelong learners), and two institutes (Temple University and Kansas State University).

The overall objective of this research is to develop a Smart Stent for post-endovascular aneurysm repair surveillance that combines a flexible, and battery-less bioelectronic system with a deep-learning algorithm to realize automated diagnosis of endoleak. The central hypothesis is that Smart Stent, created by conformally weaving piezoelectric porous membrane sensors inside and outside of the conventional stent graft, will bring a novel electromechanical wireless biotelemetry scheme whose sensor data can be directly analyzed by a deep-learning model for classification of complex hemodynamics. The intellectual merits of the proposed research include 1) design of an auxetic porous piezoelectric membrane for the Smart Stent that is optimized for the multi-modal sensing of blood pressure and flow, 2) microfabrication  of complex 3D structure and surface-integrated micro coils for near-field magnetic induction communication, 3) a novel electromechanical interrogation scheme that converts energy from physiological information (e.g., blood pressure and flow) into wireless magnetic induction signals, 4) a comprehensive evaluation using a precise aneurysm phantom model to build baseline data for cardiovascular research, and 5) a deep learning-enabled sensing classification algorithm that offers real-time, quantitative, and automated assessment of five different types of endoleak. The research will establish a machine learning-enabled wireless sensing system that will spur new theory and understanding for the next generation implantable biomedical system.

Project Outcomes Report for the General Public

Award Title: Collaborative Research: Smart Stent for Post-Endovascular Aneurysm Repair Surveillance

Federal Award ID: 2326938

This project aimed to develop an innovative Smart Stent for post-endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) surveillance to address critical challenges in monitoring abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) treatment. Abdominal aortic aneurysms, if left untreated, can rupture and lead to life-threatening complications. EVAR, a common preventive procedure, uses a stent graft to reinforce the weakened artery wall. However, post-EVAR complications, such as blood flow leakage into the aneurysm sac (endoleak), demand regular and invasive clinical monitoring using imaging techniques. This project resolves these challenges by introducing a Smart Stent capable of real-time, non-invasive, and wireless hemodynamic monitoring. This was achieved through the development of a porous piezoelectric membrane optimized for multi-modal sensing, the fabrication of a 3D-printed stent with integrated coils for wireless communication, and the validation of its performance in a simulated aneurysm model. These advancements reduce the reliance on frequent imaging, enable early detection of complications through automated data analysis, and improve patient outcomes while minimizing healthcare costs.

Intellectual Merit:

The Smart Stent integrates a porous piezoelectric membrane, 3D microfabrication techniques, and a machine learning-enabled diagnostic framework. One key achievement of the project was the development of a unique polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membrane with engineered pore architectures, optimized for multi-modal sensing capabilities. These membranes enable precise measurement of blood pressure and flow within the aneurysm, forming the foundation for real-time hemodynamic sensing. Additionally, a three-dimensional (3D) porous piezoelectric hollow cylinder was designed and fabricated using advanced techniques such as laser micromachining and 3D printing. This stent integrates surface-coated coils that allow wireless, magnetic induction-based communication, facilitating non-invasive hemodynamic measurements. The wireless pressure-sensing capability of the stent was experimentally validated within a 3D-printed aneurysm phantom model, where the resonance frequency influenced by pressure changes was successfully measured through inductive coupling with an external antenna. Furthermore, the collected data was utilized to develop and test a deep-learning model for endoleak classification, showcasing the Smart Stent’s potential for automated diagnosis and an innovative approach to post-EVAR surveillance. Lastly, a novel method for directly printing piezoelectric smart stents using PVDF-TrFE material was investigated. These stents demonstrated the ability to harvest energy from mechanical stress, offering a promising pathway to self-powered sensing devices.

Broader Impacts:

This project addressed key healthcare challenges by introducing a transformative technology that improves patient outcomes and reduces healthcare costs. The Smart Stent enhances patient care by providing continuous and remote monitoring, reducing the need for frequent in-clinic visits and minimizing exposure to harmful imaging techniques such as CT scans. This innovation promotes long-term surveillance compliance among patients, thereby reducing the risk of undetected complications. Furthermore, the project contributed to the advancement of bioelectronic systems by integrating piezoelectric materials with wireless communication technology, paving the way for future implantable devices with similar capabilities. It also supported educational and workforce development by offering research and learning opportunities to graduate and undergraduate students at partner institutions. The project extended its impact through community outreach programs, including workshops aimed at fostering interest in STEM fields. Additionally, the Smart Stent demonstrates significant potential to lower healthcare costs by reducing the frequency of expensive diagnostic procedures, hospital visits, and treatments associated with undetected complications.

Summary:

Over the course of this project, we successfully demonstrated the feasibility of the Smart Stent as a novel bioelectronic device for post-EVAR surveillance. The project achieved significant outcomes, including the development and optimization of porous piezoelectric membranes for hemodynamic sensing, enabling precise and multi-modal monitoring of blood flow and pressure. A functional Smart Stent prototype was fabricated with wireless pressure-sensing capabilities, and its performance was validated in a 3D-printed aneurysm model under simulated physiological conditions. The project also explored self-energized stents using piezoelectric materials, demonstrating the feasibility of sustainable, long-term operation for implantable devices. These achievements establish the Smart Stent as a promising solution for addressing challenges in post-EVAR monitoring and lay the groundwork for further research and commercialization. The project highlights the intersection of biomedical engineering, materials science, and healthcare innovation, emphasizing its transformative potential to improve patient outcomes and advance medical technologies.

award.abstractText:
Advances in low-cost low-power silicon radio frequency (RF) integrated circuits (ICs) in the last two decades have opened up the commercial applications for millimeter wave (mmWave) frequencies which are an order of magnitude beyond those used in WiFi and cellular today. Large-scale deployment of mmWave communication networks, such as NextG cellular infrastructure outdoors and NextG WiFi infrastructure indoors, implies that these resources can be leveraged for RF imaging at scales that are not otherwise possible. The project develops foundational algorithms, architectures and protocols for such Joint Communication and Imaging (JCAI) systems. Each sensor in such a system provides 4D measurements (range, Doppler, azimuth angle and elevation angle) whose resolution improves by going to higher frequencies.  The project establishes US leadership in a critical technology by developing large-scale RF imaging using frequencies beyond 100 GHz. Outdoor applications include pedestrian and vehicular tracking for global situational awareness supporting vehicular autonomy, and addressing security challenges such as timely detection of illegal drones or unauthorized personnel.  In indoor settings, the technology enables fine-grained inference/prediction of human actions for eldercare and smart home applications. RF imaging technologies are especially useful in low-light or high-smoke/fog conditions when visible light or infrared technologies are not effective.

The project develops and demonstrates a framework for JCAI at mmWave frequencies.  A core aspect of the technical plan is to drastically improve resolution by synthesizing large apertures (Thrust 1). This employs a combination of novel approaches to single sensor design which utilize large antenna arrays developed for communication, and networked collaboration between multiple sensors. A complementary aspect (Thrust 2) is the strategic utilization of unmanned vehicles to image difficult-to-reach areas, utilizing the fixed infrastructure to reduce the robot payload. In Thrust 3, hardware at 140 GHz previously developed by the PIs for communication will be adapted to support demonstration of networked RF imaging at 100+ GHz.  Thrust 4 develops a control plane for networked imaging, including a resource management framework based on imaging demand and imaging capacity, and protocols supporting collaborative imaging. The concepts and methods to be developed have potential impact in a vast array of applications, including vehicular autonomy and road safety, manufacturing automation, indoor and outdoor security, eldercare, and healthcare.  The PIs will work closely with industry partners, building on their strong track record in transitioning mmWave research, and plan to incorporate this research into the undergraduate curriculum through courses, capstone projects, and REU projects.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Overview and Objectives
The recent advances in low-cost, low-power silicon radio-frequency integrated circuits have enabled commercial deployment of millimeter-wave (mmWave) systems at higher frequencies than current wireless infrastructure. The large-scale rollout of mmWave cellular infrastructure with larger bandwidths and shorter wavelengths presents a unique opportunity to leverage these devices for both communication and high-resolution radio-frequency imaging. This project, 4D100, laid the intellectual foundations for Joint Communication and Imaging (JCAI) at city scales, exploring how networked mmWave devices capturing 4D measurements (range, Doppler, azimuth, and elevation) could be used to achieve unprecedented imaging. 

The 4D100 project consisted of a cross-disciplinary team from Rice University and UCSB with expertise in wireless communication, MIMO radar, imaging and signal processing, robotics for sensing and control, RFIC design and packaging for massive mmWave arrays, and large-scale programmable networks. The project goals were focused in three main thrusts related to (1) significantly increase imaging resolution by creating large effective apertures with networked collaboration, (2) develop a control plan and resource management framework for multi-function JCAI networks, and (3) build experimental JCAI platforms using off-the-shelf and emerging mmWave technology.

Technical Approach
Our work exploited the fundamental advantages of mmWave systems: large bandwidths for fine range resolution, high carrier frequencies for improved Doppler resolution, and short wavelengths enabling compact large-scale 2D antenna arrays for high angular resolution imaging. Key accomplishments of the project included creating large effective apertures via networked sensing, designing protocols and control mechanisms for collaborative imaging, and developing experimental platforms spanning 60–77 GHz commercial hardware through 140 GHz and beyond.

Major Research Outcomes

RF Edge-Based Imaging of Static Objects - Imaging static objects is challenging when Doppler information is absent. We introduced a new paradigm that focuses on object edges rather than surfaces, leveraging diffraction effects described by the Geometrical Theory of Diffraction. By exploiting the distinctive “Keller cone” signatures produced when mmWave signals interact with edges, we developed a novel processing pipeline capable of tracing edges and imaging stationary objects.

Beyond-Field-of-View Target Localization - We demonstrated that natural multi-bounce propagation in real environments can be exploited to localize and image objects outside a radar’s direct field of view, such as around corners. Our approach requires no additional hardware or prior environmental knowledge and supports single-, double-, and triple-bounce paths through a sequential matched-filtering framework. Experiments on commercial mmWave MIMO radar platforms showed 2×-10× reductions in localization error for humans outside the radar’s field of view. 

Collaborative Inference with Networked MIMO Radar - We developed core components of a collaborative sensing architecture in which multiple mmWave radars jointly track targets. A central challenge is self-calibration where the relative radar poses need to be estimated without external references. We proposed an autocalibration method based on joint target tracking and pose estimation, deriving a closed-form optimal solution for 2D scenes. Experiments with mmWave radars demonstrated successful self-calibration using only a moving human target. Building on this, we showed that calibrated radars can perform one-shot fusion to estimate full target velocity vectors instantaneously.

Instantaneous Velocity Estimation via Multi-Bounce Scattering - We showed that a single MIMO radar can estimate a target’s full velocity vector by exploiting angle-resolvable multi-bounce paths from static landmarks, eliminating the need for multi-frame tracking. 

Implicit Shape Estimation with mmWave SAR - Using an experimental 110–260 GHz synthetic aperture radar, we achieved millimeter-resolution point clouds and introduced an algorithm that fuses traditional radar detection with advanced computer vision signal processing to recover smooth 3D object shapes. This work has the potential to aid in radar downstream tasks such as object classification and remote sensing.

Crowd Analytics with Commodity mmWave Radar - We developed new mathematical models and signal processing pipelines for crowd counting and semantic analysis using off-the-shelf mmWave radar. A closed-form model was derived to characterize undercounting due to human-body shadowing, enabling accurate estimation of large crowds. In parallel, we introduced a framework that extracts high-level crowd semantics by transforming radar flow fields into directed geometric graphs.

100+ GHz Hardware and Testbed Development - The project supported the development of a 140 GHz MIMO radar testbed at UCSB, leveraging CMOS ICs, LTCC packaging, and advanced antenna integration. First-generation 4-channel transmitter chips achieved 20 dBm EIRP with 8% power-added efficiency, and receiver building blocks demonstrated 7.5 dB noise figures in D-band.

Broader Impacts and Future Directions

This project established novel algorithms, systems, and hardware for large-scale joint communication and imaging networks. The outcomes advance sensing for urban safety, autonomous systems, crowd management, and road safety. The research and experimental platforms developed during this project position the community to further explore city-scale RF imaging and tightly integrated joint communication and imaging systems in future NSF and industry-supported efforts.

award.abstractText:
The majority of machine learning algorithms rely on the assumption that data are sampled from a fixed probability distribution. This assumption is often violated in practice, which results in classification and regression strategies that are far from optimal or even reliable. Recent work has shown that an adversary can significantly compromise the outcome of preprocessing techniques and classification. Unfortunately, a unified framework for learning in the presence of an adversary from streaming data has not been addressed despite the growing number of applications that need such techniques. 

This CAREER will study to understand when and why feature selection fails with an adversary. Not only will this research focus on understanding why feature selection fails, but also the transferability of black and white box attacks on feature selection. This project also proposes to develop novel methods to attack information-theoretic algorithms and approaches for resilient information-theoretic feature selection. This CAREER also addresses the problem of learning in a nonstationary environment with the presence of an adversary. A comprehensive set of synthetic and real-world benchmarks will be performed for each of the tasks. The research focuses on this unmet need and tackles a variety of adversarial learning problems drawn from different subfields of machine learning: specifically, algorithms for feature selection and learning in nonstationary environments.

A successful implementation of the proposed research plan will have broader impacts on machine learning and application-driven domains. The education plan includes mentoring and training the future workforce for data scientists, who are currently in high demand, by introducing machine learning through multiple levels of education in a collaborative learning environment at the university. The CAREER project also includes integrated then integration research, revise research and learning with a community-based integration of research in education to draw more students at all levels for STEM and machine learning. This CAREER will engage K-12 students in Tucson to promote STEM education and also machine learning through hands-on teaching techniques. There will also be public talks to the data science community based on the CAREER research outcomes and the most recent trends in machine learning.

award.projectOutComesReport:
The primary research goal is to develop and evaluate a pipeline for modeling adversaries from the preprocessing phase to the classification phase, specifically by addressing adversarial learning in four CAREER objectives. One objective was to develop novel information-theoretic feature selection techniques that directly overcome the issues associated with learning in the presence of an adversary as well as techniques to degrade the performance of feature selection. This project also focuses on establishing, composing, and deriving a framework for learning and evaluating with an adversary. This project also studies new algorithms that can learn in a nonstationary environment while in the presence of an adversary. We have spent a significant amount of time developing continual learning algorithms, and we are beginning to investigate how adversarial attacks influence the objectives of continual learning methods. 

 The broader impacts of this project involved hosting two summers of REU students whose focus was in adversarial machine learning, computer science, software engineering, and data science. Further, the PI has taught machine learning courses at the University of Arizona and Rowan University, which included lectures that were based on the research in this project. The Engineering Clinic sequence at Rowan University allows undergraduate students to participate in sponsored research which was another mechanism to bring undergraduate students into the project.

award.abstractText:
Machine learning has emerged to be an indispensable tool for addressing many decision-making problems, e.g., autonomous driving. As applications of machine learning algorithms for decision-making broaden and diversify, the requirements on security, fairness, interpretability and generalization have been pushed to higher standards. These emerging issues have brought great challenges to the design of machine learning algorithms in the presence of big and complex data.  Traditional machine learning methods by minimizing an unconstrained or simply constrained convex objective have become increasingly unsatisfactory. This project seeks to advance learning with complex objectives and constraints by designing and analyzing efficient and effective optimization algorithms for addressing computational challenges in new machine learning paradigms. The project will enhance the ability to solve large-scale, real-world problems from more diverse and broad applications. Furthermore, the project will strive to communicate the significance of machine learning and optimization and provide excellent research experience to students at different levels.

Although both constrained optimization and non-convex optimization have been studied and applied to machine learning in the literature, great challenges and many problems remain unaddressed. The primary focus of this project is to design and analyze a set of efficient optimization algorithms and statistical learning methods for advancing machine learning with complex objectives and constraints at large scale. The technical aims of the project are divided into two thrusts. The first thrust is to (i) develop faster and provable stochastic algorithms for learning with complicated non-convex objectives, and (ii) improve the generalization performance of deep learning by advanced regularization and compression methods through design of efficient optimization algorithms. The second thrust is to (i) design computationally efficient constrained optimization algorithms for learning with complicated and complex constraints, and (ii) investigate their applications in adversarial learning, fair learning, interpretable learning, etc. The optimization tools and techniques developed will enable more advanced regularization and loss minimization methods in machine learning, and should greatly influence other areas, such as operations research, signal processing, data mining, etc.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Overview. This award supported a cohesive research program on the algorithms and theory of non-convex optimization (min-max, compositional, and bilevel forms) and constrained optimization, with direct impact on ML/AI applications including non-decomposable loss minimization, self-supervised contrastive learning, continual learning, federated learning and fair ML, and open-source software. The work advances both provable methodology and practice at scale.

Non-convex min-max optimization and applications in ML. We published 17 papers at top ML conferences and journals, including ICML, NeurIPS, ICLR, and JMLR. We initiated the study of stochastic algorithms for solving non-convex–concave min-max optimization problems, developing the first algorithms with established complexities. This work has been widely cited more than 300 times and is ranked as the second most impactful publication in Optimization Methods and Software over the past five years by Google Scholar Metrics. Building on these theoretical results, we initiated a new research direction on deep AUC maximization for deep learning, which formulates the problem as a non-convex, strongly concave min-max optimization. Our algorithms for deep AUC maximization not only achieve fast theoretical convergence but also deliver strong practical performance, helping us secure first place in the Stanford CheXpert competition. We also developed federated AUC maximization in distributed environments, achieving the best-known communication and iteration complexities. Furthermore, we proposed efficient algorithms for non-convex–non-concave optimization and demonstrated their practicality for solving generative adversarial networks.

Non-convex compositional optimization and applications in ML. We published 25 papers on this topic at leading venues including ICML, NeurIPS, ICLR, JMLR, and TMLR. We were the first to formulate distributionally robust optimization (DRO) as stochastic compositional optimization and developed efficient stochastic algorithms that achieve the same complexity as SGD for solving empirical risk minimization. These algorithms enhance robustness to imbalanced and noisy data, and our attention-biased SGD for DRO achieved the best performance using ResNet50 on the iWildCam benchmark of the Stanford WILDS leaderboard.

We also introduced a new learning paradigm by optimizing a family of compositional objectives called X-risks, and formalized finite-sum coupled compositional optimization (FCCO). We developed extensive convergence theory for FCCO across smooth, non-smooth, convex, and non-convex objectives, and achieved the optimal complexities for these problems. Our algorithms have been applied to a broad range of problems in machine learning, including optimizing AUPRC for highly imbalanced data classification, optimizing NDCG for ranking tasks, and optimizing global contrastive loss for self-supervised learning. Our AUPRC optimization algorithms helped us win first place in the MIT AI Cures Challenge, while our NDCG optimization methods significantly improved over Google’s TensorFlow Ranking library.

We have also extensively investigated FCCO for self-supervised contrastive learning. Our algorithms for optimizing global contrastive loss, such as SogCLR, resolve the large-batch bottleneck of earlier approaches, enabling training in resource-limited environments. Moreover, we developed efficient FCCO-based algorithms for contrastive language–image pretraining (CLIP), making it possible to scale training to billions of data points with limited GPUs. Our algorithm for CLIP not only improves training efficiency but also delivers stronger performance, producing a model that surpasses OpenAI’s CLIP while using twice less data, one-tenth the compute budget, and achieving improved results across downstream tasks.

Non-convex bilevel optimization and applications in ML. We published 5 papers on bilevel optimization and its applications in machine learning. We were among the first to develop variance-reduced stochastic algorithms for non-convex bilevel optimization, achieving a complexity of O(1/epsilon^3) for finding an epsilon-stationary solution. We further proposed efficient algorithms for solving multi-block bilevel optimization problems with multiple lower-level objectives. Importantly, we were the first to formulate top-𝐾 NDCG optimization as multi-block bilevel optimization, and to cast partial AUC maximization as a bilevel optimization problem.

Non-convex constrained optimization and applications in ML. We published 6 papers on non-convex constrained optimization in top venues such as ICML, NeurIPS, and JMLR. We developed stochastic algorithms based on level methods, penalty methods, and switching gradient methods, and established rigorous convergence guarantees. These algorithms have been applied to a variety of machine learning problems, including learning with fairness constraints to ensure equitable model performance, and continual learning with zero-forgetting constraints to enable stable lifelong learning.

Software & translational impact. We developed LibAUC, a PyTorch-based deep learning library implementing a range of algorithms for X-risk minimization. LibAUC demonstrates clear advantages over existing libraries, including outperforming TensorFlow Ranking in both efficiency and accuracy. It has been widely adopted across academia and industry, with more than 94,000 downloads from over 90 countries. LibAUC has accelerated applications in medical imaging, recommendation systems, and representation learning.

Broader significance. This project provides a unifying algorithmic foundation for modern ML objectives that are non-convex, compositional, bilevel, or constrained, precisely the regimes that underpin today’s foundation-model training and responsible AI. By replacing ad-hoc, resource-intensive heuristics with provably efficient methods, the work advances both rigor and sustainability.

award.abstractText:
Graph neural networks (GNNs), which translate the success of deep learning to graph-structured data, have numerous applications spanning from recommendation systems and fraud detection to medicine to finance. In such applications, the extent to which similar entities connect with each other---known as homophily---is unknown and cannot be computed empirically due to limited labeled data. Though homophily is common, it is not universal; there are important real-world settings where "opposites attract", leading to heterophily (low homophily). By moving beyond a reliance on graph homophily and introducing new GNN models, this project will generalize GNNs to work effectively in a wider range of domains. It will also help rectify some negative consequences of GNNs that are tailored to homophilous graphs, including biased, unfair, or erroneous predictions when applied to heterophilous data. Focusing on robustness, fairness, and explainability will help support accountable algorithmic decision-making in the domains where GNN models are employed. In addition to research, this project will support the training of a diverse cohort of undergraduate and graduate students at the University of Michigan, the New Jersey Institute of Technology, and Michigan State University via integration of this research in advanced courses, capstone projects, and other opportunities to directly contribute to this research program.

The inability of GNNs to generalize their strong performance on homophilous or assortative graphs to many heterophilous graphs has attracted significant attention, and has led to empirical demonstration of the existence of "good heterophily", where GNNs can perform well. However, there is still limited understanding about the types of heterophily that are easy or difficult to handle with GNNs, especially beyond the limited, typically-studied settings (i.e., node classification on small homogeneous graphs). This project will advance the theoretical underpinnings of the interplay between different types of heterophily and GNNs, considering properties beyond just accuracy, which are necessary for deployment. Specifically, it will contribute: (a) New Theory: It will formally characterize the heterophily-related challenges of GNNs to provide a deeper understanding into "good" and "bad" heterophily, and enhance our understanding of "good" types of heterophily, which some architectures can model effectively, but have been vastly ignored until now. (b) New Models: Based on the new theory, it will introduce new GNN designs and architectures that not only have strong performance across different levels and types of heterophily, but are also robust, fair, and transparent, which are crucial for algorithmic decision-making. (c) New Applications: The project will also go beyond the traditional tasks and heterophilous network types investigated in the literature, and will include exploration of high-impact applications along with collaborators in academia and industry.
