award.projectOutComesReport:
This project pioneers a quantum-enhanced AI platform that dramatically reduces training time and boosts performance, enabling real-time learning on rapidly growing datasets. By leveraging annealing quantum computers, the project accelerates AI development for applications in science, healthcare, logistics, and national security. This effort emphasizes immediate commercialization using available quantum hardware. Educationally, it supports interdisciplinary STEM training through outreach at New York City College of Technology, CUNY. The initiative aims to build a talent pipeline and foster innovation across fields such as physics, engineering, and computer science, ensuring long-term societal and technological impact.

A patent application for was filed by the project team to protect the core innovation developed through NSF PFI-TT funded research. Although no patents have been granted yet, a key outcome was the execution of an exclusive licensing option agreement between the CUNY Technology Commercialization Office and a university spinoff startup formed to commercialize the research outcomes in quantum computing. While revenue has not yet been realized, the team is preparing a Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) proposal for submission to the NSF, with CUNY serving as the university partner.

The team actively collaborated with industry partners throughout the project. These partnerships provided infrastructure, technical support, and access to quantum computing platforms, enabling the team to test and validate their algorithms. Collaborations also demonstrated the applicability of the developed technology to real-world use cases, particularly in biomedical fields, enhancing the technology's commercial potential.

A major educational outcome of the project was the entrepreneurial training of one doctoral student. This student played a central role in managing project milestones, co-inventing the core technology, and maintaining strong relationships with external collaborators. Their training included leadership development, commercialization strategies, and participation as an industrial mentor in a regional NSF I-Corps program in 2025. This doctoral student is expected to lead the upcoming NSF STTR application and assume a leadership role at the startup following anticipated PhD completion. Additionally, several undergraduate students were involved in the project and received training in quantum computing and artificial intelligence, gaining valuable hands-on experience in these cutting-edge fields.

The project team also completed regional I-Corps training, identifying promising commercial applications. Their commercialization roadmap includes submitting NSF STTR Phase-I and Phase-II proposals, followed by seed funding efforts.

award.abstractText:
Machine learning systems have become prominent in many applications in everyday life, such as healthcare, finance, hiring, and education. These systems are intended to improve upon human decision-making by finding patterns in massive amounts of data, beyond what can be intuited by humans. However, it has been demonstrated that these systems learn and propagate similar biases present in human decision-making. This project aims to develop general theory and techniques on fairness in AI, with applications to improving retention and graduation rates of under-represented groups in STEM graduate programs. Recent research has shown that simply focusing on admission rates is not sufficient to improve graduation rates. This project is envisioned to go beyond designing "fair classifiers" such as fair graduate admission that satisfy a static fairness notion in a single moment in time, and designs AI systems that make decisions over a period of time with the goal of ensuring overall long-term fair outcomes at the completion of a process. The use of data-driven AI solutions can allow the detection of patterns missed by humans, to empower targeted intervention and fair resource allocation over the course of an extended period of time.  The research from this project will contribute to reducing bias in the admissions process and improving completion rates in graduate programs as well as fair decision-making in general applications of machine learning.

This project will focus on machine learning algorithms for resource allocation, which can be used at various points throughout a process such as in education. The team will propose new notions of fairness and show the applicability of those notions to settings in which limited resources, such as acceptance to the program, faculty mentoring, professional development, and paid assistantships or fellowships, are allocated to students fairly. The proposed research will also go beyond fairness in task-specific supervised learning settings and investigate fairness in unsupervised learning that guarantees to learn fair representations or generative models for multiple downstream tasks. The team will address the practical problems that arise due to uncongenial data in real-world sequential decision-making systems, including distribution shifts between training and test, imbalanced data, and missing sensitive attributes. This proposal contains a comprehensive plan to incorporate its research into education at high school, undergraduate, and graduate levels, as well as plans for within- and cross-disciplinary dissemination of research results, outreach, and other synergistic activities.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to help make consequential decisions in education, hiring, health care, finance, and other areas of public life. A central risk is that AI systems can learn patterns from historical data that reflect unequal opportunities, and then repeat or amplify those inequities. This project studied how to design fairer AI systems for decisions that unfold over time, using graduate admission and degree completion as a motivating application.
The project moved beyond the common view of fairness as a one-time classification problem, such as “admit” or “do not admit.” In graduate education, a fair outcome depends on many connected decisions: admission, mentoring, research or teaching assistantships, fellowships, professional-development opportunities, and timely support when students face barriers. The project therefore treated fairness as a long-term resource-allocation problem. Its goal was to help ensure that limited resources are allocated in ways that support equitable long-term outcomes, especially for women and underrepresented students in STEM.


The project’s intellectual contributions include new ways to define, measure, and improve fairness in AI systems. The team developed ideas for fairness that remain meaningful when budgets or decision thresholds change, which is important when the number of available admission slots, fellowships, or mentoring opportunities varies from year to year. The project also produced methods for learning fair data representations, so that the same data can support multiple downstream tasks while reducing the risk that sensitive attributes or historical bias drive decisions. A major outcome was the Equal Long-term Benefit Rate framework, or ELBERT, which adapts fairness to sequential decision-making systems. ELBERT evaluates whether different groups receive comparable accumulated benefits over time and provides an algorithmic approach for reducing long-term disparities while maintaining useful decision quality.


The project also addressed practical challenges that arise when fair AI is used outside controlled laboratory settings. These include changes in data over time, imbalanced data for different demographic groups, missing sensitive-attribute information, hidden confounding factors, and privacy concerns. The team developed and studied methods for robust representation learning, fairness under distribution shift, graph-based fairness, dynamic fairness in multi-stage decision systems, and privacy-preserving machine learning through synthetic data and differential privacy. Together, these results help build AI systems that are not only accurate on past data, but also more reliable, transparent, and fair when used in changing real-world environments.
The broader impacts of the project include potential benefits for graduate education and for other domains where people receive repeated decisions or limited resources over time. The methods developed in this project can inform fair allocation of educational support, and they also have relevance for public-interest applications such as medical resource allocation, hiring, lending, and other multi-step decision processes. The project disseminated results through peer-reviewed publications, workshops, conference presentations, invited talks, and engagement with the NSF-Amazon Fairness in AI community.


The project also contributed to workforce development and broadening participation. It supported graduate-student training, including women Ph.D. students, and provided mentoring opportunities for undergraduate researchers and summer interns. The team engaged students in interdisciplinary research spanning machine learning, signal processing, privacy, causal reasoning, graph learning, and decision-making. Outreach and community-building activities included work connected to Rising Stars in Machine Learning, fairness-focused student projects, and educational efforts to increase awareness of responsible AI. Overall, the project advanced both the science and practice of fair AI by developing tools and principles for decision systems that seek equitable long-term outcomes rather than only short-term statistical parity.

award.abstractText:
5G and beyond, the next generation of wireless communication technology, will provide higher capacity, faster speeds, and world-wide connectivity, transforming the way we live, work, learn and entertain. The development of 5G alone impacts our economy and workforce by contributing $1.4 to $1.7 trillion to US gross domestic product over the next decade and create 4.6 million 5G-related jobs through 2034. The dramatic growth and ever-increasing functionality and performance of wireless devices has crowed the electromagnetic spectrum. Dynamic spectrum sharing in 5G and beyond can meet the demands of scarce spectrum, unprecedented traffic, and better quality of service. For example, unlicensed and license-aided bands, such as 2.4 - 5 GHz industrial, scientific and medical bands, 6 GHz radio frequency bands, 60 GHz millimeter wave bands, are being shared for commercial and scientific use. However, dynamically sharing spectrum poses additional challenges to share autonomously, reliably, and securely among civilian, government, and defense. Therefore, learning surrounding wireless signals is essential to support wireless user coexistence over shared spectrum. This project focuses on developing an adaptive incremental deep learning architecture to infer radio frequency signals in dynamic spectrum sharing environments in real time. The proposed research will provide recommendations to Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) Standard P1900.8 on criteria for evaluating the performance of machine learned spectrum awareness models. The integration of research and education activities and outreach activities will broaden participation of underrepresented groups in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics fields and benefit local community collaborations through service learning-based curriculum development.

The goal of this project is to develop an incremental deep learning architecture for adaptively and efficiently detecting, classifying, and demodulating radio frequency signals in dynamic spectrum sharing environments in real time with online learning capabilities. The proposed incremental deep-learning architecture will (1) adaptively learn a wide range of wireless communication scenarios, starting from a small dataset with limited known signals or scenarios and then incrementally learning new signals or scenarios as well as updating the deep learning network in an online manner without interruption to re-train the whole network and a man-in-the-middle to label the signal; (2) advance self-learning the spectrum including spectrum sensing, signal classification and radio frequency parameter characterization in real-time; and (3) improve deep learning-based signal demodulation with the adaptive incremental learning, which can replace conventional block-based demodulation processes and preserve the same performance with high flexibility.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This project explored how artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) can help wireless communication systems adapt to new and unfamiliar radio signals. Most machine-learning systems are trained to recognize a fixed set of signal types. When a new signal appears, the system often must be retrained from the beginning. This process can be slow and impractical in crowded or rapidly changing wireless environments. 

To address this challenge, the project developed and tested incremental-learning architectures that allow an AI/ML system to learn new radio-frequency signals while retaining previously acquired knowledge. The research worked directly with raw, digitized baseband signal samples rather than relying on manually selected signal features. It also developed an automated method for designing convolutional neural networks, reducing the time and computing resources needed to identify an effective network architecture. 

A major focus of the research was catastrophic forgetting, which occurs when an AI/ML model learns new information but loses its ability to recognize previously learned classes. The project designed and assessed several architectures to address this problem, including retaining representative examples, or exemplars, of previously learned signals; knowledge distillation; and bias correction. Tests using a dataset containing twenty-four modulation types showed that bias correction generally produced the strongest results among the methods evaluated. The experiments also showed that retaining more exemplars improved performance. The research further found that the order in which new signal types are introduced can have a major effect on learning stability and final classification accuracy. By studying ten different class orderings, the project developed practical guidance for designing adaptive radio systems when memory, computing capacity, or the number of stored exemplars is limited. 

The project also investigated a unified neural-network receiver architecture designed to perform functions traditionally handled by separate signal-processing components, including filtering, phase correction, timing recovery, and demodulation. The unified neural-network performed receiver functions such as detecting signal frames with dynamic frame sizes, correcting timing and frequency errors, reducing noise, and recovering transmitted symbols. This work supports the long-term development of wireless receivers that are more flexible, reconfigurable, and efficient. 

The intellectual merit of the project extends beyond wireless communications. Similar learning challenges arise in cybersecurity, radar, autonomous systems, robotics, cognitive electronic warfare, and other areas in which AI/ML systems must respond to changing conditions without losing previously acquired  capabilities. The project therefore contributes to broader research in continual learning, trustworthy AI, intelligent sensing, and reliability engineering. 

The project also produced important educational and workforce-development outcomes. Graduate and undergraduate students gained hands-on experience in software-defined radio, machine learning, experimental design, RF hardware, over-the-air testing, data analysis, and technical communication. One supported doctoral student completed his dissertation and later joined the Department of Defense. Project findings were also introduced into the principal investigator’s software-defined radio course and will support a new course module on adaptive signal classification and catastrophic forgetting. 

Results were shared through peer-reviewed publications, workshops, conference presentations, tutorials, invited talks, and panel discussions. The project also supported outreach and service-learning efforts involving community organizations in New Bedford, MA. In addition, the work contributed to professional discussions on trustworthy, reliable/robust, understandable, and explainable AI for future wireless and mission-critical systems.

award.abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase II project is to improve the resiliency of the supply chain by implementing flexible robotic systems for materials handling.  The robotic systems that are controlled by artificial intelligence. E-commerce sales are increasing 20% year over year. During the COVID-19 pandemic additional retail volume shifted online and many customers became accustomed to sourcing essentials using e-commerce. This shift has put a greater burden on asupply chain infrastructure that has traditionally relied on human labor to pick, sort, pack, and process items for delivery. These manual processes are monotonous, error-prone, and sometimes dangerous, have extremely high worker turnover. The automation of these processes elevates worker roles and brings greater consistency to the processes. The innovation developed during this Phase II project may enable broader automation of complex materials handling processes by creating novel training systems for artificial intelligence-enabled robotic systems that are configured specifically for individual customer needs. This innovation may increase US supply chain resilience, enabling citizens to rapidly and reliably obtain necessities such as food, medicine, and health supplies without needing to leave their homes. The commercial opportunity is large, with over $20B spent on US pick and pack wages annually.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase II project seeks to develop new methods for rapidly training artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled robotic systems built for object identification and manipulation. Warehouse object manipulation tasks are variable and automating them often requires custom solutions for each customer and facility. These custom solutions are often prohibitively expensive. To solve these problems, an industrial operating system that can be deployed across many configurations of materials handling processes is required. This project aims to develop modules critical to scaling commercial deployments, such as quality control vision systems, automated assessments of item pickability, and enhanced AI systems for robotic picking. The anticipated result of this project is an industrial AI-enabled robotic operating system that allows rapid configuration of robotic systems to implement highly-optimized processes for picking and packing individual items in e-commerce logistics.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Ecommerce sales in the US have grown a staggering 85% from 2019 to 2023 in part due to the Covid-19 pandemic, and sales are expected to increase over 50% by 2028. However, a major challenge for on-time online order delivery is the high dependence on manual processes for sorting and packing individual items. Existing processes are tedious and injury-prone, making it challenging to attract and retain labor. 

Robots that can be rapidly configured to pick and pack applications with a wide variety of items have the potential to automate repetitive motions and enable humans to focus on less strenuous tasks such as exception handling and value-added services. However, the ability to pick, scan, and pack novel objects without tedious item-specific training has been a major technological barrier to automation in ecommerce fulfillment. New robotic capabilities and technologies are needed to adapt to new items and packages in response to the high variance of real-world warehouse operations.

This NSF SBIR Phase II project extended developments from the NSF SBIR Phase I project to enable AI-powered robots to operate with high reliability and throughput in real warehouse environments. The project focused on five core tasks: developing detection systems for multi-item picks to avoid costly missorts, developing classification systems for unpickable items, improving picking vision systems using novel neural network training paradigms, implementing continuous learning systems, and integrating these develops into a commercial system for sorting and packing a wide variety of items.

A key outcome of this project was the development of several AI models that serve to increase the productivity of robotic machines in production. We developed quality control neural networks to accurately detect when a robot has picked multiple items, helping improve production sort accuracy to well above 99%. We also deployed an item tracking system that can be used to detect repeated failures and unpickable items, helping to improve throughput and reduce interventions. We built a new version of the robotic pick planning AI that can rapidly plan a set of grasps on each item, improving pick success rate and throughput to well over 400 sorts an hour. We deployed a continuous learning pipeline that automatically re-trains neural networks based on production data. Finally, we developed enhancements to the AmbiSort A-Series robotic machine for parcel sorting that would enable the machine to automatically feed itself packages and reject unpickable items.

During the course of this project, Ambi Robotics deployed a large number of the AmbiSort A-Series robotic package sorting machines into commercial production with customers. Most enhancements developed in this project were moved into production as software or hardware updates, resulting in significantly improved performance. Over the peak holiday season 2023, Ambi Robotic machines sorted well over 1 million packages per week in production at a throughput over 30% higher than the contracted rate, with over 99.5% uptime. Through surveys of operations managers and robot operators who use the machines, we also identified that the machines are perceived as a significant improvement over previous processes and provide a better working environment for employees.

Ambi Robotics has now raised over $67 million in private venture funding and continues to grow its commercial deployments.

Overall, the results of this project have led to significant utilization of robots for parcel sorting in ecommerce order delivery, contributing to the advancement of US welfare and prosperity by improving the reliability of the ecommerce supply chain and increasing worker satisfaction.

award.abstractText:
Visualizing a protein’s 3D structure at atomic resolution is essential to understand its function. Historically, a technique called X-ray crystallography was preferred to obtain atomic-level structures of proteins. However, crystallography is undesirable for studying large and dynamic protein assemblies or proteins that reside in lipid membranes. But because proteins with these traits are key to many biological processes, new techniques to visualize their atomic structures are required to understand their cellular functions. An advanced form of microscopy called cryogenic electron microscopy (cryoEM) is ideal for studying these challenging proteins, and recent advances have made it capable of achieving atomic resolution. This fellowship will support the PI and research team in acquiring hands-on training in cryoEM by experts at the Pacific Northwest Center for CryoEM (PNCC), a state-of-the-art user facility operated by the Oregon Health & Science University and the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. Upon completion of the fellowship, the researchers will be cryoEM specialists, and apply this new knowledge to visualize structures of the large membrane-embedded protein assemblies they study in atomic-level detail. Further, the fellowship will bolster research and education in the molecular life sciences at the University of Nebraska (NU) by importing cryoEM expertise there. This expertise will be passed to other researchers and students across Nebraska via lab-based and in-class experiences that will impart the theory and practice of this state-of-the-art structural technique to them. As no institution in the state has cryoEM capability, infrastructure, or expertise, this fellowship has potential to be transformative to Nebraskans.

The PI’s group use the specialized training in cryoEM to propel their structural biology capacities in new and transformative directions. CryoEM will enable the PI’s group to resolve 3D structures of the small membrane protein-comprised supramolecular machines they study that will help define the mechanistic principles that drive self-assembly of these proteins. These membrane protein assemblies warrant in-depth comprehension because they control two key biological processes in animals—fortification of epithelial intercellular spaces called tight junctions, and synthesis of fatty acids that produce lipids vital to membrane organization. The fellowship will function by establishing a collaborative training ecosystem between the PI’s group and PNCC, with the primary goal to acquire deep knowledge of the cryoEM workflow, which includes sample preparation; negative stain EM; grid screening and evaluation; image collection; image processing and particle classification; 3D model building and refinement; and structure determination by cryoEM. This cryoEM expertise will foster new independent and collaborative research in Nebraska by creating a core of specialists at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln (UNL) that will train additional NU researchers, allowing many groups to use cryoEM and national centers like PNCC to determine structures of other important macromolecular systems. Educational objectives to teach future generations the theory and practice of state-of-the-art structural techniques like cryoEM will also be realized by integrating this training into the advising activities and undergraduate biochemistry courses the PI conducts at UNL. Because UNL, NU, and other regional institutions currently lack abilities in cryoEM, this fellowship will provide an essential knowledgebase that will have wide-reaching impacts on the research and educational trajectories of many individuals and groups throughout Nebraska and the Great Plains.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Researchers at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln (UNL), Drs. Vecchio and Kapoor, have used this RII Track-4 Fellowship to learn a new scientific technique called cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) at the Pacific Northwest Center for Cryo-EM (PNCC) in Portland, Oregon over the course of two years. We intended to learn this technique due to its unique capabilities to resolve the 3D structures of dynamic and challenging integral membrane proteins, to better discern these protein's functions. This endeavor was also undertaken because neither UNL nor any institution in Nebraska possesses cryo-EM infrastructure--although UNL is in the process of installing it--so, resident expertise in cryo-EM was a necessity to keep UNL on the cutting-edge of science. We have taken membrane protein samples isolated in our lab and learned the cryo-EM technique first-hand from experts at PNCC through multiple on-site visits as part of this fellowship. In the process, we have become successful independent practitioners, which was the major goal of this fellowship, as demonstrated by structure determination of several new membrane protein complexes using cryo-EM. As a lab, we will refine this expertise and continue to use this technique to bolster our structural biology platforms, which intend to resolve the principles and structures of small membrane protein-comprised supramolecular assembly. Further, we have used this fellowship to organize training sessions and a symposium in cryo-EM, and teach it to scientists within Nebraska. This has been accomplished through integrating cryo-EM into a course taught to 36+ undergraduate biochemistry majors at UNL, lead two training session in negative stain electron microscopy and sample vitrification, as well as assisting with the organization of a cryo-EM symposium that will bring experts from across the US to UNL to inform its researchers and scholars on the practice and application of this ground-breaking technology. In sum, this RII Track-4 Fellowship has transformed the future research, teaching, and professional development trajectories of Drs. Vecchio and Kapoor, and the broader training enabled by this fellowship will have wide-reaching impacts on the research and educational trajectories of many scientists across UNL and the state of Nebraska.

award.abstractText:
Mental illnesses, including depression and anxiety, are chronic, disabling, and devastating conditions. However, many people are not receiving the care they need to fully recover from their illnesses because of a shortage of health services and a lack of state-of-the-art treatment options. Studies have documented that up to two-thirds of patients who seek standard pharmacological and/or psychological interventions to emotional disorders will not respond. Noninvasive neurostimulation methods, such as transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), are emerging techniques to treat patients who have failed multiple attempts of standard interventions. However, issues of variable response effects and inter-subject variability have arisen in numerous investigations of treating depression and other mental illnesses, which have prevented the broad application of noninvasive neurostimulation for clinical use. This EPSCoR Research Fellows RII Track-4:NSF fellowship will enable the PI from the University of Oklahoma, to partner with psychiatrists and scientists at the Medical University of South Carolina to develop a novel neurostimulation technology that is integrated with neuroimaging in a closed-loop design. This research and the associated partnerships will pave the way for developing individualized treatment with much improved outcomes in people with mental illness. This success can be further generalized to the neurostimulation treatment of other disorders.

Noninvasive neurostimulation is an emerging technology that is rapidly booming in the recent decade for treating many neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders. However, the responses to a standard protocol varied greatly among individuals. Addressing the issue of heterogeneous responses will be an important step forward to exploit the full potential of neurostimulation as the treatment option. The key innovation of the project is to leverage the large-scale neural networks as biomarkers, using the algorithms previously established by the PI, to individually optimize the therapeutic outcomes of neurostimulations. A high-density, whole-head montage of multimodal electroencephalogram (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) will be used in the project for recording in the human participants. The computational analysis of the multimodal imaging data will primarily focus on identifying the functional connectivity of neural networks as biomarkers in response to neurostimulation treatment. Addressing these research questions will be important steps towards the next-generation neurostimulation methods via a biomarker-based, closed-loop approach to optimize individual treatment.

Mental illness, including depression and anxiety, are chronic, disabling, and devastating conditions. Hundreds of thousands Oklahomans suffer from mental illness, ranking Oklahoma in the highest quintile of state in the United States for prevalence of mental illness. However, most people are not receiving the care they need to fully recover from their illnesses because of shortage in health services and lack of state-of-the-art treatment options. The long-term goal of the project is to develop a novel and state-of the-art technology for treating depression and other mental illness, specifically a closed-loop, biomarker-based neurostimulation system. During the project period, the PI Dr. Han Yuan as well as undergraduate and graduate students in her lab at the University of Oklahoma travelled to a world-leading brain stimulation lab led by the host Dr. Mark George at the Medical University of South Carolina and they learned the state-of-the-art neurostimulation methods. PI and the host together have developed an integrated system of multimodal imaging and stimulation. Their testing results showed live images of brain activations during the intensive stimulations of a clinical treatment protocol for depression, suggesting that a more accurate and efficient treatment could be further built. Moreover, after learning the technology at the host lab, PI and her students have brought the technology to their home institute, the University of Oklahoma, and they installed such an advanced neurostimulation technology via partnership with the University of Oklahoma Health Science Center. Beyond the project duration, PI and her students continue to work on the neurostimulation technology that will benefit the state of Oklahoma in battling mental illness.

award.abstractText:
NONTECHNICAL SUMMARY

This award supports research and education towards discovering new kinds of fluids that can exist in nature. The most well-known fluids are liquid water or the air around us. The equations that govern such liquids and gases have been understood for hundreds of years.  More recently, fluid-like behavior has also been discovered in gases of ultracold atoms, electrons flowing through metals, and even in plasmas of quarks and gluons created at high energy particle colliders.  

The PI has recently predicted infinite families of exotic generalizations of these previously discovered fluids. The goal of this project is to develop a systematic way of classifying and understanding new kinds of hydrodynamic behavior and to predict how to discover these new fluids in experiments with ultracold atoms and quantum materials. The proposed activities will lead to a more systematic approach to predicting the collective behavior of a broad range of physical systems, ranging from quantum fluids of electrons or spins in metals, to the dynamics of liquid crystals and other soft or active matter, and even to the collective behaviors of non-equilibrium biological systems such as bacterial suspensions or flocks.  

This award also supports educational and outreach activities, including the development of a new course on modern hydrodynamics to be delivered to senior-level undergraduate and first-year graduate students. Rather than focusing on the physics of everyday liquids or gases, as is done in conventional treatments of the subject, this new course will emphasize all of the many physical settings in which hydrodynamics arises in both classical and quantum fluids: the atmosphere, electron liquids, quark-gluon plasma, liquid crystals, and the collective motion of living organisms.  These efforts will culminate in a set of book-like lecture notes, which will be freely available to the public. The PI also will lead a summer school, tentatively scheduled for July 2025,  at which a broad and diverse set of the nation's top graduate students will learn about cutting edge advances in condensed matter physics.  Undergraduate and graduate student researchers will participate in the activities funded by this award, and the PI will further disseminate results through public lectures aimed at his local community through departmental outreach programs.

TECHNICAL SUMMARY
 
This award supports research and education towards the discovery and classification of infinitely many new universality classes of hydrodynamics, and infinitely many new non-equilibrium dynamical fixed points which generalize the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang universality class.
 
The research has three main thrusts. (1) The discovery of many new universality classes of hydrodynamics, which arise in constrained quantum systems with multipole and/or subsystem symmetries.  By incorporating further conservation laws such as momentum, or by breaking spacetime symmetries, these hydrodynamic theories can become unstable in the presence of thermal fluctuations, and flow to new non-equilibrium universality classes.  (2) The PI will develop new effective field theory methods to systematically predict and analyze these new universality classes. These field theories will naturally describe nonlinear fluctuating hydrodynamics and help lead to better understandings of the foundations of statistical physics (including fluctuation-dissipation theorems and the existence of thermodynamics) in far-from-equilibrium settings. The mathematical methods developed will also help to uncover if and when exotic non-relativistic fracton matter can be coupled consistently to gravity.  (3) Lastly, the PI will work to predict experimental realizations of these new kinds of fluids. Two natural settings include Fermi-Hubbard-like models in ultracold atoms confined in tilted optical lattices, and frustrated quantum magnets. The PI will deduce the appropriate hydrodynamic description for these exotic dynamical systems, which are expected to lead to the discovery of exotic generalizations of magnetohydrodynamics and other models with higher-form symmetries.  Together, these three thrusts will help usher in a more systematic and predictive approach to hydrodynamics in classical and quantum many-particle systems with unconventional symmetries.
 
This award also supports educational and outreach activities, including the development of a course on hydrodynamics as an effective field theory for first-year graduate students and senior undergraduate students. Course materials from this class, including an eventual set of lecture notes, will be freely available to the public.  The PI will also lead a summer school on dynamics in strongly correlated quantum materials, helping to train the diverse next generation of physicists in the state-of-the-art in the field.  Undergraduate and graduate student researchers will participate in the activities funded by this award, and the PI will further disseminate results through public lectures aimed at his local community through departmental outreach programs.

This Boosting Research Ideas for Transformative and Equitable Advances in Engineering (BRITE) Synergy award supports research into new wearable robotic systems created with a unique manufacturing process. This project aims to develop a new class of garment-like robots that will provide assistive technology for patients with neuromuscular disorders and other disabilities, as well as augmentive capabilities for workers in everyday use. In clinical applications, this new class of wearable robots will be able to provide vital-signal monitoring for diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation with high comfort, biocompatibility, and operability, improving personalized healthcare. The assistive robots can augment upper limb capabilities and prevent injuries in challenging working conditions. This project will disseminate the research products to a broad audience in both classrooms and communities through various activities. It will also provide training to students, especially those from groups underrepresented in STEM.

The research goal of this project is to establish a new class of smart and programmable wearable textile robots for upper extremity assistance. The robots will integrate sensing, understanding, and mimicking of skeletal muscle behaviors in real time, through mechanisms based on textile materials made by novel manufacturing techniques. To achieve the goal, multidisciplinary knowledge needs to be integrated, including wearable sensing, continuous feature recognition, distributed actuation, and wearable robot design and control. Two research tasks are planned for achieving the research goal: 1) Developing smart and robust textile-based human interfaces and building understanding of muscle behaviors and 2) developing wearable textile robots based on programmable distributed actuators controlled by human inputs. The success of this project will promote the mass production of textile robots as a next-generation technology for ubiquitous assistance.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Neuromuscular disorders, including conditions such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), muscular dystrophy, and spinal muscular atrophy, affect millions of people worldwide by progressively reducing muscle strength, movement, and independence. Because most of these conditions cannot be cured, improving mobility, rehabilitation, and quality of life remains a critical healthcare challenge. At the same time, healthy individuals, caregivers, and workers in physically demanding occupations also face risks of fatigue, overuse injuries, and musculoskeletal disorders during everyday activities. Wearable robotics, also called exoskeletons, have emerged as a promising approach to augment human movement and provide physical assistance. However, existing systems are often built using rigid mechanical structures that can be bulky, uncomfortable, and difficult to integrate into daily life. These limitations highlight the need for a new generation of soft, lightweight, and wearable robotic technologies that seamlessly combine comfort, functionality, and long-term usability.

This project created a new class of soft wearable robots, also called soft exosuits, that seamlessly integrate sensing, actuation, and intelligent control within textile materials using scalable textile manufacturing techniques. Unlike conventional exoskeletons, these exosuits are designed to function as comfortable everyday garments while naturally interpreting users’ movement intentions through brain-computer interfaces. In particular, the project developed multiple electroencephalography (EEG) based motor imagery control methods that real-timely decode human motion intention for soft exosuit control, enabling the exosuit to anticipate user actions and provide timely assistance. By combining lightweight textile-based hardware with intelligent human-machine interaction, the project lays the foundation for wearable robotic systems that provide intuitive, personalized assistance while preserving comfort, mobility, and long-term wearability.

In order to better control soft actuators, this project also generated new modeling methods for understanding and controlling soft robots. The research developed physics-informed neural network (PINN) techniques that combine the fundamental laws of soft matter mechanics with machine learning to accurately model the highly nonlinear deformation of soft actuators. Compared with conventional data-driven approaches, these physics-guided models require less training data while providing improved accuracy, robustness, and physical consistency. The resulting framework enables faster prediction of soft actuator behavior and lays the groundwork for real-time control, optimization, and digital simulation of wearable soft robotic systems.

In addition to advancing wearable robotics, this project established a new design-to-manufacturing platform for embroidered electronics that enables functional electronic systems to be directly fabricated onto everyday garments. The platform integrates digital circuit design, automated embroidery, and textile manufacturing into a streamlined workflow, allowing sensors, electrodes, conductive traces, and human-machine interfaces to be seamlessly embedded within fabrics. By eliminating many of the complex fabrication steps traditionally required for textile electronics, the platform makes the development of smart garments more accessible, reproducible, and scalable. This open and programmable manufacturing capability provides a foundation for the rapid development of next-generation wearable technologies for healthcare, rehabilitation, human performance, and human-computer interaction.

Beyond its research contributions, this project also made broader impacts through education and workforce development by providing multidisciplinary training for undergraduate and graduate students at the intersection of wearable robotics, textile electronics, biomechanics, artificial intelligence, and human-centered design. Students gained hands-on experience through research, prototype development, human subject studies, and collaborations with clinicians and industry partners, preparing them for careers in academia, healthcare technology, and advanced manufacturing. The project's research outcomes were also integrated into undergraduate capstone design courses, enabling students to develop next-generation wearable systems using technologies created through the project. In addition, the project fostered an open research ecosystem by disseminating hardware designs, software tools, and manufacturing workflows to the broader research community, helping to accelerate innovation and lower barriers to entry in wearable robotics and smart textiles.

Called for in the FY 2020 National Defense Authorization Act, the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine has convened the Roundtable to bring together individuals from the research agencies, national intelligence, law enforcement, academic research, and business communities to explore critical issues related to protecting U.S. national and economic security while ensuring the open exchange of ideas and the international talent required for American leadership in science and technology. The Roundtable is tasked with: 1) exploring critical issues related to protecting US national and economic security; 2) identifying and considering security threats and risks associated with federally funded
research and development; 3) identifying effective approaches to communicating threats and risks; 4)sharing best practices for addressing and mitigating the threats and risks; and 5) examining potential near and long-terms responses by stakeholders in the research enterprise to mitigate and address the risks associated with foreign threats.

The National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine organized a two-day Meeting of Experts that was open to public participation on January 25-26, 2023.  The meeting followed up on the recommendation in the 2022 NASEM report ?Protecting U.S. Technological Advantage? related to NSDD-189 on protecting the open research environment. The meeting examined whether now is the time to revisit NSDD-189 and the practical effects of doing so, based on views of the foreign policy, security, scientific, and legislative communities.  The event was formed around four questions: 

  • What boundaries should exist between fundamental research that should be undertaken in an open environment and research that should only be pursued in a closed environment?  Should restrictions be limited to classification? 
  • How do we protect research that is fundamental, that is not technology focused, and/or requires the use of platforms with clear dual-use implications?
  • If the commercial sector is now the center of platform production, as opposed to the past in which military research preceded commercial deployment, how are we to assess when technology becomes of interest to national security?
  • How might foreign actors react to changes in the U.S. research security policy landscape, given foreign interest in achieving scientific and technological pre-eminence, leadership, or at least parity with the United States?

Participants also received briefings from individuals closely tied to the national security communities to help them understand where research security fits in the broader scope of the international technology competition.

Given the meeting of experts format, an uncorrected transcript was provided to the National Science Foundation at the conclusion of the event. 

As a follow on from the event, the University of Maryland suggested a closed meeting for senior research officers take place on protecting research in the university environment.  That event, which took place under the National Science, Technology, and Security Roundtable funded by the Department of Defense and National Institutes of Health, took place on March 31, 2023, and featured presentations from Congressional staff and current and former research security professionals from the U.S. government.

award.abstractText:
Non-Technical Description: 
Philosophers of science analyze the logical and conceptual foundations (i.e. the epistemologies) of scientific knowledge. Epistemologies of science elucidate why and how science works. Understanding the nature of science enables philosophers and scientists to work together to improve scientific methods and further scientific progress, as well as to employ science to improve the welfare of the nation and the world. This EPSCoR Research Fellowship will produce the first analysis of the epistemology of agricultural science. Agricultural science is an interdisciplinary and applied set of scientific practices that will feature prominently in solutions to urgent, global 21st-century problems, including the energy crisis and food shortages anticipated by climate change. Understanding the epistemology of agricultural science will improve the abilities of scientists and policymakers to employ the results of agricultural science to solve large-scale social problems.  The PI and a postdoctoral scholar will collect field data, receive additional training members in science and values, and strengthen an existing research collaboration at Michigan State University, to advance the PI’s research on the epistemology of agricultural science.

Technical Description:
This EPSCoR Research Fellowship will fund a research residency for the PI and a postdoctoral scholar to collect field data, receive additional training, and strengthen an existing research collaboration at Michigan State University (MSU), in order to advance the PI’s research on the epistemology of agricultural science. The Fellowship is co-sponsored by the MSU Department of Philosophy, the MSU Socially Engaged Philosophy of Science (SEPOS) group, and the MSU Center for Interdisciplinarity. The overall objective of the Fellowship is to accelerate research in the epistemology of agricultural science by strengthening the research partnership between philosophers at the University of Kentucky and MSU. This will be accomplished via two types of research activity: 1) Collaborative philosophical research with members of the sponsoring institutes.  The PI and postdoc will additionally receive training from SEPOS members in science and values, a branch of philosophy of science for which MSU and SEPOS are widely renowned; and 2) Collection of data from philosophical fieldwork on the agricultural scientific activity being conducted at MSU. The PI employs fieldwork methods to conduct research, including interviewing and shadowing practicing agricultural scientists to examine how they generate concepts and theoretical frameworks. Due to the localized nature of agricultural science, comparative data across multiple locations, e.g. Kentucky and Michigan, is required. Analysis of applied science, especially agricultural science, innovates on the way epistemology of science understands the nature of the scientific practice. This advances inquiry in the epistemology of science, particularly impacting existing research in the philosophy of scientific classification and the study of science and values. This Fellowship will expand the scope of philosophy of science, and, via the collection of field data, it will also generate a dataset that will catalyze additional new scholarship in the epistemology of science.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This award produced the first modern, systematic, philosophical investigation of scientific reasoning in agricultural science, focusing primarily on cropping practices in Michigan. The research team employed philosophical, historical, and social-scientific methods in order to map the complex network of technological, biological, physical, social, institutional, governmental, and economic factors affecting the design of modern agriculture and the scientific research that supports it. Members of the research team conducted interviews, extended observation, archival research, and philosophical analysis to obtain results.

 

Intellectual Merit: Key finding 1. Agricultural science is meliorative. Unlike some areas of the sciences, which aim to describe and characterize aspects of the world as it is, meliorative sciences conduct research with the explicit or implicit aim of improving some aspect of the world. Typically, “improvement” is defined relative to human interests. Medical scientific research is meliorative, aiming not simply to understand human health but to improve it; our team found that agricultural science is importantly analogous. The aims and epistemic structures of medical science are well-studied in the philosophy of science, and insight from those findings can be used to inform future research into the philosophy of agricultural science.

 

Key finding 2. A complex network of professionals and content experts who are not trained scientists play essential roles in defining the goals, methods, and measures of success in agricultural scientific research (ASR). ASR experiments are frequently conducted on commercial farms, monitored and maintained through crop development by farm workers as opposed to scientists or laboratory technicians. This is a unique type of scientific activity that sets ASR apart from most other forms of contemporary experimental research. The role of extension workers from county agents to university faculty members adds further complexity to this picture, particularly in the mechanisms by which ASR experiments are defined in response to commercial- and community-reported problems in production. Further, industry is deeply integrated into ASR in ways that impact research agendas. This integration does not directly parallel industry integration in medical/pharmaceutical research, and requires further epistemic analysis.

 

This key finding holds a number of implications for philosophy of science (PS). Notably, it complicates standard PS stories about the epistemic roles of non-scientists in the production of scientific knowledge, offering an alternative to standard citizen-scientist accounts. Similar complications arise for industry. It also generates a challenge to the standard PS assumption that products of scientific research are separable from producers of research. 

 

Key finding 3. The products of ASR are best characterized and classified through endemic classificatory schemes, rather than by extending biological or economic classification practices. This finding is best understood by example. Consider potatoes: the biological taxonomy of potatoes is well-established as solanum tuberosum. This classification embeds important scientific information about the lifecycle of potatoes and their connections to biological relatives in the nightshade family, and it can be used to draw inferences about many other topics of interest, such as the geographic history of potato plants. The biological taxonomy of potatoes cannot, however, inform many important aspects of ASR, such as research on potato storage or optimal sugar–starch ratios for chipping. Instead, agricultural classification systems that distinguish finer-grained differences between potato types (e.g. cultivars) must be implemented in order to achieve the meliorative aims of many ASR experiments. These classification systems operate on features of potatoes that are not considered to be biologically significant to solanum tuberosum as a species, but which are nonetheless deeply significant to the agricultural uses to which grown potatoes will be put.

 

Broader Impacts: STEM workforce. Grant activities provided essential training in cutting-edge research methods for all members of the research team. Team members trained in interview methods, archival methods, and philosophical methods that advanced members’ ability to perform research and, in that case of two junior researchers, led directly to further career opportunities. In one case, a junior researcher previously trained as a philosopher of science became sufficiently proficient in interview and data analysis methods to receive employment as a social scientist with the USDA. In another case, a junior researcher previously trained as a historian of science had work accepted for presentation at two competitive philosophy of science conferences.

 

Inclusion. The research team consisted of 6 central researchers. The three seniormost team members each fall into at least one recognized category of minorities underrepresented in STEM. One of the junior team members falls into a recognized category of minorities underrepresented in STEM. Through efforts associated with grant activity, this team member was also placed in a competitive postdoctoral opportunity that would not have been available without their participation in grant activities.

 

Partnerships. By highlighting and analyzing the role of industry in the production of ASR findings, this research strengthens understanding of how to efficiently, effectively, and ethically partner with industry in the production of ASR.

This award is funded in whole or in part under the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 (Public Law 117-2). 

Almost 1% of the world's population lives with epilepsy and half of them are women, whose seizures and antiseizure medicines affect their menstrual cycle, pregnancy, menopause, and bone health. Hormonal changes in women can influence seizure risk and are associated with changes in biological signals measured by wearable devices, such as temperature and heart rate variability, and can be linked to seizure patterns. This Engineering Research Initiation (ERI) award focuses on improving the quality of life of women with epilepsy by creating forecasting algorithms that can help manage dosing of antiseizure medication based on predicted seizure risk. The proposed research will provide training opportunities for a diverse group of undergraduate and graduate students and the focus will be to engage female students in research. 

The proposed research investigates hormonal changes associated with the menstrual cycle and their effects on seizure risk in women by analyzing physiological signals recorded with non-invasive wearable devices. The ability to forecast seizures, minutes to hours in advance has already been verified using data from invasive EEG (Electroencephalography) devices; however, it is still a challenge to do this using noninvasive wearable devices. The performance of the machine learning algorithms for seizure forecasting could be significantly improved if the seizure risk associated with hormonal changes be considered in the design to mitigate false alarms and improve sensitivity. Designing a reliable seizure forecasting algorithm will allow patients to use lower baseline doses of medications, with escalated doses given during times of high seizure risk. Additionally, investigating the gender-specific parameters affecting seizure risk and implementing them in managing epilepsy will lead to significant improvements in quality of life for women with epilepsy.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Approximately one percent of the US population is affected by epilepsy, with half of this number being female. Despite the application of various treatment techniques, such as medication therapy and resective surgery, many individuals with epilepsy continue to experience seizures. A reliable seizure forecasting algorithm has the potential to enhance the quality of life for people with epilepsy by enabling them to modify their activities or take fast-acting medication in response to predicted seizures.

Recent advancements in wearable technology have demonstrated the feasibility of seizure forecasting through the implementation of machine learning techniques. Previous research indicates that the temporal distribution of seizures is non-random, and the risk of seizure occurrence can be forecasted in some people. In particular, hormonal changes in women exhibit a non-random and cyclic nature as well, and it is known that hormonal changes influence brain excitability and can modulate seizure risk. However, this has remained largely unstudied despite the importance of this phenomenon.

The hormonal changes in women are associated with measurable changes in bio-signals such as temperature and heart rate variability. This study correlates hormonal changes and bio-signals using data recorded from non-invasive devices during the menstrual cycle. Continuous data from 21 healthy female subjects, wearing wristbands for at least two menstrual cycles and tracking their menstruation and ovulation days, revealed that, in addition to temperature and heart rate variability, skin conductance level can also serve as a representative indicator of hormonal changes.

Machine learning algorithms were developed to accurately track menstrual cycle phases, achieving a 91% accuracy in detecting menses, ovulation, and luteal phase. The application of these algorithms to data collected from patients with epilepsy (”My Seizure Gauge” project funded by Epilepsy Foundation of America), allowed for the detection of menstrual phases and recognition of ovulating and non-ovulating patients. Mapping menstrual phases and seizure cycles suggests a correlation between hormonal changes and seizure patterns in some patients. Furthermore, the analysis of data from male subjects contributes to defining differences in natural cycles.

Intellectual merit and broader impacts: These findings hold the potential to better manage the health of patients with epilepsy, offering insights that may improve their quality of life. Additionally, automating the tracking of menstrual cycle phases, especially ovulation, can alleviate the need for traditional methods like urine strip tests or thermometers. This automation is not only beneficial for epilepsy patients but also holds relevance for broader studies related to women's physical and mental health. As a result, the impact of this interdisciplinary project extends across various disciplines focused on women's health.

Thus far, the project has generated several publications and presentations, with additional papers currently in progress. Three female graduate students and two undergraduate students from the departments of Electrical Engineering, Computer Science, and Data Science underwent training, enhancing their expertise in data science, signal processing, and artificial intelligence. Furthermore, the acquired devices will be utilized in the physiological signal processing course and other associated research endeavors.

The project aims to serve the national need of developing highly effective STEM teachers with knowledge of data science. Since data driven discovery is a high priority across all areas of science and engineering education and research, future STEM professionals, including today’s students, will need to be able to gather and analyze data to solve problems. In order to help students to thrive in a data-intensive society, teachers themselves require opportunities to develop their own skills and understandings related to data science and scientific research. To meet this need, this project will engage prospective secondary STEM teachers in mentored summer research experiences related to biological applications of data science. Accompanying the research experiences will be a professional development program. This professional development program will be aimed at increasing pedagogical and content knowledge. It is also aimed at developing communication skills and incorporating enrichment experiences to illustrate and emphasize ways research can be applied to build prospective teachers' capacity to incorporate research and other inquiry-based learning in the classroom. By providing prospective teachers with firsthand research experiences involving data analytics, the project has potential to improve the quality of STEM teaching related to data science as well as to contribute to teachers’ satisfaction and retention.

This project at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston includes collaborations with teacher preparation programs at University of Houston, University of Houston Clear Lake, and the Texas Education Agency Region 4 Service Center. The project will immerse six future secondary STEM teachers per year in authentic research experiences related to life sciences data mining and analysis, with a total of 18 participants over three years. The project has four fundamental goals. A primary project goal is for these prospective teachers to receive authentic research experiences involving a variety of data analytical approaches to investigate questions from neuroscience as well as molecular and cellular biology. A second goal is to incorporate accompanying professional development opportunities designed to expand the research experiences and to equip these perspective STEM teachers with the skills and understanding to bring research and professional development experiences to their future classrooms. A third goal is to evaluate the impact of project components on prospective teachers’ growth and preparation. To meet the project's fourth goal, project outcomes will be disseminated to other investigators and institutions interested in improving and enhancing STEM pre-service teacher preparation. Project evaluation will include studying the impact of the research experiences and engagement in the professional development program on the participants, and will include information from completion of the project's curriculum, analysis of reflective journal entries, assessment of science identity and science teaching efficacy, and results emanating from continued engagement with partnering researchers and the host institution. Project results will be disseminated through communications with project collaborators, publications in peer-reviewed journals, presentations at local and national meetings, and web-based strategies. This Noyce Research Experiences for Pre-Service Teachers project is supported through the Robert Noyce Teacher Scholarship Program (Noyce). The Noyce program supports talented STEM undergraduate majors and professionals to become effective K-12 STEM teachers and experienced, exemplary K-12 teachers to become STEM master teachers in high-need school districts. It also supports research on the retention and effectiveness of K-12 STEM teachers in high-need school districts.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Data‑driven discovery—using large data sets, computational tools, and increasingly artificial intelligence (AI)—now underpins much of modern science. Yet most future middle and high school STEM teachers have few opportunities to experience how scientists actually use quantitative data to answer real research questions. The Baylor College of Medicine Research Experiences in Data Analytics Program was created to address this gap by immersing future STEM teachers in authentic, data‑intensive biosciences research and preparing them to bring these experiences into their classrooms.

From 2022 through 2025, the project engaged undergraduate students pursuing STEM degrees and teacher certification in a multi‑stage program combining hands‑on training in data analytics with summer research experiences in active biosciences laboratories. Participants first completed an intensive short course introducing data science concepts using a free, visual data‑mining platform that does not require programming experience. In the final two years, the course included foundational instruction in artificial intelligence (AI), reflecting the growing role of AI in research and education. Participants then spent five weeks as members of scientific teams focused on genetics, genomics, neuroscience and bioinformatics, analyzing real research data and contributing to ongoing studies. Weekly professional development sessions supported participants in translating these experiences into classroom‑ready instruction aligned with state standards.

Intellectual Merit. The project advanced understanding of how authentic research experiences shape future teachers’ knowledge, skills, and professional identities in data‑driven science. Across all project years, evaluation data showed that participants entered the program with little or no prior experience in data analytics or computational research methods. Following the short course and lab experience, participants consistently reported increased knowledge of data analysis, data visualization, and the role of computation in scientific discovery. They also learned how scientific questions are developed, how teams of scientists collaborate, and how evidence is generated and interpreted in real research settings.

Importantly, the project demonstrated that complex topics such as data mining, genomics, and neural networks can be taught effectively to future teachers in a research setting. Participants progressed from self-reported novice to competent levels of confidence in multiple data‑science skills and reported improved ability in communicating scientific findings. These findings contribute to the research base on teacher preparation by showing that immersive, data‑focused research experiences can meaningfully enhance teachers’ understanding of modern biology without requiring advanced technical backgrounds.

Broader Impacts. The broader impacts of the project extend directly to K–12 classrooms. Across all cohorts, participants reported strong intentions to apply what they learned in their future teaching. Evaluation data show that most pre‑service teachers planned to incorporate data analytics concepts, examples of real scientific data, and discussions of authentic STEM careers into their classrooms. In earlier cohorts, participants specifically identified plans to introduce data visualization, classification, statistics, and inquiry‑based lessons in their future classrooms.

Participants consistently reported increased confidence in their ability to explain how scientists work on real problems and to provide concrete examples of authentic research to their students. Many indicated that the program prepared them to mentor students interested in STEM careers and to help learners understand the interdisciplinary nature of modern science, particularly the connections among mathematics, biology, computer science, and data analysis. It is likely that each of the program participants will interact with more than 300 secondary school students after teaching for three years, so the total number of  secondary school students reached will exceed 8,000.

The project also strengthened connections between biomedical researchers and the education community. Scientists and trainees in host laboratories gained experience mentoring future teachers and increased their understanding of secondary education contexts. These partnerships helped bridge the gap between cutting‑edge biosciences research and K–12 education, fostering mutual learning and collaboration.

Overall, the project demonstrates that immersive research experiences centered on data analytics in the context of biological research can play a critical role in preparing future STEM teachers. Evaluation evidence shows that participants not only gained knowledge and skills, but also left the program with clear intentions to bring data‑driven science and authentic research examples into their classrooms. By equipping teachers with firsthand experience in how modern science works, the program helps ensure that future students learn about science as a dynamic, evidence‑based process and are better prepared to engage with an increasingly data‑rich world.

award.abstractText:
This study aims to improve the methods surrounding surface landform dating, and thus methods for determining rates of fault slip. Accurate slip rates are essential for tectonics and earthquake hazards research, and often require numerous surface ages. Such dating efforts can be challenging due to a lack of datable materials, cost concerns, or accessibility of field sites. Recent investigations have directly correlated specific remote sensing observations to the absolute age of surface landforms. Using a large repository of remote sensing data and recent advances in data science and machine learning, this study will integrate multiple, distinct types of remotely sensed data with published age data, to develop a calibrated age model that will be applied to faulted landforms in southeastern California. The methodology will be applied to the eastern Garlock fault, a major strike-slip fault in this region, and aid in answering longstanding questions about the role of the fault in southern California tectonics. This study will make a significant contribution to earthquake hazard analysis of many active faults in southeastern California, a region under threat of damaging earthquakes and with a population of more than 3 million people. Improved earthquake hazard assessments are critical for federal, state, and local agencies and regulatory bodies, a broad spectrum of industry, and the public. The model produced by this study can also form a framework for future surface age studies around the world. Additionally, this study will contribute to the development of the STEM workforce by advancing the education and training of a female graduate student and at least two undergraduate students, as well as the professional development of two early-career researchers, including a female assistant professor.  

Geologic slip rates are essential components of seismic hazard analysis and critical to addressing many pressing questions at the forefront of tectonics and seismological research. However, discrepancies of Late-Cenozoic and present-day slip rates continue to be debated, particularly when slip rate estimates span different timescales of activity. Discriminating true slip rate discrepancies from observational biases / limitations requires an accurate (and self-consistent) view of slip rates and their temporal and spatial variability.  However, obtaining robust slip rates remains challenging, due to lack of dateable materials, cost concerns, or accessibility of field sites. Addressing these challenges, recent investigations have directly correlated specific remote sensing indices to the absolute age of landforms. Using the broad combined repository of remote sensing data from the past 20 years and recent advances in data science and machine learning, the investigators will expand on these efforts and integrate several types of remotely sensed data with published geochronology data to develop a calibrated surface property-age model that will be applied to faulted landforms in the Eastern California shear zone / southern Walker Lane of southeastern California. The ensemble model will incorporate different modeled responses between sensed values and surface age. Ensemble modeling uses a variety of statistical and computational models to fuse an array of single variate models to solve classification and regression problems. With the variety of remote sensors, bands, and spatial scales available, a wealth of data can be consolidated into a cohesive, robust model. The investigators believe such rigorous data treatment may yield significantly improved uncertainties on resulting ages compared with individual models. When implemented, the proposed effort will yield a calibrated means of estimating surface ages using remote sensing data and new slip rates for the eastern Garlock fault.
