The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) to solve cybersecurity problems has been gaining traction within industry and academia, in part as a response to widespread malware attacks on critical systems, such as cloud infrastructures, government offices or hospitals, and the vast amounts of data they generate. AI- and ML-assisted cybersecurity offers data-driven automation that could enable security systems to identify and respond to cyber threats in real time. However, there is currently a shortfall of professionals trained in AI and ML for cybersecurity. This project will  address the shortfall by developing lab-intensive modules that enable undergraduate and graduate students to gain fundamental and advanced knowledge in applying AI and ML techniques to real-world datasets to learn about Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI), malware analysis, and classification, among other important topics in cybersecurity. The proposed project will impact more than 400 students annually and is uniquely poised to provide opportunities to a diverse student population.  Tennessee Technical University and University of North Carolina Wilmington are located in economically challenged regions.  Manhattan College has a student population that is 31% minority (20% Hispanic) and 33% first generation college students. In addition, this project proposes to increase participation of underrepresented groups in STEM by conducting workshops and participating in professional conferences, such as The Women in Cybersecurity Conference, Community College Cyber Summit, and Society of Hispanic Professional Engineers.  Providing undergraduate and graduate students with training in the use of AI in malware analysis is an important step towards bridging the current cybersecurity talent gap. 

The project will develop six self-contained and adaptive modules in "AI-assisted Malware Analysis." Topics will include: (1) CTI and malware attack stages, (2) malware knowledge representation and CTI sharing, (3) malware data collection and feature identification, (4) AI-assisted malware detection, (5) malware classification and attribution, and (6) advanced malware research topics and case studies such as adversarial learning and Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) detection. The course modules will be evaluated and assessed to determine their impact on students. Workshops and tutorial sessions at conferences will be used to expand the project’s impact and provide students and enthusiasts with hands-on experience of aspects of AI-assisted malware analysis using real-world datasets. A two-day training workshop for external faculty will also be arranged to enable further dissemination of the modules. The suite of activities proposed in this project will train students, researchers, and professionals in AI-assisted malware analysis and prepare them to meet future cybersecurity challenges. 

This project is supported by the Secure and Trustworthy Cyberspace (SaTC) program, which funds proposals that address cybersecurity and privacy, and in this case specifically cybersecurity education. The SaTC program aligns with the Federal Cybersecurity Research and Development Strategic Plan and the National Privacy Research Strategy to protect and preserve the growing social and economic benefits of cyber systems while ensuring security and privacy.

The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is to broaden access to healthcare data. Users of the system developed in this project can take biometric measurements such as heart rate, muscle-activity, and body mass calculations in real-time, with data collected through sensors embedded into clothing.  The innovation enables vital measurements to be taken, both inside and outside of clinical environments, while reducing instrumentation weight and cost requirements. This fabric-based technology can potentially serve users ranging from medical professionals to everyday consumers who will more easily adopt wearable soft-material products in lieu of traditional hardware devices. Specialized sectors such as physical therapy, pre-surgical studies, sports labs, and out-patient care have the highest growth opportunity for new technology adoption. Complementing the rapid growth of telehealth, bio-sensing capabilities for real-time and remote tracking will improve patient compliance and aid health care workers by providing better access to comprehensive vital measurement data.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project involves material science research in conductive threads and fabrics. These soft goods can bend, stretch, and compress along the body where they are worn. In addition, their electromechanical characteristics allow them to pick up small voltage and current signals that are naturally generated from the body, specifically from the heart, muscles, and the brain. By strategically weaving these materials within a shirt, small voltages for EKG (heart), EMG (muscle), EEG (brain), and BIA (water and body mass content) can be simultaneously captured and measured for heart rate, muscle activity, brain activity, and water and fat content measurements. The technical research will involve innovation in fabric-materials optimized for small signal and low noise pickup and design of a comfortable garment incorporating multiple fabric-based electrodes for simultaneous pickup of EKG/EMG/BIA signals. The project will also develop new signal processing algorithms to transform raw voltages to real-time signals transmitted wirelessly. The desired technical result is a functional and wearable prototype with end-to-end communication from the fabric through the garment to a receiving mobile or desktop app visualizing the processed data for heart rate, muscle activity, and body mass analysis.

award.projectOutComesReport:
The goal of Nextiles' NSF SBIR Phase I grant was to develop conductive fabrics and yarns as more flexible and affordable substitutes for dry and wet electrodes for biometric sensing used in clinical and commercial settings. The purpose of the project's research into fabric-based conductive materials was to improve the form-factor, accessibility, and comfort-level of current electrophysiology equipment used for EKG (electrocardiography), EMG (electromyography), and EOG (electrooculography).

Nextiles was able to develop several conductive fabrics and yarns, with more than ten different fabrics assessed. Each material was assessed both mechanically and electrically. Mechanically, each material was made to be cut, died, sewn into, and embroidered for mostly all cut-and-sew machines and operations. Manufacturing and prototyping experiments were tested at the Nextiles' facility. In addition, each material was electrically analyzed for their internal resistance, sheet resistance, and changes in resistance due to mechanical deformation or perturbation such as applied pressure, twisting, and bending.

During the project, Nextiles developed accessory technologies that allowed the conductive fabric to be embedded with standard electronic devices such as electromechanical connectors and Bluetooth devices. The purpose was to construct a final prototype that could be delivered at the conclusion of the project. The final prototype(s) being a shirt for EKG, compressive sleeve for EMG, and a facemask for EOG. These additional hardware components were also made to be sewable into the prototypes using Nextiles patent (pending) flexible and sewable connector technology. The research and development involved in the final prototype included pattern making, techpack assembly which includes a bill of material (BOM) and point of measurement (POM), as well as customizing the sewn routes between the connectors and controller to the fabric electrodes.

With the deliverable, the prototypes were used to collect preliminary data to compare against gold standard electrophysiological waveforms. The results in this project show a strong feasibility for commercial use, as well as for potential application in clinical studies. Signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) and waveforms such as heart rate (EKG), heart pulse pattern (EKG QRS complex), muscle activity (EMG), and eye movement (EOG) were within 10%-15% of off-the-shelf devices. In addition, data acquisition bandwidth was observed to go as high as >100 Hz, allowing granular signal analysis for peak phase and frequency response. Ongoing work will focus on further enhancing the data acquisition circuitry, as well as developing algorithms to further filter and implement machine learning insights for consumer use once the prototypes evolve into a commercializable form.

Work that can be conducted in a Phase II is to develop algorithms in which to transform raw data into easily interpretable metrics for consumer, sport, and medical personnel. Examples of metrics could be heart rate (EKG), time of intense or low muscle activity (EMG), and types of eye activity (EOG). With these promising results, we plan to further expand to other fabric-based electrophysiology capabilities such as BIA (bioelectric impedance analysis), EDA (electrodermal activity), and SIA (skin impedance analysis). The goal is to combine these modalities into a unified system, such as a shirt or leggings, to reduce the equipment burden and cost when performing any electrophysiological measurements and experiments.

award.abstractText:
This award provides support to U.S. researchers participating in a project competitively selected by a 9-country initiative on global change research through the Belmont Forum.  The Belmont Forum is a consortium of research funding organizations representing over 55 countries focused on support for transdisciplinary approaches to global environmental change challenges and opportunities.  It aims to accelerate delivery of the international research most urgently needed to remove critical barriers to sustainability by aligning and mobilizing international resources. Each partner country provides funding for their researchers within a consortium to alleviate the need for funds to cross international borders. This approach facilitates effective leveraging of national resources to support excellent research on topics of global relevance best tackled through a multinational approach, recognizing that global challenges need global solutions. This award provides support for the U.S. researchers to cooperate in consortia that consist of partners from at least three of the participating countries.  The research teams will address key areas of arctic resilience understanding and action. This collaboration of academic and non-academic knowledge systems constitutes a transdisciplinary approach that will advance not only understanding of the fundamentals of arctic resilience but also spur action, inform decision-making, and translate into solutions for resilience.  

The project seeks to address the challenge of building resilience in a rapidly changing Arctic by focusing on human activities that impact Arctic wetlands ecosystems.  The project will support and help communities to strengthen their capacity to engage in wetlands restoration and stewardship.  At a local scale, wetlands buffer heavy precipitation and snowmelt and filter and store water. They provide crucial habitat for biodiversity, providing nesting and breeding areas for migratory bird species and spawning areas for fish species. As such, they support traditional livelihoods activities including reindeer husbandry, hunting and fishing, other cultural and recreational activities, and tourism. Less widely known is that intact wetlands store a large amount of global carbon. While they make up only about 3% of the Earth's land area, wetlands store an estimated 20% of the worlds terrestrial carbon – the largest regional store of carbon on the planet. Identifying and testing approaches for strengthening the engagement of local communities and other actors in the restoration and stewardship of Arctic wetlands ecosystems helps increase community resilience though shared engagement - and through the ecosystem service benefits derived from improving wetlands ecosystems' resilience.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Arctic Wetlands are thawing at increasing rates. Understanding how wetlands with permafrost thaw under climate warming is important to impacted communities and decision makers. That information can increase our capacity to predict the impacts of climate change in the Arctic. Wetlands have similar regional ecosystem characteristics across the Pan-Arctic, which includes parts of eight nations, there is no common language for how to classify wetlands. Lack of a common language across the Pan-Arctic to be able to discuss wetlands has both short and long-term implications.  For instances, regional and national governments lack a common classification system for arctic wetlands.  Eight Arctic nations, all have wetlands that are rapidly changing due to climate change or development. Unfortunately, each nation has its own classification system and typology.

Our research developed an approach for how two different wetland classifications for Arctic wetland systems could be merged to develop a common system. Building upon the foundation of a Russian and a Alaskan field sites and reports, we adapted two existing classification systems for rapidly assessing wetland conditions on the Coastal Plain (North Slope) of Alaska, USA, and the Coastal Plain of the Barents Sea in (Nenets Autonomous Okrug) Northern Russia. Synthesizing knowledge across natural sciences and classifications systems we intend to strengthen links between knowledge holders, policymakers and practitioners. We include in our draft report a refined land class typology and wetland indicators that could be used at a regional scale with desktop technology. Our research seeks to provide an approach for how differing wetland classifications can be adapted to enable decision and policy makers to communicate about Pan-Arctic wetlands.  Due to the war in Ukraine, the research team was delayed in finishing its report. The draft report is currently out for external review.

One aspect of the proposed research has to do with the geometry and topology of manifolds with scalar curvature lower bounds. Scalar curvature is the simplest curvature invariant of a Riemannian manifold. It represents the amount by which the volume of a small geodesic ball in a Riemannian manifold deviates from that of the standard ball in Euclidean space. Scalar curvature also arises in natural sciences. For instance, in general relativity, it is the Lagrangian density of the Einstein-Hilbert action. A natural and deep question in geometry, topology and mathematical physics is to understand the affect of scalar curvature conditions on a manifold. The other main area of investigation concerns minimal surfaces. Minimal surfaces arise as the mathematical model of a number of interfaces in nature. In mathematical model of general relativity, minimal surfaces occur as “apparent horizons” of black holes; soap films and capillary interfaces also provide examples of minimal surfaces. The PI will investigate the existence, regularity and topology of minimal surfaces. The two aspects proposed here are deeply connected via geometric variational theory.

The project concerns a range topics on differential geometry, geometric measure theory and partial differential equations. A main theme of the research in geometry will be a geometric comparison theorem for scalar curvature using Riemannian polyhedra, with the aim to define weak notions of positive scalar curvature on spaces with low regularity. The PI plans to continue his investigations into such a theorem for more general polytopes, especially simplexes of higher dimensions, and its connection to quasi-local mass in general relativity. The PI also plans to continue his investigation on the structure of moduli spaces of manifolds with positive scalar curvature and mean convex boundary, including studying its high homotopy groups, and the structure of moduli spaces defined by other related curvature conditions. In addition, the PI will study singular spaces with scalar curvature lower bounds, and understand when such a singular manifold arises as a certain limit of smooth manifolds with same assumptions. A central tool in the PI’s research is the theory of minimal varieties. The PI plans to understand the existence and regularity of minimal surfaces with free boundary and capillary boundary conditions in general Lipschitz domains, especially in locally convex polyhedral domains. He also plans to establish a general existence theory of capillary surfaces via a min-max construction.

award.projectOutComesReport:
During the award period, the PI has made progress in all the four directions of proposed research. Specifically, the PI has completely settled two proposed projects (project 7 and 12): the PI has proved that the space of Riemannian metrics with positive first eigenvalue of -\Delta + 1/4 R is path-connected, and used this fact to illustrate surprising flexibility phenomenon in the Riemannian Penrose inequality; the PI has also constructed capillary surfaces with any mean curvature and contact angle in any 3-manifolds with boundary. The PI has also made significant progress towards other projects.

New ideas and novel approaches have emerged in the course of investigations into these proposed projects, leading to other important discoveries in the area. For example, the PI has obtained classification results for manifolds with positive scalar curvature in 4 and 5 dimensions. The PI also proved the stable Bernstein theorem for minimal hypersurfaces in R^4 (and other 4 dimensional manifolds).  These results were built upon proposed projects in this award. 

In the past three years, a total of 12 research papers were written (all acknowledging the award) and submitted to journals. Although many of these papers are still under peer review, some of them have already been accepted to top journals (including Acta, CPAM, JDG, CMP and Geometry and Topology). Some of these papers relied on collaborations that were only made possible with the support with this award. 

The PI has put lots of efforts in disseminating the new findings. The PI has written a survey article on recent progress on the topology of manifolds of positive scalar curvature. This article has appeared in a book published by World Scientific. The PI has given a mini-course in Rutgers University, where most of the attendees were PhD students. The PI has also given various seminar and conference talks on related results, and organized several conferences and meetings. Given the opportunity, the PI will continue his efforts in publicizing the new developments in the area.

Although the PI has not got any PhD students, he has mentored several undergraduate and master students through several semester-long reading courses, on a wide range of topics including elliptic PDE, Riemannian geometry, and the Hawking-Penrose singularity theorem in general relativity. He has also participated in high school research days and math Olympiad in Princeton International School of Math and Science. In particular, the PI has proctored the International Math Olympiad in 2021, where the exam was carried out remotely due to Covid.

award.abstractText:
Wearables are poised to transform health and wellness through automation of cost-effective, objective, continuous, real-time, and remote health monitoring and interventions. These technologies utilize machine learning algorithms to detect important health events and to predict impending medical complications. Currently, however, machine learning algorithms for these systems are designed based on sensor data that are collected and labeled/annotated in controlled environments such as laboratory settings and clinics. This process of data collection, data annotation, and algorithm training has created great impediments to scalability of wearable systems because (1) collecting and labeling sufficiently large amounts of sensor data is a time consuming, labor-intensive, expensive, and often infeasible task; and (2) wearables are deployed in highly dynamic environments of the end-users whose physical, behavioral, social, and environmental context undergo consistent changes. Such changes result in drastic decline in the accuracy of the machine learning algorithms trained in controlled environments. Therefore, it is important to develop autonomously reconfigurable machine learning algorithms as wearable sensors, settings in which they are utilized, and their configuration changes. This project introduces computational autonomy as an overarching solution for training accurate machine learning algorithms, without human supervision, in highly dynamic, unpredictable, and uncontrolled settings. The successful conclusion of this work will enable future wearables to learn in-situ autonomously, operate in-the-wild reliably, and adapt to the changing context of their users automatically. 

This project will develop foundations of computational autonomy for wearable-based health monitoring and interventions through the following research objectives: (1) investigating methods of automatic and autonomous labeling of sensor data in a new setting based on labeled sensor data collected in a different setting by designing combinational optimization methodologies for cross-subject, cross-context, cross-platform, and cross-modality sensor data mapping; (2) developing non-parametric label refinement algorithms to reliably infer labels in a new setting based on uncertain and sporadic knowledge obtained from another, potentially unreliable and heterogeneous, sensor; (3) exploring methodologies for training machine learning algorithms that are robust to unknown parameters of a source sensor and adaptive to dynamically changing signal attributes of the new setting; and (4) validating the developed algorithms and tools through both in-lab experiments and in-the-wild user studies.

This interdisciplinary project will not only address the technical challenges in developing highly performant wearable systems but will also enable actual monitoring of a variety of populations. The work has major broader impacts on conducting high-precision chronic disease management and on the availability of wearable-based consumer applications. This has the potential to lead to the development of products around the concept of computational autonomy and its use in automation of health management, as well as, applications yet to be envisioned. The interdisciplinary nature of this work will provide unique opportunities for integrated research and education. To  this end, the educational objectives will focus on developing a new ambassador program to increase interest of underrepresented minority community college students in Science, Technology, Engineering and Math (STEM) careers in general and in computer science and engineering careers in particular, developing a novel patron program to improve retention of transferred underrepresented minority students through student and parental exposure to wearable-based health monitoring research, engaging undergraduate students in research, and establishment of an interdisciplinary research-based curriculum on computational autonomy. All the data produced over the course of this project, including design methodologies, software algorithms and tools, experimental data, publications, and curriculum will be made publicly available at http://epsl.eecs.wsu.edu/. The data will be stored and hosted on local servers and replicated on external public web servers.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This project developed robust machine learning algorithms for health monitoring and clinical decision making using wearable technology. On one hand, it is well-studied that machine learning models perform poorly when distribution of the test data is different from that of the training data. On the other hand, wearables are deployed in highly dynamic environments leading to consistent change in distribution of the sensor data. For example, when the devices are deployed in new users who did not participate in data collection for constructing the training dataset, the model performance declines dramatically. Similarly, the model performance degrades substantially when the previously trained model is used with new sensors or in new contexts different than those of the training data. To address these challenges, the project designed algorithms and tools for making wearable systems robust to distribution shift in the sensing data. The technical focus of the project was on developing transfer learning, semi-supervised learning, and robust and resource-efficient prediction techniques. The methods were developed and evaluated for activity recognition, image classification, stress detection, gait monitoring, and blood glucose forecasting. These detection and monitoring tasks are central to providing proactive health solutions for the prevention and management of many chronic diseases. The findings from this project are significant because they offer solutions for utilizing pervasive sensors in real-world settings to provide accurate health monitoring and intervention outside traditional confines of clinical environments.

award.abstractText:
This award is funded in whole or in part under the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 (Public Law 117-2).

This project brings together researchers from seven Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) and three National Research Laboratories (NRLs) to develop the AI-CyS research partnership at the intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) and cybersecurity. Cybersecurity vulnerabilities are growing at a scale and speed that strains human capacity to proactively address threats; developing AI and machine learning (ML) techniques to support prediction and detection capabilities is thus an important area of research. The HBCUs involved in AI-CyS either already have or are rapidly developing cybersecurity research capacity that would be further developed by increasing student and faculty involvement and training. To develop that potential, the project team will leverage its existing research activities and collaborations to deepen relationships with both other HBCUs and with the NRLs. The NRLs will provide additional research resources and mentoring through both regular remote meetings and on-site visits to the NRLs around projects of mutual interest, and opportunities for student internships and faculty visits at the NRLs. The team will also work to expand the impact of the partnership by (a) hosting an annual research conference to bring researchers together across the partners, (b) adding additional research projects, HBCUs and national lab partners with complementary research and educational interests to the existing partnership, and (c) developing cross-university curricula and mentoring programs to train HBCU students to be future research and workforce leaders in cybersecurity. Together, these efforts will advance research in cybersecurity, research capacity at the partner institutions, and research and educational opportunities for students at HBCUs, who are often members of underrepresented groups in computing. 

The partnership will be organized around five seed research projects chosen to maximize existing capacity and collaborations. The first will use reinforcement learning to improve target selection by current autonomous network mapping software agents. The second involves analyzing network traceroute data to better understand and work around limitations of its ability to map paths in order to better detect and classify network anomalies. The third focuses on developing, then defending against, adversarial attacks on computer vision algorithms in which attackers add visual patches to objects to fool object detection and classification tools. The fourth will analyze existing tools and algorithms for generating “deepfake” videos to develop methods to detect forged video in near real-time, with applications to surveillance and authentication tasks. The fifth will extend probabilistic sequential models to develop threat detectors at multiple levels of the network stack in the context of Internet of Things devices. Beyond these specific seed research projects, the project team will also analyze its activities to develop evidence-based best practices for research capacity-building efforts. These efforts will include developing mechanisms to expand current collaborations and foster resources, sharing expertise between HBCU members, and hosting an annual research conference that allows faculty and students from both current and potential partner HBCUs to showcase their cybersecurity research and create connections to other researchers and resources.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This project, HBCU Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity (AI-CyS) Research Partnership, was designed to strengthen research capacity at Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) while advancing knowledge in artificial intelligence (AI) and cybersecurity. The project focused on two key goals: building a collaborative research incubator among HBCUs and exploring how machine learning techniques can improve cybersecurity tasks such as intrusion detection and risk assessment.


Over the course of the award, the project successfully developed a collaborative research model that brought together faculty, students, and national research laboratory partners. Through workshops, research meetings, and mentoring activities, participating institutions strengthened their ability to conduct advanced research in computer science and cybersecurity. Faculty expanded their research networks, developed new collaborations, and increased their readiness to compete for external funding. The project also supported shared educational opportunities, allowing students from multiple institutions to engage in joint learning and research experiences.


A major outcome of the project was the training and development of students in high-demand areas such as AI, machine learning, and cybersecurity. Undergraduate students participated in hands-on research, working with real-world datasets and developing models to detect and analyze cyber threats. Many students contributed to research presentations and publications, gaining valuable experience that prepares them for graduate study and careers in technology fields. These efforts help build a more diverse and skilled workforce in areas critical to national security and economic competitiveness.


From a research perspective, the project explored a range of machine learning methods for improving cybersecurity performance. The team developed and tested models for identifying potential cyber threats, evaluating their effectiveness using standard performance measures. These efforts contribute to ongoing research on how AI can be used to strengthen digital security systems.


The project had broader impacts beyond research by promoting educational innovation and expanding access to advanced technology training. By integrating research into classroom experiences, students gained practical, real-world skills in addition to theoretical knowledge. The collaborative model also provided a framework that can be adopted by other institutions seeking to build research capacity and partnerships.


Overall, this project strengthened research infrastructure at HBCUs, advanced knowledge in AI and cybersecurity, and contributed to the development of a diverse and well-prepared STEM workforce. The partnerships, training opportunities, and research outcomes established through this effort provide a strong foundation for continued growth and innovation beyond the life of the award.

award.abstractText:
The coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic has exposed a critical set of vulnerabilities that have impacted community resilience in responding to escalating societal, economic, and behavioral issues. Unfortunately, there are no established solutions or proven models for us to depend on to tackle the complex challenges with significant uncertainties and unknowns. This project engages novel disciplinary perspectives to help address the devastating effects caused by COVID-19, i.e., leveraging the extracted information of experiences, ideas and support from positive-energy communities who are successfully navigating threats that can be transformed and transferred into actionable information to assist vulnerable communities to cope, progress and move forward. More specifically, by advancing artificial intelligence (AI) innovations, the goal of this project is to design and develop an AI-driven paradigm for collective and collaborative community resilience in responses to a variety of crises and exposed vulnerabilities in the COVID-19 era and beyond. With additional validation, this research will provide foundation to assist the federal and state governments, corporations, societal leaders to develop and implement strategies that will guide local and regional communities, and the nation into a successful new normal future.


This exploratory yet transformative high risk-high payoff work that involves radically different approaches will have three main research components. First, the research team will construct a novel attributed heterogeneous information network (AHIN) to comprehensively model the up-to-date multi-source pandemic related data for abstract representation. Second, to understand how users interact and how information are propagated within and cross-community in social media, the team will develop an innovative nonnegative matrix factorization regularized deep graph learning model for community detection in the AHIN by considering the heterogeneity of the network. Third, the team will propose an integrated adversarial disentangler to separate the distinct, informative factors of variations hidden in the milieu to learn post embeddings for emotion and topic analysis for community classification and framing, and thus to derive supportive and constructive information for community resilience improvement. The developed AI-driven paradigm in this project will provide in-depth insights and customized guidance that can help public health experts, social workers, law enforcement, economists, and policy makers in decision-making and also enable a conceptual framework for the development of resilient community engagement strategies in responses to a variety of crises created by COVID-19 and future natural or health-related disasters. The research will be beneficial to multidisciplinary areas, including data mining, machine learning, epidemiology, economics, social and behavioral sciences. The outcomes of this project will be made publicly accessible and broadly distributed. The project will integrate research with education through curriculum development, the participation of underrepresented groups, and student mentoring activities.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
The prolonged global pandemic has created a variety of crises and exposed vulnerabilities impacting community resilience; whereas there were no established solutions or proven models to tackle the complex challenges. To tackle this challenge, this project aims to design and develop an artificial intelligence (AI) driven paradigm for collective and collaborative community resilience in responses to various exposed vulnerabilities in the COVID-19 era and beyond. With the support of this grant, during the two-year project period, the team has had 28 publications (including 1 Ph.D. dissertation and 1 MS thesis) in recognized journals (e.g., IEEE TBD, IEEE TKDE, ACM TIST) and in proceedings of highly competitive conferences with acceptance rate about or less than 20% (e.g., WSDM'2023, ICDM'2023, SGIKDD'2022, AAAI'2022, SIAM SDM'2022, CIKM'2021-2022, NeurIPS'2021-2022, etc.). The research outcomes have been widely disseminated to research communities and practitioners through the publications, presentations, seminars, project website and demos, media presses, etc. Specially, with partial support of this project, the PI and her team have received the SIGKDD 2022 Best Paper Award Shortlist (Research Track), the prestigious ACM CIKM 2021 Best Paper Award (Full Paper Track), and the ACM CIKM 2021 Best Paper Award Runner Up (Applied Paper Track).

The proposed techniques and developed systems in this project have had significant societal impacts by improving community resilience in responses to a variety of crises and exposed vulnerabilities when facing health-related disasters like the pandemic.  Specifically, we have developed an AI-driven system (named α-Satellite) to estimate the spread of COVID-19 and predict near real-time risks at community levels for community mitigation, which has attracted positive media/public attention from WKYC, NPR, Fox8, WTAM, etc. As of June 19, 2023, the system has had 654,522 users with positive feedback on its utility of dynamic risk estimations. In addition, we have developed novel techniques to combat the increase of drug abuse and explosive growth of cyberattacks for community resilience improvement during the pandemic. Furthermore, we have also developed novel machine learning models to extract and transform the constructive ideas, experiences, and support to facilitate actionable information to improve community mental resilience in responses to the socio-economic impacts induced by the pandemic. In addition to the broader societal impacts, the proposed research will be beneficial to research and engineering communities when large-scale multi-source data is involved. The outcomes of this project (including open-source codes and large-scale datasets) have been made publicly accessible; and broadly distributed through publications, presentations, seminars, demonstrations, etc. The project has integrated research with education through curriculum development, K-12 outreach activities and engaging graduate and undergraduate students in research (e.g., four Ph.D. students and one master student have been recruited). The project has also increased the involvement of underrepresented groups, including minority and women (e.g., three female graduate students have involved in working on AI and data driven research related to this project).

award.abstractText:
The objective of this IRES project is to provide U.S. students with valuable research experience in the exploration of novel artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms for congenital heart diseases (CHDs) in Guangdong Provincial Cardiovascular Institute (GCI), located at Guangdong General Hospital (GGH). Located in Guangzhou, China, GGH is one of the biggest hospitals in China, and the GCI affiliated with it is constantly ranked top three in terms of cardiovascular disease research. The project will select three (3) graduate students and three (3) undergraduate students nation-wide each year and support them to visit GCI over a period of twelve (12) weeks to work with world-renowned researchers on cardiovascular medicine in an immersive setting, addressing some of the most critical and challenging problems through innovative AI algorithms that can benefit the large population suffering from CHD.

CHD is the leading cause of mortality from birth defects, which occurs 1 in every 110 births in the United States, and even more in developing countries. CHD comes with very large structure variations which makes it time-consuming and tedious to diagnose manually. In addition, the most common treatment for CHD is cardiac surgery, which is rather complex and is widely regarded as the jewel in the crown of surgery. Currently, only radiologists and surgeons with extensive experience in CHD can handle them confidently. The outcome of this project will potentially boost the effectiveness and efficiency of CHD treatments, and benefit the large population worldwide who suffer from CHD. The project will also enable U.S. students to conduct high-quality research on AI for CHD, in collaboration with their research mentors at GCI. Such experiences expose them to the international research community at a critical early stage in their careers. It is expected that through participating in this program, U.S. students will gain extensive experience on the research of deep learning with medical applications, on the international healthcare prospects, on Chinese culture, and on performing and collaborating in an international environment in general. The experience will also be shared to the broader community through personal social media as well as outreach events such as KidAI webinars for national K-12 students interested in AI. To ensure sustainability, the project will provide professional development support for the participating students. It will also focus on minorities and underrepresented groups.

The scientific objective of this IRES project is to explore innovative AI algorithms that can benefit the diagnosis, treatment planning and prognosis of CHDs. The proposed research, through the collaboration
between doctors at GCI and the IRES visiting students in the engineering fields, targets fundamental
issues in medical image processing and diagnosis of CHD that need to be addressed urgently. Although AI has shown great potential in general medicine, the large heart structure and great vessel connection variations in CHDs cannot be handled well by existing AI algorithms developed for other diseases. The proposed research will be the first to tackle this challenge and innovative algorithms are expected to be developed. It can also be anticipated that with the close interaction with leading research group on cardiovascular diseases in China, the breakthroughs made from these projects at GCI can have a direct impact on AI-based medicine research, clinic usage, and social welfare.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This International Research Experiences for Students (IRES) project provided U.S. undergraduate and graduate students with immersive research opportunities in artificial intelligence (AI) for congenital heart diseases (CHDs) at the Guangdong Provincial Cardiovascular Institute (GCI), located within Guangdong General Hospital. Over the lifetime of the award, cohorts of six U.S. students per year (three undergraduate and three graduate students) completed 12-week research residencies, working alongside leading cardiovascular physicians and researchers to address critical challenges in diagnosing and treating CHDs.

Congenital heart disease is the most common birth defect and a leading cause of infant mortality worldwide, affecting approximately 1 in 110 births in the United States and even more in many developing regions. CHDs are especially challenging because each patient’s heart may have unique structural variations. Diagnosing these complex conditions from medical images requires extensive expertise and years of training. Through this project, students developed novel AI algorithms to assist with image analysis, surgical planning, and prognosis prediction, helping to make diagnosis and treatment planning more accurate, efficient, and accessible.

Intellectual Merit

The core scientific achievement of this project was advancing AI methods tailored specifically for CHDs. Most existing AI tools in medicine are trained on relatively consistent disease patterns; however, CHDs present large structural variations in heart chambers and blood vessel connections. Students and mentors co-developed new deep learning approaches that better capture anatomical variability and improve segmentation and classification of cardiac images. These efforts addressed fundamental research challenges in medical image processing, including handling limited labeled data, improving model generalization across diverse patient anatomies, and integrating clinical knowledge into AI model design.

The project resulted in peer-reviewed publications, conference presentations, and new international research collaborations. Participating students gained hands-on experience in interdisciplinary research at the intersection of AI and cardiovascular medicine, preparing them for advanced study and careers in biomedical engineering, computer science, and medicine. Several students continued their research in related areas, contributing to sustained scientific impact beyond the duration of the award.

Broader Impacts

Beyond scientific advancement, the project delivered significant educational and societal benefits. By embedding U.S. students in a leading international medical research center, the program fostered global collaboration and cross-cultural understanding at an early stage in students’ careers. Participants reported increased confidence in conducting research in international settings and a deeper understanding of global healthcare challenges.

The project prioritized recruitment of students from underrepresented and minority groups in STEM. Through structured mentorship and professional development activities, including research seminars and cultural exchange events, the program supported students’ academic growth and long-term career development.

Overall, this IRES project strengthened international research partnerships, advanced innovative AI solutions for complex heart diseases, and trained a diverse cohort of young researchers equipped to tackle pressing global health challenges.

award.abstractText:
Groups appear in numerous areas of mathematics, chemistry and physics and have had tremendous impact as an organizational tool within mathematics. They often appear as the set of symmetries of a geometric object, for example, of 3-dimensional space, a molecule or a crystal. Oftentimes, the set of symmetries themselves, i.e., the group, has a natural topological structure. That is, one can speak of one symmetry being close to another, as in the case of two rotations of 3-dimensional space being close if they differ by a small angle. These latter groups are called topological transformation groups and are trivially related to geometry via the geometric object of which they are the set of symmetries. However, other topological groups are not so easily viewed as coming from geometry. This is, for example, the case for the systems of solutions to many differential equations which form a group under addition called a Banach space. However, one of the principal ideas of the present project is that all topological groups have natural intrinsic geometric structure which is defined jointly by their topological and algebraic structure. Moreover, this geometric structure can in many cases provide significant insight into the structure of the group by blotting out finer details that obscure the global or large scale properties of the group.

The primary aim of this project is to investigate the coarse geometry of topological and, in particular, Polish groups. In earlier research, the PI has established and investigated a natural coarse structure that every topological group is equipped with and which coincides with that traditionally studied on finitely generated or locally compact groups, Banach spaces or even homeomorphism groups of compact manifolds. Particularly interesting subclasses to be studied are the Polish groups of bounded geometry for which the geometric structure theory is well-advanced. Several interesting questions on the extent of this class of groups remain open, for example, whether every Polish group of bounded geometry is coarsely equivalent to a locally compact group. The research program is by nature interdisciplinary. While its origins lie in descriptive set theory, the main examples of groups to be studied arise in various disciplines of mathematics, including functional analysis, logic, and geometric and differential topology.

award.projectOutComesReport:
The concept of a group originates in the work of E. Galois as the collection of symmetries of solutions to polynomial equations. However, the concept was subsequently found to have numerous uses beyond polynomials, for example, by modeling more general versions of number and coordinate systems. Furthermore, it has applications far from mathematics, most notably in chemistry, in the classification of crystals, and in physics, as the set of symmetries of various physical systems. The present award aimed to support foundational research into this and neighbouring topics from the point of view of mathematical logic and set theory, specifically concerning large topological groups arising as the symmetries of discrete mathematical structures.

One of the major outcomes of the award concerns so called amenable groups. Whereas it has been well-known that amenable groups allow for a good concept of integration that permits one to integrate bounded real valued functions defined on the groups or their phase spaces, the PI introduced tools from the theory of optimal transport and functional analysis to show how this may be done every for potentially unbounded functions, leading to unexpected geometric consequences for these groups.

A second study done in collaboration with the PI’s postdoc J. Zomback concerns the geometric structure of groups. A major theme of mathematics over the past half a century has been geometric group theory, namely the study of groups as geometric objects. This ties together numerous branches of mathematics and begins with the fundamental observation that, if a group is generated by a finite set of elements, then it is possible to measure the distance between arbitrary elements of the group. However, this distance is in general only well-defined up to some bounded distortion and thus only provides a somewhat fuzzy picture of the group. However, in this study, a new class of group is isolated, the so called asymptotically spherical ones, that has the property that distances between elements are no longer defined up to a bounded distortion, but where large distances are in fact inherently determined up to a fixed multiplicative factor. This significantly removes some of the fuzziness of the picture when passing to larger scales. Furthermore, numerous and prevalent examples of such groups are given, especially among larger topological groups.


A third project pursued in collaboration with A. Aviles, M. Taylor and P. Tradacete concerns coordinate systems in Banach lattices. The latter can be viewed as the general model for systems of real valued functions equipped with the usual algebraic operations of addition of functions and rescaling. Furthermore, the lattice has an order corresponding to the pointwise majorisation of functions. Banach lattices have a well-understood concept of coordinate system originating from Banach spaces, which unfortunately squares very poorly with the order structure, in the sense that the coordinate expansion of a function need not converge in order. Thus, it is imperative to have other concepts of coordinate systems that recuperate the full order structure. This has been done in several works by other authors, which introduce three primary notions of order, uniform and norm bases. However, the interrelationship between these notions was very much undetermined. In the above mentioned study, the PI and coauthors settle this completely using additional tools from mathematical logic and set theory, including infinite games of perfect information, forcing and large cardinal axioms. In particular, it is shown that all order bases are uniform and, in turn, that uniform bases are norm bases. It remains an open problem to decide if the use of additional axioms is needed in this presumably innocuous are of mathematics.

This award is funded in whole or in part under the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 (Public Law 117-2).

This project brings together researchers from seven Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) and three National Research Laboratories (NRLs) to develop the AI-CyS research partnership at the intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) and cybersecurity. Cybersecurity vulnerabilities are growing at a scale and speed that strains human capacity to proactively address threats; developing AI and machine learning (ML) techniques to support prediction and detection capabilities is thus an important area of research. The HBCUs involved in AI-CyS either already have or are rapidly developing cybersecurity research capacity that would be further developed by increasing student and faculty involvement and training. To develop that potential, the project team will leverage its existing research activities and collaborations to deepen relationships with both other HBCUs and with the NRLs. The NRLs will provide additional research resources and mentoring through both regular remote meetings and on-site visits to the NRLs around projects of mutual interest, and opportunities for student internships and faculty visits at the NRLs. The team will also work to expand the impact of the partnership by (a) hosting an annual research conference to bring researchers together across the partners, (b) adding additional research projects, HBCUs and national lab partners with complementary research and educational interests to the existing partnership, and (c) developing cross-university curricula and mentoring programs to train HBCU students to be future research and workforce leaders in cybersecurity. Together, these efforts will advance research in cybersecurity, research capacity at the partner institutions, and research and educational opportunities for students at HBCUs, who are often members of underrepresented groups in computing. 

The partnership will be organized around five seed research projects chosen to maximize existing capacity and collaborations. The first will use reinforcement learning to improve target selection by current autonomous network mapping software agents. The second involves analyzing network traceroute data to better understand and work around limitations of its ability to map paths in order to better detect and classify network anomalies. The third focuses on developing, then defending against, adversarial attacks on computer vision algorithms in which attackers add visual patches to objects to fool object detection and classification tools. The fourth will analyze existing tools and algorithms for generating “deepfake” videos to develop methods to detect forged video in near real-time, with applications to surveillance and authentication tasks. The fifth will extend probabilistic sequential models to develop threat detectors at multiple levels of the network stack in the context of Internet of Things devices. Beyond these specific seed research projects, the project team will also analyze its activities to develop evidence-based best practices for research capacity-building efforts. These efforts will include developing mechanisms to expand current collaborations and foster resources, sharing expertise between HBCU members, and hosting an annual research conference that allows faculty and students from both current and potential partner HBCUs to showcase their cybersecurity research and create connections to other researchers and resources.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This project focused on strengthening artificial intelligence and cybersecurity research at the University of the District of Columbia (UDC) in collaboration with other Historically Black Colleges and Universities. The goal was to enhance research in machine learning for cybersecurity, but also to expand research opportunities for students.

Faculty and students worked together on several cybersecurity challenges. These included improving how network intrusions are detected using reinforcement learning, studying ways to identify manipulated or "deepfake" images and videos, and examining how cyber-physical systems can remain secure under attack. The research contributed to a better understanding of how machine learning can be applied to real cybersecurity problems. Findings were shared through peer-reviewed conference publications and national and international presentations.

A central outcome of the project was student development. Undergraduate and graduate students participated directly in research activities, gaining hands-on experience in coding, data analysis, simulation, and model development. They presented their work at conferences, responded to questions from research audiences, and strengthened both their technical knowledge and communication skills. These experiences helped prepare them for graduate study and careers in cybersecurity, AI,  and related fields.

The project also contributed to long-term institutional growth. Faculty expanded their expertise in cybersecurity and machine learning, and computational research environments were developed to support deep learning and cyber-physical system simulations. These resources continue to support research and mentoring beyond the life of the award.

Overall, the project advanced research in machine learning-based cybersecurity while expanding research capacity at a minority-serving institution and helping develop the next generation of cybersecurity professionals.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This NSF-supported project focused on strengthening undergraduate research capacity in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and computer networking at Mississippi Valley State University (MVSU), with collaboration across HBCU partners. The project addressed two central goals: (1) building a collaborative research environment to enhance Computer and Information Science and Engineering (CISE) capacity, and (2) engaging students and faculty in research on machine learning methods for cybersecurity applications, including network analysis and intrusion-related data interpretation.

Throughout the life of the award, the project successfully created structured opportunities for undergraduate students to participate in faculty-mentored research experiences. Students engaged in the exploration of network measurement data, particularly traceroute analysis, to improve understanding of computer network behavior. This work helped students learn how data science and machine learning concepts can be applied to real-world cybersecurity and networking problems. Although an external laboratory collaboration was initially planned, the project adapted to faculty-led research at MVSU, ensuring continuity and sustained student engagement.

A major outcome of the project was the development of student research skills and increased exposure to cybersecurity and artificial intelligence concepts. Students gained experience in literature review, data analysis, technical problem solving, and scientific communication. Faculty mentorship played a key role in guiding students through research processes and strengthening their academic preparation for graduate study and STEM careers.

The project also contributed significantly to broader impacts by increasing participation of underrepresented students in computing research. Students and faculty presented their work at multiple venues, including the AI-CyS Expo in conjunction with the ADMI Symposium, the Mississippi Academy of Sciences Annual Meeting, and Mississippi Valley State University Research Day. These dissemination activities provided opportunities for participants to share findings with academic peers, industry professionals, and the broader scientific community, while also receiving valuable feedback to improve their work.

In addition to student development, the project strengthened institutional research capacity within the Computer Science program at MVSU. Faculty enhanced their ability to mentor undergraduate researchers and integrate research experiences into academic training. The project also fostered collaboration among HBCU institutions and supported the development of a sustainable research culture focused on cybersecurity and artificial intelligence.

Overall, the project contributed to both intellectual merit and broader impacts by advancing knowledge in cybersecurity and network analysis while also expanding opportunities for undergraduate research, workforce development, and participation in computing fields. The experience helped prepare students for future careers and graduate education in cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and related STEM disciplines, thereby contributing to a stronger and more diverse computing workforce.

award.abstractText:
The research in this project concerns a branch of mathematical logic called model theory, which studies mathematical structures at the linguistic level, and classifies structures according the complexity of their behavior with respect to a fixed choice of mathematical language. The tools for testing whether a mathematical structures is suitable for classification are various hypotheses called "dividing lines", which forbid some fixed pattern in the behavior of a structure. A main focus of this project is one such dividing line called VC-dimension, which originated in machine learning, and uses ideas from graph theory to measure randomness in mathematical objects. In model theory, this notion emerged in the study of so-called "NIP theories". Conant will apply this model theoretic framework to questions in group theory, from both the discrete and topological perspectives, and also in the newer field of arithmetic combinatorics, which is a fusion of algebra, analysis, and discrete math. 

A large part of past research in model theory has focused on structures which exhibit tameness at the global level, in the sense that every definable relation in the structure omits a combinatorial configuration of some fixed type. This research focuses on the local level, in which one analyzes a single tame relation inside an otherwise complicated structure. A major aim is to develop an algebraic theory of NIP formulas in arbitrary groups, which continues prior research of Conant and Pillay in the case of pseudofinite groups. A second aim is to extend this work on pseudofinite groups outside of the NIP environment. This setting is suitable for applications to arithmetic combinatorics in finite groups, for example previous research of Conant, Pillay, and Terry on tame arithmetic regularity. In the proposed research, Conant will use Lie theory and representation theory to develop arithmetic regularity in the pseudofinite setting without extra tameness assumptions. The goal is to give a model theoretic account of arithmetic regularity results of Green and Tao, and extend these results to non-commutative groups.

award.projectOutComesReport:
The research outcomes of this award are based in the field of model theory, which is a branch of mathematical logic. A major research focus was on interaction between model theory and a branch of discrete mathematics called additive combinatorics. When taken at face value, this latter area appears quite far from model theory in motivation, tools, and objectives. However, there is a deep connection between these two fields, which exploits the power of model theory to make analytic and "continuous" tools effective in a discrete setting. This connection has its roots in celebrated work of Ehud Hrushovski from 2009 on the structure of "approximate groups", although it took nearly ten more years to develop an active research community centered on the synergy between these previously disconnected areas of mathematics. The catalyst for this change was research of Conant (PI), Pillay, Terry, and Wolf, which connected the combinatorial notion of "arithmetic regularity" with ideas from mathematical logic on abstract notions of "tameness" for mathematical structures. 
Over the course of this award, several new developments and breakthroughs were obtained. On the more technical side related to objectives in additive combinatorics, this includes a full quantitative proof of the "stable arithmetic regularity" lemma with explicit polynomial bounds and a structure theorem for approximate subgroups of bounded VC-dimension in noncommutative groups. On the broader side, the research done during this project also uncovered several mistakes and gaps in existing mathematics literature on model-theoretic "neostability theory". Consequently, Conant and coauthors have produced a series of research papers which clarify and shore up this important area, while also extending the relevant tools (namely, probability measures on "definable sets") well beyond the limits of what was previously known. In the final stages of the project, Conant and coauthors have widened the perspective of model theory on additive combinatorics by studying arithmetic regularity in the more analytic setting of real-valued functions on groups. This has resulted in a new and powerful approach toward the ideas of Hrushovski's original work from 2009, including applications to additive combinatorics which unify the model-theoretic foundation for several results in existing literature. This also serves as a stepping stone from this award to future research. 
This award has also contributed to building a strong and lasting community connection between two major mathematical fields. For example, Conant co-organized a high profile international workshop at the University of Cambridge in 2022, which was attended by a diverse audience ranging from beginning graduate students to two Fields medalists. The project also supported summer stipends for two undergraduate students in The Ohio State University program Research Opportunities in Mathematics for Underrepresented Students. Finally, the project funds were used to support graduate level education  through Conant's website "The Map of the Universe", which is a well-established online reference for model theory used by students and researchers worldwide.

award.abstractText:
This project will focus on the interaction between two different aspects of mathematical logic: categorical logic and descriptive set theory.  Broadly speaking, mathematical logic is the formal study of mathematical language and its meaning.  For example, the assertion "between every two numbers, there is a third" changes meaning depending on which ambient universe of "numbers" (integers, fractions, etc.) one is referring to.  Categorical logic provides tools for constructing a "universal abstract universe" in which the interpretation of mathematical statements captures their meanings in all possible "real" universes at once.  Descriptive set theory provides tools for classifying all such possible "real" universes, or in certain cases, proving that no such classification exists.  Recent work has pointed toward a deep connection between these two historically disparate subfields of logic, and this project aims to further develop this connection.

In this project the PI studies categorical logic and descriptive set theory as dual "syntactic" and "semantic" representations of infinitary propositional and first-order logic.  In the propositional setting, a long line of work points to locale theory ("point-free topology") as an uncountable generalization of classical descriptive set theory in Polish and standard Borel spaces, and this project aims to extend this analogy by developing localic counterparts of more advanced classical techniques, such as projective sets, effective descriptive set theory, and forcing.  In the first-order setting, recent work by the PI has shown that the Joyal-Tierney representation theorem for toposes yields a duality between theories in infinitary first-order logic and their standard Borel groupoids of countable models.  This project aims to extend this duality to continuous logic for metric structures, which will involve first developing the foundations for a metric analog of topos theory.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This project studied the interaction between two different aspects of mathematical logic: categorical logic and descriptive set theory.  Broadly speaking, mathematical logic is the formal study of mathematical language and its meaning.  For example, the assertion "between every two numbers, there is a third" changes meaning depending on which ambient universe of "numbers" (integers, fractions, etc.) one is referring to.  Categorical logic provides tools for constructing a "universal abstract universe" in which the interpretation of mathematical statements captures their meanings in all possible "real" universes at once.  Descriptive set theory provides tools for classifying all such possible "real" universes, or in certain cases, proving that no such classification exists.  Recent work has pointed toward a deep connection between these two historically disparate subfields of logic, and this project contributed to the further development of this connection and its applications.

Specific results obtained as part of this project, that have been published or submitted for publication, include the following:

(1) A new proof of the Becker–Kechris theorem on topological realizations of Polish group actions, using methods inspired by point-free topology, as well as several generalizations of the theorem, such as to groupoid actions via homeomorphisms on topological bundles.

(2) An application of the same machinery to develop a theory of abstract equivalence relations and groupoids equipped with "componentwise topologies", that are modeled on such topologies induced by a Polish group action, but without reference to the action itself.

(3) A precise correspondence (namely, an equivalence of categories) between the global structure of all locally countable Borel combinatorial problems on equivalence relations and groupoids, and certain classes of countable first-order structures axiomatizable in infinitary logic.

(4) An application of Stone duality and related dualities (namely, for median graphs/algebras) to solve a problem in locally countable Borel combinatorics, showing that every Borel graph whose large-scale structure is "tree-like" can be definably turned into a tree.

(5) An axiomatic theory of topological spaces "parametrizing" countable structures, generalizing well-known classical instances (structures on the natural numbers, marked groups), that is based on the theory of groupoid representations for Grothendieck toposes.

This project supported mentorship of 3 REU students and 1 Master's student, that produced several joint papers including (3) above.

In addition, this project supported travel to several conferences, seminars, and research visits with collaborators, which provided opportunites for dissemination of research results and exchange of ideas with the mathematical community.

award.abstractText:
As the Internet becomes increasingly ubiquitous, it offers a low-risk harbor for cybercrime -- illegal activities such as hacking and online scams. Cybercrime is increasingly enabled by an online underground ecosystem, within which are anonymous forums and so-called dark web platforms for cybercriminals to exchange knowledge and trade in illicit products and services. To better protect the trust of legitimate institutions and users within cyberspace, and to disrupt or mitigate the harm of illegal markets, there is an urgent need to gain deep insights into the online underground ecosystem and understand its intricate relationships. The goal of this project is to design and develop an integrated computational framework for in-depth investigation of the online underground ecosystem and thus to help secure cyberspace by producing data-driven interventions of cybercrimes. 

The research will have three main parts. First, the research team will design methods and develop algorithmic and scalable techniques to automate the analysis of online underground markets. Second, the team will develop a novel framework for cross-market user identification and profiling. Third, the team will design an innovative model and propose algorithms for structural analysis of cybercriminal social networks to gain deep insights into the organization and operation of cybercriminals in the ecosystem. The broader impacts of this work include benefits to scientific communities and society as a whole by developing interventions into online crime to secure cyberspace for its users. The establishment of a cybersecurity lab through this project will enhance education and workforce training in cybersecurity. The project integrates research with education through curriculum development, the participation of underrepresented groups, and student mentoring activities for a newly-established cybersecurity degree program.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Cybercrimes have become increasingly dependent on the online underground ecosystem which has evolved into a complex and decentralized system resistant to infiltration. As more and more social activities have moved online, society’s overwhelming reliance on complex cyberspace makes its security more important than ever. To protect legitimate users in cyberspace against evolving cyber threats, this CAREER project aims to design and develop an integrated framework (algorithms, scalable techniques) for in-depth investigation of the online underground ecosystem and thus to help secure cyberspace by producing data-driven interventions of cybercrimes. The work in this project includes three key research components: (1) design methods and develop an effective model to automate the analysis of online underground markets in the forms such as social media platforms, underground forums and dark webs; (2) design methods and develop a novel framework for cross-market user identification and profiling; and (3) design an innovative model and propose algorithms for structural analysis of cybercriminal social network to gain deep insights into the organization and operation of cybercriminals in the ecosystem. With the support of this grant, during the project period, the PI and her team have had 66 publications in recognized journals (e.g., ACM TIST, ACM TKDD, IEEE TBD, Decision Support Systems, Information & Management, TMLR) and in proceedings of highly competitive conferences with acceptance rate about or less than 20% (e.g., AAAI'2021-2023 & 2025, NDSS'2025, ACM IUI'2025, UAI'2024, WWW'2019, 2021 & 2023-2024, ICLR'2023-2024, ICML'2023-2024, NeurIPS'2021-2023, ICDM'2023, CIKM'2021-2023, WSDM'2023, SIGKDD'2022, SDM'2022, IJCAI'2019 & 2022, ACSAC'2019-2020, etc.). The project also resulted in 5 Ph.D. dissertations and 1 Master Thesis. The research outcomes have been widely disseminated to research communities and practitioners through the publications, presentations, seminars, project website and demos, media presses, etc. Especially, with partial support of this project, the PI has received the prestigious IJCAI Early Career Spotlight (2019), the AICS 2019 Challenge Problem Winner, the ACM CIKM 2021 Best Paper Runner Up (Applied Track), WWW 2021 Best Paper Award Shortlist, SIGKDD 2022 Best Paper Award Shortlist, and the AAAI-DCAA 2023 Best Paper Runner-Up.

By probing into the evolving online underground forums, the proposed techniques and integrated framework developed in this project will help law enforcement and security defenders identify threats driven by the online underground ecosystem, produce effective countermeasures to disrupt underground market operations, and predict evolving trajectories of cybercrimes. Specifically, by engaging with the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), PI Ye's extensive work on combating online opioid trafficking received the award-winning "What Would You Fight For (WWYFF)?" series, which was aired on NBC to millions of audiences to raise awareness of this critical societal issue on October 28, 2023 in the "Red Robbin Week"; due to the significant societal impact, it was re-aired on NBC-Peacock and the stadium during the Notre Dame football game on September 28, 2024. In addition to the broader societal impact, the proposed research in this project will be beneficial to researchers and practitioners in multidisciplinary areas. The techniques developed in this project can be used in various security domains (e.g., spammer detection, combat against mis/disinformation) and applicable in different learning tasks in AI/data science (e.g., classification, network/graph embedding). Moreover, this project will also generate interdisciplinary research impacts - i.e., developing innovative links between AI/data science and cybersecurity to gain deep insights into the online underground ecosystem is likely to have increasingly significant impacts across different disciplines. The innovations in AI and data science that are advanced in this project will reshape the landscape of research combating evolving cybercrimes. The outcomes of this project (including open-source code and benchmark datasets) have been made publicly accessible; and broadly distributed through publications, presentations, seminars, demonstrations, etc. The project has integrated research with education through novel curriculum development, engaging postdoc, graduate and undergraduate students in research. Through various K-12 and community outreach activities, this project has also broadened participation in computing especially in the areas of AI, data science, and cybersecurity.
