award.projectOutComesReport:
This project addressed several key questions on the complexity of semi-definite and polynomial optimization (SDO and PO, respectively) within the broader context of real algebraic geometry. Real algebraic geometry is the study of semi-algebraic sets and functions described by polynomial equations and inequalities, and it has widespread applications in computer sciences, applied mathematics, and optimization. Both SDO and PO are of significant theoretical and practical importance, with applications spanning theoretical computer sciences, control theory, quantum information sciences, and statistics. However, they are provably hard, in the languages of arithmetic and bit complexity. Thanks to real algebra, PO can be “numerically” solved using a sequence of SDO problems. Although these SDO sub-problems are “very efficiently” solvable using interior point methods (IPM), they may become intractable, even approximately. This poor performance can be linked to analytic or algebro-geometric features of the so-called central path, a fundamental concept in IPMs.

In this project, we leveraged the semi-algebraic structures inherent in the problem and applied techniques from real algebraic geometry and topology to achieve three main objectives: 1) new complexity measures -- including the degree and worst-case convergence rate of the central path, the Lojasiewicz exponent, error bounds, and Betti numbers -- to provide a finer classification of computational complexity for SDO and PO; 2) efficient numerical and symbolic algorithms to compute these complexity measures, and 3) quantitative bounds on the complexity measures. By utilizing algorithmic real algebraic geometry, we developed symbolic algorithms to describe the central path as a Puiseux series, and we proved bounds on its degree and convergence rate. The key outcome of this work, however, is an analytic reparametrization of the central path, that retrieves higher-order derivatives of the central path at the limit point. This analytic reparametrization paves the way for significant algorithmic improvements in the area of IPMs, leading to a higher-order IPM for general SDO problems that converges super-linearly fast.

The notion of an error bound is crucial in the computational complexity of PO, particularly because the central path is no longer well-defined. Error bounds measure proximity of an algorithm iterates to a set, providing insights into the convergence behavior of the algorithm. By leveraging bounds on the effective quantifier elimination, we proved a tight upper bound for the Lojasiewicz inequality (which includes error bounds as special cases) in the semi-algebraic category. Our bound not only improves the best existing bound on the Lojasiewicz exponent, but it also has the key advantage of being independent of the cardinality of the descriptions of the given semi-algebraic set and functions. This distinct feature enables tighter error bounds for polynomial and nonlinear semi-definite systems, leading to more accurate convergence rates for sums of squares and gradient projection techniques for PO.

The topological complexity of semi-algebraic sets has been a very active area of research in real algebraic geometry. It is well-known that the topological complexity reflects the hardness of checking the emptiness of a semi-algebraic set. In this project, we measured computational complexity of PO in terms of the Betti numbers of the feasible set. The main intuition is the poor performance of iterative algorithms on feasible sets with non-trivial topology (which unlike SDO, it could be very complicated for PO). By applying techniques from the stratified Morse theory and real algebraic geometry, we proved upper bounds on the sum of Betti numbers in terms of the critical points of the objective function, thus extending the classical Morse inequalities to semi-algebraic sets.

award.abstractText:
In settings from shipping to sailing to surgery, thousands of different types of knots are used every day, each requiring a specific amount of force to tighten. This force depends on the material properties, friction, and the topology of the knot. A knot typically also has a load-bearing capacity; force beyond this level causes the knot to be undone, and excessive force may result in material failure in the knot. Moreover, some knots hold tight without any external force while others easily get untangled. In other words, the knots can store energy in the material. This concept is called a topological battery with implications in nanometer-sized knots in DNA to macroscopic knots in structural engineering. This award supports research to understand the fundamental science of knots. The work will develop modeling and computational methods for the analysis of the mechanics of knots and tangles. In parallel, it will formulate experimental techniques to systematically study this mechanics. The research will be complemented by developing teaching tools (videos, notes, and demonstrations) for undergraduate and graduate courses. The computational software will also be made publicly available. 

The research objective of this project is to quantify the mechanical response of knots tied in elastic rods. The project will employ (1) fast numerical simulations inspired by computer graphics, (2) innovative materials with customizable friction, and (3) autonomous robotic experiments to untangle the mechanics of knots. Even in the case of the most basic type of knots (overhand knots), the force required to tie the knot depends on an intricate interplay of (1) elasticity, (2) friction, and (3) topology. Interestingly, the overhand knot may undergo a snap-through buckling instability beyond a critical amount of pull. Such instability in a basic knot points to the richness of the mechanical behavior of knots. After developing simulation and experimental tools, the mechanical response and instabilities of a few common knots, e.g. overhand and shoelace knots, will be investigated. Exploiting the computational speed of the simulation tool and autonomy of robotic experiments, the mechanical response of several types of knots will be quantified to build a library of their mechanics. This data will be used to rationalize the variation of a knot’s mechanical response as a function of the topological, material, and frictional parameters. Similar to the periodic table of elements, a mechanics-based classification scheme of knots will be formulated, where the knots will be grouped into various classes, such as, friction-dominated knots, bending-dominated knots, and others.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Knots are a familiar part of everyday life, from tying shoes and securing loads to surgical sutures and fishing lines. Despite their widespread use, the physical principles that govern how knots tighten, resist slipping, and ultimately fail have remained poorly understood. This National Science Foundation–supported project addressed this long-standing gap by uncovering the fundamental mechanics of knots and tangles formed in elastic rods, while also developing new methods for controlling friction and particle transport relevant to modern manufacturing and materials processing.

Intellectual Merit

Over the full duration of the award, this collaborative research established a comprehensive framework combining experiments, computer simulations, and theory to understand how elasticity, friction, and geometry interact in knotted structures. The team developed and validated numerical simulation tools capable of accurately modeling contact and friction between flexible rods—an essential challenge in understanding knots, tangles, and other deformable structures.

Through systematic experiments and simulations, the project revealed how different knot designs behave when tightened. For example, studies of commonly used knots showed that some configurations rely on friction-dominated locking to prevent slipping, while others distribute forces more evenly due to their geometric symmetry. These findings provide new, mechanics-based guidelines for selecting knot types in applications where safety, reliability, and material preservation are critical, such as surgery, engineering fasteners, and soft robotic systems.

Beyond knot mechanics, the project made major advances in understanding how microscopic particles can be transferred from complex liquid mixtures onto solid surfaces for controlling surface morphology. Such particle transfer processes are central to manufacturing techniques ranging from coatings to powder-based fabrication. The research established quantitative links between stirring intensity, fluid behavior, particle clustering, and transfer efficiency in non-colloidal mixtures. New performance metrics were introduced to distinguish between uniform particle coverage and clustered deposition, enabling better prediction and control of these processes. These discoveries challenge existing assumptions in the field and expand fundamental knowledge of particle–fluid–surface interactions.

The project resulted in numerous peer-reviewed journal articles, conference publications, and publicly available simulation tools, contributing lasting resources to the scientific community.

Broader Impacts

This research produced significant educational, workforce, and societal benefits. Multiple graduate and undergraduate students were trained in experimental mechanics, computational modeling, data analysis, and scientific writing. Students supported by the project completed master’s and progressed into Ph.D. programs, and transitioned into research careers in academia and industry. Undergraduate researchers gained hands-on experience that inspired independent projects and long-term engagement in science and engineering.

Project outcomes were directly incorporated into education. Tools and methods developed during the research were integrated into a newly developed Digital Manufacturing course, reaching both undergraduate and graduate students and strengthening training in advanced manufacturing and data-driven analysis.

The project also enhanced research infrastructure. A standardized continuous dip-coating system developed under the award is now used as a shared laboratory resource for new NSF-funded biomanufacturing research. In addition, a machine-learning–based particle detection tool created through this work is being applied beyond the original project, including agricultural engineering research and scalable microalgae cultivation systems aimed at improving productivity and sustainability.

Technology transfer was another key outcome. The particle transfer and characterization methods developed during the project contributed directly to patent applications for high-throughput particle sorting and advanced particle analysis techniques, demonstrating clear potential for real-world impact in manufacturing and materials processing.

Finally, the project contributed to public engagement and STEM outreach. A high school student participated in summer research activities, gaining early exposure to engineering research and computational tools, helping broaden participation in science and engineering.

Overall Impact

By combining fundamental science with practical applications, this project advanced understanding of knot mechanics and particle transfer while delivering lasting benefits to education, infrastructure, and technology development. The outcomes continue to influence fields ranging from mechanics and robotics to manufacturing, agriculture, and biomanufacturing, exemplifying the NSF mission to support research that benefits both science and society.

award.abstractText:
Bees are vitally important to agriculture, food security, and the preservation of natural ecosystems due to their pollination services. Over 85% of the 325,000 flowering plant species on the planet depend on animal pollination and the vast majority is carried out by bees. In the U.S.A. alone bees are responsible for the commercial production of 130 crop plants, generating over $11 billion in annual revenue. The value of bees to nature and human well-being is abundantly clear. The partnership between bees and flowering plants formed over 100 million years ago, and since that time, bees have radiated globally into an astounding 20,000+ different species, many of which are specialist pollinators of particular plant species or families. The study of bee biodiversity is urgently needed because there is growing evidence that some bee species are in decline and baseline knowledge of bee diversity, distribution, and family relationships is incomplete. The Bees of the World project has the potential to significantly improve knowledge of bee biodiversity and to establish a guide to interpret key traits of bees, such as their host-plant associations. By utilizing recent advances in DNA sequencing technology, a comprehensive tree-of-life for bees will be generated for the first time, providing a framework from which to study bee diversity and their relationships with plants. To disseminate results and general bee knowledge, the project will engage in multiple outreach efforts with professional and non-professional audiences. Activities include creation of a virtual bee course, teaching of a molecular methods workshop, and, in collaboration with the Natural History Museum of Utah, development of exhibits and youth education activities focused on pollinators.

The project will use cutting edge molecular and analytical methods and engage a global network of collaborators to assemble a comprehensive phylogenomic dataset for bees. The project aims are to: (1) resolve remaining uncertainties in higher-level bee phylogeny and classification, (2) incorporate fossils to reconstruct the global biogeographic history of bees, revealing the origin and spread of bee diversity over time, and (3) analyze patterns of host-plant use across bees and for targeted clades at lower taxonomic levels, revealing how host-plant specialization has evolved and impacted rates of diversification in bees. To resolve the phylogeny of bees with improved confidence, the research team will use next-generation DNA sequencing approaches and novel laboratory methods to sequence bee species from across the globe. The project will generate low coverage genomes for most bee genera and ultraconserved element (UCE) data for over 3,000 species, filling in sampling gaps. The resulting bee phylogeny will serve as a framework to study bee classification, biogeography, and host-plant evolution. Comprehensive databases of bee fossil, distribution, and host-plant information will be created and made available to other researchers. Combining results from each component of the project will provide a comprehensive understanding of how bees have diversified and dispersed over time and how their partnership with plants has shaped their evolutionary trajectory.

award.projectOutComesReport:
The interaction between bees and flowering plants represents one of the most important co-evolutionary stories on earth. The origin of bees (between 110 and 130 my ago) coincides with a rapid increase in angiosperm diversification and the appearance of the largest and most species rich clade of flowering plants – the eudicots. Flowering plants, with over 350,000 described species, are currently the dominant group of plants in all terrestrial habitats and their dominance is due, at least in part, to their partnership with mobile pollinators – primarily insects and most importantly bees. Bees provide angiosperms plants with pollination services and plants, in return, provide bees with food for building nests, attracting mates, and rearing offspring. One key to unraveling how the bee-angiosperm partnership evolved over time is to reconstruct both the temporal and spatial patterns of bee diversification, biogeography, and host-plant use.

Our research focused on the bee tribe Emphorini, a group of 97 exclusively Western Hemisphere bee species ranging from Canada to the southern tip of South America. Emphorines are unique among bees in that they have remarkably narrow host-plant preferences, with most species restricting pollen collecting to a small group of unrelated host-plant families, including Malvaceae, Convolvulaceae, Portulacaceae, Cactaceae, Onagraceae, Zygophyllaceae, and Asteraceae. Emphorines are both behaviorally and anatomically highly specialized upon their preferred host-plants. To get a good representation of the extant Emphorini diversity and floral associations, we partnered with several international institutions, by visiting entomological collections in Mexico, Argentina, and Brazil. By utilizing high-throughput DNA sequencing techniques (ultra-conserved elements, or UCEs), we reconstructed the most comprehensive phylogeny of the group to date, including 86 species (89% of described species). By mapping geographic range and host-plant use onto the phylogeny, we were able to reconstruct the historical changes that occurred in geographic range and host use since the origin of the group approximately 35 million years ago. Our biogeographic analysis shows that the group originated in South America, specifically in a region encompassing the Southern Andes and the Southern Cone. Four subsequent dispersal events led to the spread of the tribe into North America. Based on our analysis of host-plant use, the ancestor of the group was a specialist on the family Malvaceae (mallows) with subsequent shifts to other families, most notably Cactaceae (cactuses) and Convolvulaceae (morning-glories).

Over the course of our work, we mentored Cornell undergraduate students, who learned molecular biology, taxonomy, and phylogenetic methods. Our international partnerships also allowed us to conduct fieldwork in Mexico, which contributed to the growth of the Cornell Insect Collection. In addition, we interacted with the general public, including backyard naturalists, birders, and master gardeners, through public presentations on bee biology. We published numerous peer-reviewed scientific papers and helped train the next generation of bee biologists. Our work will have broad impacts across the fields of bee-plant interactions, pollination biology, historical biogeography, and biodiversity.  Our study adds to the growing literature on the evolution of bee-plant interactions and paves the way for a more general understanding of the history of bee-plant interactions.

award.abstractText:
How do we segregate the distinct objects in a complex visual scene? Since most real-world objects are opaque, and therefore partly occlude one another, the eye receives a patchwork of overlapping surfaces, and the brain is then left with the task of determining how to perceptually group these various surface patches into unified objects. Although we do this effortlessly every day, we still do not understand the underlying neural computations that accomplish this scene analysis. Perceptual grouping cues (e.g., two surface fragments moving together or possessing the same texture) provide important clues that can be used to organize the visual scene into complete objects, but the specific computations performed, and the brain regions involved, are largely unknown. This project employs brain imaging to quantify the relative strength (and “pecking order”) of the many possible perceptual grouping cues used in constructing perceived objects from their component structures. This has been achieved by the development of a novel method for visual stimulation and analysis using noise-based image classification (i.e., reverse correlation) during functional brain imaging. This method has been used extensively in behavioral laboratory testing, but until recently, has not been practical for application to brain imaging because it typically requires a very large number of trials. However, by optimizing this technique to achieve reverse correlation during brain imaging, it is possible to uncover the brain regions driving the perception of objects in our environment. A more complete understanding of the brain mechanisms underlying perceptual grouping will lead to optimized designs for visual displays in our environment including street signs, occupational safety warnings, medical equipment instructions, and virtually all dynamic displays of visual information, as well as better artificial intelligence and robotic visual scene analysis, crucial for new technologies such as driverless cars.
 
Neuroscientific studies of object perception have previously focused primarily on the specificity of object representations in the brain. In contrast, the new approach in this research is to study the psychological and neural underpinnings of the formation of these object percepts. A key innovation is the development of a novel quantitative metric to reliably and quantitatively measure perceptual grouping that is flexible enough to be used both behaviorally and during functional magnetic resonance brain imaging (fMRI). Using this approach, it is possible to determine the critical grouping cues for object perception and detail their dominance relations in careful behavioral testing, and then to adapt the reverse correlation method to be used with brain imaging data and optimize the algorithm to reduce the number of trials (and total brain scan time) required. Finally, this new technique, comparing internal templates of neural structures to behavioral templates, can be utilized to specify the network computations driving brain-behavior relations during perceptual grouping. The results of this research will advance our understanding of visual cognition, and resolve where in the brain, and specifically at which level of the visual processing cortical hierarchy, the visual grouping cues are operating. This research will reveal computational algorithms used by the human brain for perceptual grouping and scene segregation that can also be utilized to enhance artificial intelligence (AI) visual scene analysis.

Project Outcomes Summary

Overview

Our brains constantly organize the visual world into meaningful objects, grouping together features like edges, colors, and textures to recognize everything from street signs to human faces. This project developed and optimized a powerful brain imaging technique to reveal how different brain regions perform these grouping computations. Understanding these mechanisms has important applications ranging from improving visual displays and safety warnings to advancing artificial intelligence systems like those used in self-driving cars.

Major Findings and Intellectual Merit

The project achieved a significant breakthrough in brain imaging methodology through an unexpected discovery. We initially hypothesized that sophisticated mathematical algorithms would be the key to making reverse correlation practical for brain imaging studies. However, our research revealed something different: carefully designing the visual noise patterns used in experiments was far more effective at reducing the number of trials needed.

Reverse correlation is a technique that reveals which visual features the brain uses to make perceptual decisions. Traditionally, this method required 5,000-10,000 experimental trials to produce interpretable results—far too many for practical brain imaging studies. Through systematic testing, we discovered that customizing noise patterns to match the spatial frequency characteristics of the objects being studied reduced the required trials to fewer than 1,000, and in some cases as few as 500 trials. This ten-fold improvement makes the technique practical for routine use with fMRI brain imaging.

We tested this optimized method by studying how people group visual objects using different cues: luminance (brightness differences), common region (boundary enclosures), and texture. Our brain imaging experiments revealed that these grouping cues operate through distinct neural computations. Luminance grouping highlighted entire objects in participants' mental representations, while common region grouping preferentially emphasized occluded (hidden) portions of objects. These findings demonstrate that different brain regions use different computational strategies to construct our perception of objects.

An important lesson emerged from pandemic-related constraints. When unable to test human participants early in the project, we pivoted to computer simulations. This pivot led directly to our key discovery about noise optimization—a finding we likely would have missed with our original experimental approach. This serendipitous result has inspired a new NSF grant proposal focused entirely on further optimizing noise parameters for brain imaging applications.

Broader Impacts

Training and Workforce Development: The project directly supported one postdoctoral researcher and one PhD student, both of whom attended four consecutive Vision Science Society conferences and received intensive mentoring through biweekly meetings and Career Development Plans. Two undergraduate students also gained research experience, receiving mentorship from the project team. The PI incorporated project findings into seven different graduate and undergraduate courses, exposing approximately 150 students to cutting-edge vision neuroscience methods.

Public Engagement: We maintained an active community outreach program throughout the project period, presenting to diverse audiences including the MCW Neuroscience Research Center Governing Board and the Greater Milwaukee Parkinson's Disease Support Group. Our team developed and hosted multiple exhibits at the MCW Brain Expo in 2023 and 2024, including new displays on perception, executive function, and hands-on neuroscience demonstrations with the Backyard Brains SpikerBox, directly engaging hundreds of community members in accessible neuroscience education.

Technology Transfer and Innovation: The project's success in demonstrating the feasibility of optimized fMRI reverse correlation has opened pathways for clinical translation. We have initiated discussions with Prism Clinical Imaging, a local neuroimaging software company, to explore implementation of these new methods in clinical diagnostic applications. This collaboration holds promise for jointly developed intellectual property that could translate basic neuroscience discoveries into practical medical tools.

Societal Applications: The optimized reverse correlation technique provides a foundation for understanding how the brain constructs object representations, knowledge that can improve the design of visual displays throughout society—from street signs and occupational safety warnings to medical equipment interfaces. These insights also advance artificial intelligence and robotic vision systems, which are crucial for emerging technologies including autonomous vehicles that must reliably perceive and interpret complex visual environments.

Conclusion

This project successfully developed and optimized fMRI reverse correlation as a practical neuroscience tool while uncovering fundamental differences in how the brain processes different types of visual grouping information. The unexpected discovery that stimulus noise optimization outperforms computational optimization for reducing trial numbers represents a paradigm shift that will enable future researchers to apply this powerful technique more broadly across vision science and cognitive neuroscience.

award.abstractText:
This proposal provides support for students, mentors, speakers, and postdoctoral attendees for professional development activities in conjunction with the IEEE International Conference on Digital Health (ICDH). ICDH and its associated activities will take place virtually, between September 5 and 10, 2021. The funds will be used to fund about 40 students’ registration fees, research competition prizes, and small stipends for faculty mentors, distinguished speakers, and postdoctoral scholars, with the goal of providing high-quality mentoring experiences and broadening participation in the conference to include more members of groups historically underrepresented in STEM fields. Doing this will serve both societal goals around broadening participation, enrich the intellectual diversity of the conference, improve dissemination of the latest results around digital health to a wider population, and further the training of the next generation of researchers interested in digital health. 

The mentoring will be structured around two main activities. The first is a research project-based competition targeting biomedical engineering and healthcare projects in the domains of diabetes, blood pressure management, cancer management, and independent living for older adults. Graduate students (and postdocs, on a case-by-case basis) will apply to conduct projects of their choice in the competition as either individuals or small teams, with the competition advertised widely including to minority-serving institutions. Accepted project proposals will be chosen by a panel of judges; these proposers will participate in a one day research workshop and presentation competition where they will receive feedback and mentoring from the panel of judges. Participating students will also have half-day virtual mentoring sessions guided by distinguished faculty speakers with expertise in the focal areas of the competition, in which students and mentors will collaboratively explore research challenges in the areas above. The funding will also support participation from experts that will broaden the ICDH in two conference-wide panels on the topics of AI-supported cancer and cardiology treatment.

The IEEE International Conference on Digital Health (ICDH, (https://conferences.computer.org/icdh/)) is a premier international forum for researchers and industry practitioners to exchange the latest fundamental advances in the state of the art and practice of digital health technologies, emerging research topics, and the future of digital health. It was held during September 5-10, 2021 virtually, and During July 11-15, 2022, as Hybrid in Barcelona, Spain. Both of the ICDH events brought together leading researchers, community leaders and visionaries from academia and industry, end-users, and healthcare professionals, in the area of digital health to share their research, practical experience, and visions of the future of sustainable health and social care transformations.

 

This NSF award has positively impacted over 20 student researchers from 16 USA-based Universities who attended the conference and pursuing various research topics in the domain of digital health. With the support from NSF, the student research competition programs provided the platform to the selected participant gaining first-hand experience of demonstrating early research work to experts and receive mentoring. The program further provided interaction opportunities via digital health related panels, speaker series for the participants. The list of participants included minority and underrepresented students from US-based institutes pursuing programs from computer science, medical science, social science, and electrical and computer engineering.   

The organized programs covered broader area of digital health. Participating students presented research work covering areas such as health equity partnership, explainable healthcare framework, wheelchair navigation for patient, ethical digital health communication for vaccination hesitancy, improving Improved Cardiac Arrhythmia Classification, privacy preserving data sharing of healthcare organizations, Family-based Digital Lifestyle Intervention for Hispanic Adolescents, mhealth tool development of children with autism spectrum disorder, non-invasive blood glucose monitoring, security aware robust healthcare system, overcrowding management of emergency department. The program motivated students to pursue career and further research and education opportunities related to digital health area.

award.abstractText:
Visual recognition is a remarkable task performed by the human brain. Computational methods trained to emulate this capability rely on observing millions of examples of visual input paired with human annotations. These computational methods have made great progress and are being increasingly adopted in many user-facing applications such as image search, automated image tagging, semi-autonomous navigation systems, smart virtual assistants, etc. However, the underlying visual recognition models in these systems often produce errors by associating sensitive variables of societal significance with their predictions. The goal of this project is to measure and mitigate such errors in a systematic fashion. For example, if a method is able to recognize images of scenes such as 'classroom', the goal of this project is to ensure that such predictions are obtained based on cues such as the presence of a whiteboard, chairs, desks, and other elements typically needed for a space to function as a classroom and not based on incidental elements such as the characteristics or attributes of people present in the classroom. To this end, this project aims to make it easier to determine to what extent methods for computational visual recognition rely on spurious associations with incidental elements.

This project will provide a study of societal biases present in current methods and models for computational visual recognition that are widely used as a source of generic visual representations. The developed methods will be based on solid foundations drawn from both the machine learning, computer vision, and software testing communities. The project introduces association tests to probe models trained under a variety of conditions to systematically disentangle the biases introduced during generic visual representation learning. The project will be 1) developing a general assessment methodology to measure various types of biases in generic visual representation learning, 2) proposing methods to diminish the impact of these biases in existing generic visual representation extraction models, and 3) measuring the impact of these biases on some key downstream tasks. These three research aims will be complemented by a comprehensive evaluation plan and broadening participation activities. This research effort will bring novel insights into the sources of biases in the predictions of computer vision models and methodologies to make informed decisions about the risks in the deployment of such models.

award.projectOutComesReport:
Computer vision systems that are trained to automatically recognize people, objects and actions from images are increasingly powerful. These systems are built on top of powerful deep neural network models that make predictions based on internal representation states that are trained on millions of images. These internal representations of the visual input can be used for many tasks such as classification, detection, and answering questions conditioned on input images. Our work was set to investigate how to best uncover biases in these representations that might propagate to applications and systems used by people. We summarize the significant outcomes of this project as follows:

 

[1] In order to understand the extent to what computer vision models encode biases in their internal representations, we proposed a methodology and associated benchmark based on image association tests. Particularly, we aimed to test computer vision models in their ability to associate groups of images belonging to a particular category to images belonging to another group and uncover to what these associations are maintained during model development -- pre-training -- and during model deployment -- post-training or finetuning.  Our benchmarks have been made publicly available and show a nuanced set of results across model sizes and model types for various publicly available visual recognition models.

 

[2] In recent years, computer vision models have become one with Large Language Models (LLMs) that are trained to generate arbitrary text on a multitude of domains. In general, Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are capable of associating images with arbitrary information encoded as text. Our project has also produced a benchmark that measures statistical biases in VLMs at large scale. We have released a tool and associated dataset that extends our work on generic visual representation measuring toward models that can associate images with text. We found that as models become more powerful, their reliance on spurious associations tends to become less of an issue. However, there is a more nuanced analysis to be made as various types of models do not exhibit a straightforward association between model capacity and reliance on spurious associations. Our work enables this type of analysis for current and upcoming VLMs.

 

[3] Our technical work also produced a series of methods to alleviate the disparities in performance exhibited by current visual recognition models in data rich vs data scarce domains. In particular, we have shown the extent to which synthetic data can be used as a source of knowledge for alleviating issues in the data scarce domain. We particularly proposed F-SWAP or feature swapping, a strategy that consists in swapping visual features in real images with the visual features obtained from synthetic images generated using computer graphics through a 3D rendering engine. We show the effectiveness of this technique on extending the capabilities of a model in answering questions about images without significantly compromising their performance on their current capabilities. Furthermore, our work has shown that synthetic data can extend the capabilities of multimodal models in tasks that involve attributes and object-object relationships.

 

[4] We have explored complementary domains to the visual recognition domain where models based on deep neural network models might exhibit problematic behavior. We particularly proposed PropTest, a technique to mitigate the errors of methods used to answer questions about images that first generate a computer program to answer the question. We show that PropTest can improve a baseline method by 6% on the GQA question answering benchmark and 8.1% on the RefCOCO+ referring expression comprehension benchmark. We also extended our work to Code LLMs by developing dynamic evaluation frameworks that test models in more realistic settings. To assess generalization, we introduced a novel methodology that transforms standard coding tasks into domain-shifted variants, for example, converting a sorting task into sorting words from a blog post. Our results show that even state-of-the-art Code LLMs suffer significant accuracy drops under such transformations. We also created a benchmark to evaluate LLMs' ability to diagnose and fix system-level crashes, testing their reasoning and debugging capabilities in practical scenarios.

 

[5] We have developed rigorous testing methodologies to evaluate the safety and reliability of self-driving cars. Using the CARLA simulator, we created diverse corner case scenarios, rare but high-risk situations often missed in training data, such as a pedestrian suddenly crossing while the car is turning or a bicyclist emerging from a blind spot. These controlled simulations allow us to probe the limits of the driving stack and identify failure modes in perception and decision-making, enabling targeted improvements of autonomous vehicles before deployment.

 

 

Our work demonstrated methodologies to uncover implicit biases encoded in intermediate representations learned for large complex systems relying on deep neural networks, as well as methodologies for alleviating these issues.

Deep learning has shown great promise in solving many open challenges in wireless networking research and applications. Deep learning is data hungry, and one of the critical obstacles towards fulfilling its promise is facilitating the acquisition of sufficient amounts of data to train and validate deep learning models. The primary goal of this project is to devise innovative approaches that enable wireless researchers and practitioners to acquire data more efficiently at reduced cost and to utilize existing data more effectively. Findings from this project are expected to fuel future breakthroughs in wireless research by making deep learning models more widely applicable. By integrating research and education, the proposed work will provide excellent hands-on exercises, research, and educational opportunities for undergraduate and graduate students at the three collaborating universities. The project will leverage the existing diversity-related outreach programs at the three institutions to broaden participation from under-represented groups. 

A team of four investigators with complementary expertise from Auburn University, Temple University, and California State University, Sacramento will carry out a coherent research agenda consisting of the following four thrusts: (1) Spectrum data synthesis and augmentation aided by generative adversarial networks; (2) Exploiting historical and synthetic wireless networking data through novel transfer learning algorithms; (3) Characterizing the relationship between dataset size and performance; (4) Integrate, validate and apply approaches developed in the first three thrusts on spectrum database construction, RF spectrum anomaly detection, and transmitter classification. Thrusts 1-3 are application-agnostic and focused on studying fundamental concepts and techniques that facilitate the acquisition of sufficient amounts of wireless data, enable more effective utilization of existing data, and enable the prediction of how much data is needed to meet desired performance. Thrust 4 is application-specific and focused on specific wireless applications where deep learning has been applied and demonstrated great potential. The data, software and education materials developed from this project will be widely disseminated. The project will engage industry stakeholders on project-related issues, with the aim to disseminate ideas and learn relevant challenges faced by the industry when applying deep learning to wireless applications.

award.abstractText:
Throughout the course of the twentieth century, distances have played a significant role in important areas of statistics, which include classification, clustering, discriminant analysis, multidimensional scaling, sampling, spatial statistics, scoring rules, and kernel methods in machine learning. Distances are also central to the definition of divergence measures, relative entropy and information gain, some of which are fundamental to the concept of C.R. Rao's quadratic entropy and the analysis of diversity in ecology and other areas of science. Yet, at present there are significant gaps in our knowledge and in the emerging statistical literature on the use of distance-based tests and analyses for complex high dimensional data.  One example is analysis of similarity which is among the most cited and most widely used distance-based statistical methods but is limited by an absence of relevant mathematical knowledge. This research will derive new mathematical knowledge on various distance-based statistical methods, and apply this for providing answers to important scientific questions arising in a number of disciplines in forestry, ecology and marine science, such as: (1) how biodiversity changes in tropical forests? (2) how taxonomic and functional profiles of bacterial communities change with environmental conditions in different oceanic regions? The project establishes collaborations among several disciplines and between two US academic institutions and provides research and training to graduate and undergraduate students.
 
The project develops a new body of knowledge on distance-based statistical methods and computation for analyzing complex, high dimensional data that arise in the form of compositions, trees, graphs, or networks. The distances considered here are all non-Euclidean -- either non-metric dissimilarities that do not satisfy any triangular inequalities or just discrete numbers -- but they all arise from conditionally positive definite kernels. Examples of distances include the squared Euclidean distance, the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, the Jensen-Shannon distance, Unifrac or the Kantorovich-Rubinstein metric, the Aitchison distance, the edit distance, various graph kernel and spectral distances, and other distances based on optimal transport problems. Specifically, the project advances the mathematical theory and computation of exact distribution-free two and multi-sample runs tests, change points, and other related problems by counting runs along the shortest Hamiltonian path (or loop) of the pooled sample of data points. The project also considers analysis of similarity and related distance-based rank tests and derives new mathematical results that allow us to pursue more advanced statistical analyses. The project contributes to: (i) a deeper analysis of biodiversity in tropical forest; (ii)  an investigation of  how taxonomic and functional profiles of prokaryotic communities  change  with environmental conditions in different oceanic regions; (iii) a study of the variability of composition of rare earth elements in deep-sea muds of the Pacific Ocean;  and (iv) an understanding of the relationship of intertidal communities in the Oregon coast with respect to upwelling and nutrient delivery. The project integrates mathematics research, science and education and will provide opportunities for dissertation work for graduate students.

award.projectOutComesReport:
The research conducted under this award has advanced distance-based statistical methods and their applications across diverse fields: (1) distance-based run tests – deriving exact, distribution-free tests along shortest Hamiltonian paths for high-dimensional data and establishing asymptotic results under conditionally positive definite kernels; (2) asymptotic theory of ANOSIM – developing its theoretical foundations; (3) anomaly detection – advancing distance-based approaches for scalable machine-learning algorithms such as isolation forests; (4) applications to historical texts – analyzing 16th- and 17th-century English sermons; (5) uniformity testing – deriving optimal procedures for sparse high-dimensional multinomial distributions via extensions of Tukey’s Higher Criticism test; (6) two-sample testing for random graphs – identifying optimal sample complexity for inhomogeneous random graph models in the r-norm; (7) sports analytics – developing spatial hierarchical multidimensional item response theory models for ten seasons of English Premier League data; and (8) criminal justice applications – quantifying dispatch delays and spatial neighborhood effects in New Orleans police response times using a two-component mixture of accelerated failure time models and logistic regression. Collectively, these contributions provide a robust statistical foundation for analyzing complex high-dimensional data without requiring explicit probability model specifications.

The project also provided a range of educational, research, and training opportunities to undergraduate, Master’s, and Ph.D. students at Washington University in St. Louis and the University of Pennsylvania.

The project has resulted in the publication of articles, and the PIs, along with graduate and undergraduate students, have developed and implemented various distance-based algorithms on diverse complex and high-dimensional data sets.

The PIs are also disseminating results through invited talks at major national and international conferences, as well as by organizing seminars, sessions, and conferences. In particular, the PIs have presented several invited talks at major meetings, including the Joint Statistical Meetings and the Banff International Research Station workshop.

The purpose of the proposed effort is to aid future leadership development professionals (LDP) in their work to train a diverse pipeline of leaders. The future of work involves a virtual context for many occupations. Hence, two new challenges for LDP workers are to train leaders to perform effectively in a virtual context and to leverage future technology in their training of leaders. We address these challenges by proposing to create a leadership training platform to be used by LDP workers to train the next generation of diverse leaders to adapt to an online setting. The proposed platform leverages Artificial Intelligence (AI) models to provide real-time feedback to leaders. An interactive dashboard including visualization and storytelling will be developed as the front-end to provide information on leaders’ performance to improve their leadership signals. The proposed work will have practical implications for numerous stakeholders. First, LDP will be able to effectively train current and emerging leaders to work in the virtual setting. Second, future leaders and their followers will benefit from the improved training. Third, the approach aims to substantially reduce discrimination in leadership evaluations by creating objective and diverse training data.

The current scope of work within the award is focused on creating partnerships and further developing the proposed work. The award will support on-site and virtual meetings and observations of end users of the proposed AI platform (i.e., LDPs). A leadership and data science workshop will be held to share and develop ideas. LDPs will participate for training and networking purposes and to provide feedback. A consultant will be engaged to develop the project plan. Graduate students will assist in additional analytic model building and the creation of study materials for the project and subsequent data collections (e.g., developing the experimental protocol; creating recruitment and training materials).

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

In this period, we focused on creating multimodal models for classification and prediction tasks. A key necessity of these models is to be accurate as well as robust to errors. 

 

 

 

 

 

We benchmarked the accuracy of a late fusion-based multimodal model on a social media-based content classification dataset.

The datasets used are:

1) Multimodal crisis humanitarian dataset, which comprises 7, 216 Twitter posts (images + text) that are categorized into 5 humanitarian categories. The dataset covers 7 crises that occurred in 2017 all over the globe (3 hurricanes, 2 earthquakes, 1 wildfre and foods). We formulate the task of humanitarian information detection as a multi-class classifcation problem. 

2) Multimodal emotion dataset: we collect the dataset introduced by Duong, Lebret, and Aberer ( 2017) for the task of multimodal emotion detection. The dataset comprises Reddit posts categorized into 4 emotion-related classes, creepy, gore, happy, and rage, where each post contains an image and text. We crawled the images from Reddit using the URLs provided by the authors.

 

We compared DisilBERT and mBERT for unimodal models and created late fusion-based multimodal models. 


Experiments showed that using multimodality increased the F1 classification score by 0.01 to 0.06 points on the two datasets, resulting in F1 scores between 0.75 and 0.85. This shows the usefulness of the multimodal models and their universality. 

 

 

 

 

The findings from our experiments highlight the applicability and generalizability of multimodal models, which can be used to build multimodal models for leadership assessment, development, and training.

award.abstractText:
Time series data are ubiquitous in modern science and engineering. An unprecedented amount is being collected in diverse applications such as healthcare systems, the Web, cyber network monitoring, self-driving cars, and Internet-of-Things services. While deep learning has achieved enormous success in time series predictive analysis, a key bottleneck of such models is that they are ignorant about the uncertainties in their predictions. A consequence is that they can produce wildly wrong predictions without noticing---this will lead to misguided decisions, which can be catastrophic in life-critical applications. This project aims to remedy this issue and advance deep learning towards more trustworthy time series analysis. The project will enable principled deep learning models for uncertainty-aware and reliable time series regression and classification without sacrificing their predictive power. Research findings from the project will be incorporated into graduate-level classes, tutorials, and workshops to bring multiple stakeholders and domain scientists together.

The technical aims of this project are divided into three thrusts. First, the project will develop novel techniques bridging deep sequential models (e.g., recurrent networks, transformers) with Gaussian processes to quantify uncertainty in the functional space. Second, the project will explore how to learn calibrated deep sequential models and how to further decouple different sources of uncertainties to understand where a model's predictive uncertainty comes from. Third, the project will harness uncertainty to improve the reliability and efficiency of time series predictive systems. These techniques will enjoy the representation power of deep neural networks for modeling complex temporal dependencies in time-series data, while providing principled methodologies for quantifying and leveraging uncertainty for robustness and performance. The developed new models, algorithms, and techniques will be deployed in two important applications for times series analysis: 1) public health monitoring and forecasting, and 2) real-time analysis for mobile sensing time series data. The developed tools will also be open-sourced for trustworthy time series analysis that can benefit many other applications.

award.abstractText:
This Early-concept Grants for Exploratory Research (EAGER) project focuses on exploring and developing a novel operational collection of speech, language and perception-based measures to objectively assess speech intelligibility for second language (L2) speech production, as well as providing effective learner-specific feedback. With the rise of English as an international language, intelligibility-based successful communication has been emphasized over native-like accents. However, L2 teachers often raise concerns about learners’ slow or stagnant pronunciation progress. Several primary reasons for this problem may include difficulties in perceptually discerning changes in learners’ speech and interpreting learners’ speech patterns without any learner-specific intelligibility assessment profile. Today, teachers have no systematic way to assess each student’s speech changes, nor can students monitor and track feedback related to their pronunciation learning progression. Therefore, an exploratory and transformative method is introduced for measuring speech intelligibility that provides both teachers and learners with objective and individualized feedback. This  exploratory project is proposed for EAGER funding  in order to establish a baseline working framework for operational objective measure creation, and proof-of-concept assessment feedback for teachers and learners. This approach will help teachers gauge learners’ intelligibility levels and allow learners to self-regulate their learning progress incrementally over time. The long-term innovation is expected to benefit skilled US professionals from non-English speaking countries, who work in various STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) fields. Additionally, this interdisciplinary project provides various opportunities for hands-on training and experience for both graduate and undergraduate students in the fields of language education, applied linguistics, computer engineering, and speech technology.

This project explores an idea to assess intelligibility in speech communications based on multiple individual speech measures for non-native speakers. The ideas are currently in their very early stages of development, and a large portion of the research ideas are untested. In order to establish the ground truth of potential individual speech production intelligibility measures, the implementation and feasibility of this intelligibility feedback approach must be validated with evidence. By employing advanced Automatic Speech Recognition-based accent classification technology based on machine learning, the team of researchers plan to provide learners with measured speech property information through operational and a discriminating set of objective speech intelligibility measures. The current innovation builds on language skill acquisition theory with a functional analytic-linguistic approach, arguing that explicit and metalinguistic feedback plays a pivotal role in moving learners forward in their L2 development. The vision is enabled by on-going research on auditory-based neurogram and spectrogram orthogonal polynomial measures that predict speech intelligibility, employing the learners’ unconstrained speech utterances. The project will contribute to the scientific knowledge of what constitutes L2 intelligible speech, understanding how individualized objective speech intelligibility feedback affects L2 speech development, and creating a foundational collection of speech/auditory/signal processing measures as well as ASR/DNN driven measures that assess a speaker’s intelligibility and identify efficient ways of implementing this technology in L2 learning contexts.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This EAGER project represents a probe study to address the formulation of Objective Speech Intelligibility Measures (OSIM) for second language (L2) learners of English. This collaborative project involves three institutions: Northern Arizona Univ. (NAU-lead), Univ. of Texas-Dallas (UTD), and Penn State Univ. (PSU). The collaborating teams’ (NAU, UTD, PSU) efforts were divided into three interdisciplinary foci: (1) intelligibility ratings and speech properties (linguistics, NAU; speech processing, UTD), (2) intelligibility-based instruction and feedback (learning science, PSU; feedback development, NAU), and (3) OSIM development (computer engineering, UTD) and validation (NAU). This exploratory and transformative project investigated the use of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) to provide L2 learners with objective speech measures of their English intelligibility, including combining acoustic and perception measures to further understand what constitutes intelligibility, the development of automated measurement systems, and the implementation of such efforts in the tertiary language learning classroom. The project aimed to establish a baseline framework for operational objective measure creation, and proof-of-concept feedback for teachers and learners. It brought accent classification technology, repurposed for intelligibility measurement, into L2 pronunciation instruction in the form of a diagnostic and assessment framework. Traditionally, most efforts in speech detection measure native/non-native differences in speakers, striving to move accented speakers towards native-like speech production. However, the current study took a strategically alternate view by creating an inventory of measures that incorporated both native and non-native/highly intelligible accented speech production, followed by multi-dimensional weighting using Machine Learning (ML) to produce overall combined intelligibility scores. With this novel pedagogical framework, the project started with Chinese international teaching assistants (ITAs) in STEM fields in the US and expanded to other L2 speakers.

 

The focus of NAU-lead was on examining the effectiveness of OSIM feedback on L2 learners’ intelligibility as well as the relationships between raters’ intelligibility measures and acoustic properties. Initially, 30 highly intelligible speakers were identified as 95% intelligible by 15 expert listeners with various transcription tasks. Their speech, characterized as highly intelligible but still accented, was used as baseline norms for OSIM development. Then, eleven L1 Chinese ITAs received human-listener based intelligibility feedback for two-sequential interventions, from which initial findings showed the promising patterns of learner-specific intelligibility feedback. The project advanced with 108 L2 speakers who received various combinations of OSIM feedback derived from 15 trained/expert human listeners and preliminary automated intelligibility scores. A total of 405 naturalistic audio files of spontaneous speech were elicited. They were then analyzed for acoustic properties via Praat and acoustic script analysis, including lexical stress, prominence, pause, rhythm, and articulation rate. [These datasets, called the ‘L2USI’ (Second Language University Students Intelligibility’ corpus), are now publicly available through the Linguistic Data Consortium.] Major findings related to intelligibility-acoustic correlates indicate that the relationship between articulation rate and perceptual ratings of intelligibility is not linear, showing the optimal average syllables per second for intelligibility between 2.75 to 4.00. High lexical stress accuracy was associated with highly intelligible speech but severe deleterious effects were detected below 70% accuracy (See Figure 1). These findings provide scientific evidence to revamp the traditional concept of linearity in speech characteristics, which can inform the fields of linguistics, speech science, and speech engineering.  

 

As for the effects of OSIM feedback, the project involved several stages of pilot and short-term (trial) intervention approaches. In one study, 64 experimental-group L2 learners and their teachers received the OSIM feedback while 30 control-group learners did not. The OSIM group showed a statistically significant improvement (p<.001) with a large effect size on lexical stress, pause, and articulation rate (See Figure 2). The surveys of learner perceptions and interviews with eight instructors confirmed that OSIM helped not only to improve intelligibility, but also to increase motivation. Follow-up studies derived from these results included the effects of Data Driven Learning (62 L2 learners) and AI-based feedback (90 learners) on L2 intelligibility. Their findings suggested that while OSIM should be a promising approach, both learners and teachers need specific guidance/training in understanding technology-based feedback with multi-dimensional data. In addition, they verified that leveraging speech recognition model development is complex but advantageous, especially for both individual use and classroom applications, and evidence-based state-of-the-art intelligibility measure(s) should go beyond traditional phonemic recognition. With the resulting L2 speech corpus with human perception data, the foundational speech/language technology systems, and preliminary results, this EAGER research has confirms the necessity of a comprehensive investigation to advance intelligibility-based objective speech measures as a diagnostic and formative assessment tool to provide both L2 learners and teachers with the necessary actionable baselines, frameworks, and approaches to improve L2 English learners’ speech intelligibility and support their communication for personal, educational, business, and societal engagement. Overall, the project outcomes include 16 journal articles and conferene preceedings, 34 conference and invited presentations, 3 workshops, 2 audio/video product through the Linguistic Data Consortium, 1 book chapter, 1 PhD dissertation, and 1 book proposal.

award.abstractText:
Space robotics is essential for all current and future space exploration and utilization missions. Advanced space-robotic technologies will enable in-orbit servicing and refueling of satellites, and will support more elaborate missions such as in-orbit large flexible structure assembly, debris removal, inspection, hardware upgrades, etc. For instance, current communication satellites have a typical lifetime of 10 to 15 years, at which point an otherwise perfectly functioning satellite runs out of propellant and is decommissioned. Refueling the satellite can add several years of additional lifetime and revenue. Future envisioned missions to the Moon, Mars and beyond will also require advanced robotic capabilities in orbit. Many future exploration missions envision integrated teams of astronauts and free flying “co-robots” that support or monitor the human crew activities. What is currently missing from these missions is the ability to provide full 4D (space-time) situational awareness using autonomous on-board perception and planning capabilities. Recent technological breakthroughs for ground robots pave the way for similar advancements in robotic in-orbit operations to enable routine robotic operations in space in the not-so-distant future. These include perception and planning algorithms, machine learning based pattern recognition, autonomy, new computer hardware architectures, human-machine interfaces, and dexterous manipulation, among many others. The outcome of the research will be the ability of astronauts and space robots to work together to enable inspection, monitoring, and classification of resident space objects; maneuvering and proximity operations and docking; salvage and retrieval of malfunctioning or tumbling spacecraft; and servicing, construction, repair, upgrade, and refueling missions of assets in orbit.

This project will develop novel visual perception, localization, mapping, and planning algorithms that will enable new capabilities in terms of situational awareness for space robots that can work alone or alongside astronauts in orbit. The research plan includes the development of novel automated feature extraction and matching algorithms using deep neural network architectures, adapted to the challenging imaging conditions (collimated light, high contrast, lack of atmospheric scattering, paucity of distinctive features, etc.) and orbital motion constraints imposed in space. This will enable robust and reliable relative pose estimation, 3D shape reconstruction and characterization of space objects.  Novel optimal planning and prediction methods based on a factor-graph optimization framework will be matched to these new perception capabilities to account for fuel usage and orbital motion constraints.  The experimental validation of the theory will take place at the Georgia Tech Autonomous Spacecraft Testing of Robotic Operations in Space platform, a state-of-the-art spacecraft simulation platform. The research will involve both graduate and undergraduate students. The results of this research will be disseminated to the community by journal and conference publications, organization of invited workshops and seminar presentations, and by targeted exposure (press releases, interviews) to popular media.

This project is supported by the cross-directorate Foundational Research in Robotics program, jointly managed and funded by the Directorates for Engineering (ENG) and Computer and Information Science and Engineering (CISE).

award.abstractText:
Time series data are ubiquitous in modern science and engineering. An unprecedented amount is being collected in diverse applications such as healthcare systems, the Web, cyber network monitoring, self-driving cars, and Internet-of-Things services. While deep learning has achieved enormous success in time series predictive analysis, a key bottleneck of such models is that they are ignorant about the uncertainties in their predictions. A consequence is that they can produce wildly wrong predictions without noticing---this will lead to misguided decisions, which can be catastrophic in life-critical applications. This project aims to remedy this issue and advance deep learning towards more trustworthy time series analysis. The project will enable principled deep learning models for uncertainty-aware and reliable time series regression and classification without sacrificing their predictive power. Research findings from the project will be incorporated into graduate-level classes, tutorials, and workshops to bring multiple stakeholders and domain scientists together.

The technical aims of this project are divided into three thrusts. First, the project will develop novel techniques bridging deep sequential models (e.g., recurrent networks, transformers) with Gaussian processes to quantify uncertainty in the functional space. Second, the project will explore how to learn calibrated deep sequential models and how to further decouple different sources of uncertainties to understand where a model's predictive uncertainty comes from. Third, the project will harness uncertainty to improve the reliability and efficiency of time series predictive systems. These techniques will enjoy the representation power of deep neural networks for modeling complex temporal dependencies in time-series data, while providing principled methodologies for quantifying and leveraging uncertainty for robustness and performance. The developed new models, algorithms, and techniques will be deployed in two important applications for times series analysis: 1) public health monitoring and forecasting, and 2) real-time analysis for mobile sensing time series data. The developed tools will also be open-sourced for trustworthy time series analysis that can benefit many other applications.

award.abstractText:
This award to Rutgers University-Newark supports the acquisition and deployment of a High-Performance Computing (HPC) cluster (named PRICE) dedicated to research, teaching and societal outreach efforts. PRICE will have 60 general compute (CPU) nodes and one graphical processing unit (GPU) node as well as storage appropriate for the planned usage over the lifetime of the machine. The enabled research develops along three main directions: atomistic modeling, neuroscience, and data science. Some atomistic models enabled by PRICE will study the structure and dynamics of proteins to address questions related to diseases such as Alzheimer’s. New materials modeling and design is enabled both by PRICE and by the development of new quantum simulation methods. The enabled simulations will also regard new materials design by way of genetic algorithms. The enabled neuroscience research regards computational analysis of experimental data to understand brain function, connectivity, and human behavior. Enabled data science research includes the formulation of novel cooperative artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms that will improve the outcome of machine learning (ML) models of broad applicability. In addition to enabling new science, the project realizes several societal broader impacts including broadening HPC literacy of underrepresented minorities and training the future NJ workforce using HPC in the classroom and development of new undergraduate and graduate curricula.

PRICE will comprise 60 compute nodes (52 cores/node), 700 TB of redundant storage and one GPU node (4 GPUs/node) to be housed at Rutgers University-Newark. PRICE will enable several additional research projects carried out by the PI, co-PIs, and major users at Rutgers-Newark and NJIT. The GPU portion enables state-of-the-art molecular dynamics simulations that elucidate structure and dynamics of proteins for the understanding of diseases, such as Alzheimer’s. GPUs also enable the efficient and timely execution of cooperative AI algorithms aimed at improving predictivity. The CPU nodes will enable quantum simulations aimed at materials engineering through density-functional theory calculations. These simulations facilitate the development of quantum models based on density functional theory, its subsystem formulation (which parallelizes efficiently over PRICE’s low-latency network) as well as quantum mechanical frameworks based on the exact factorization of the Schrödinger equation for multicomponent systems. CPU and GPU nodes will enable data analysis associated with neuroscience experiments aimed at uncovering how the brain modulates behavior and vision-related tasks as well as the study of neuron connectivity to understand brain function. Data from these experiments is growing exponentially due to increased instrument data flow from new fMRI units and improved technology allowing recordings of local field potentials from hundreds on neurons. The project also enables new science as well as the realization of societal broader impacts, such as broadening high-performance computing literacy of underrepresented minorities, training the future NJ workforce and recruitment of new faculty.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

award.projectOutComesReport:
This Major Research Instrumentation (MRI) grant enabled the acquisition, installation, and deployment of a high-performance computing (HPC) cluster, Price, housed at Rutgers University-Newark. The cluster significantly enhanced computational resources for research and teaching, benefiting Rutgers-Newark and close-by institutions. The project directly supported research in theoretical chemistry, atomic physics, neuroscience, artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration and training across these fields.

 

Objectives and Accomplishments

The primary goal of the project was to provide cutting-edge computational infrastructure to advance scientific research and educational initiatives. Price has been fully operational, supporting both CPU and GPU-intensive workloads. Key accomplishments include:

 

Research Enablement: The cluster has facilitated breakthroughs in electronic structure methods, AI algorithm development, and multicomponent system modeling. It has directly supported 16 peer-reviewed journal publications, with many more indirectly benefiting from its resources.

Training and Education: Weekly online workshops have been conducted to train users at varying levels, ensuring broad accessibility to Price's capabilities. The system has been integrated into undergraduate and graduate courses, notably in Computational Chemistry, which utilized the cluster for student projects in Fall 2022 and 2024.

Technology Transfer: Price has been instrumental in supporting Quantum Click, a Rutgers-based spin-off project now part of the NSF I-Corps program. This initiative highlights the broader economic and innovation impact of the MRI-funded cluster.

Community Engagement: The cluster played a crucial role in hosting the Rutgers Summer Hackathon, where 40 participants (including students from Rutgers, NJIT, and Essex County College) learned Python programming using the cluster’s OnDemand interface. This initiative broadened computational literacy among underrepresented communities in Newark and surrounding areas.

 

Impact on Scientific Research

Price has supported computationally intensive projects in:

  • Electronic Structure and Multiscale Modeling: Advancing density embedding and machine learning methods for quantum chemistry.

  • Artificial Intelligence and Explainable AI: Developing Bayesian regression and deep learning models.

  • Neuroscience and Brain Research: Modeling brain function and cognitive networks using functional MRI and EEG data.

  • Materials Science and Drug Discovery: Predicting molecular interactions and designing new materials.

  • Computational Education and Outreach: Training students and early-career researchers in high-performance computing techniques.

Cluster Utilization and Performance

Since its deployment, Price has maintained a high utilization rate, with computational activity consistently reaching 50-70% of total capacity. The system's SLURM partitions have efficiently managed access for major users and general computing needs. This level of engagement underscores the critical demand for dedicated HPC resources in academic research.

 

Broader Impact and Future Outlook

The MRI-funded Price cluster has transformed computational research and education at Rutgers-Newark and its partner institutions. It has directly trained 30-40 students per year, supported diverse, federally funded research projects, and contributed to a growing computational ecosystem in New Jersey. The grant’s impact extends beyond academia, fostering industry partnerships and equipping students with skills relevant to the modern workforce. With the MRI grant concluding, the infrastructure established will continue to support research, training, and outreach activities. Plans are in place to sustain its operation through university support and external collaborations. The success of this initiative underscores the importance of continued investment in high-performance computing to drive scientific discovery and innovation in NJ and nationwide.
